World.title: Former Kanchibiya MP Chanda Says Bill 7 Vote Cost Him His Seat
World.content:
Former Kanchibiya Member of Parliament Sunday Chanda has attributed his election loss to his vote in favour of the contested Bill 7 constitutional amendment, saying constituents turned against him over the decision and that the party subsequently withheld campaign support because he was seen to have defied local sentiment.

Chanda said the practice within his party was for the leadership to consult stakeholders before major decisions, and that outcomes were meant to reflect those consultations. He said he was not deployed to campaign in Kanchibiya during the run-up to the election, a decision he linked directly to how his Bill 7 vote had been perceived among constituents and party structures.

The former legislator’s account offers a rare first-hand illustration of how constitutional reform debates, which dominated parliamentary business well before the election, continued to shape voter behaviour and party dynamics at constituency level. Bill 7 remained a politically divisive issue throughout its passage, with supporters and opponents divided along lines that did not always track neatly with party affiliation.

Chanda’s remarks suggest that his vote was interpreted locally as a break from the wishes of Kanchibiya residents, regardless of the broader political or constitutional justification he may have had for supporting the amendment at the time. He indicated that this perception hardened opposition to his candidacy well before the formal campaign period began.

He also pointed to the absence of campaign deployment as a compounding factor, describing it as a signal that the party itself had distanced itself from his position. Without that support, Chanda suggested, an already difficult path back to the seat became considerably harder to navigate.

The episode highlights a broader dynamic playing out across several constituencies this election cycle, where MPs who supported contentious legislation faced consequences at the ballot box regardless of their standing within party structures. Chanda’s case adds a personal dimension to that pattern, illustrating how quickly parliamentary votes on divisive national issues can translate into local political costs.

Chanda has not indicated whether he intends to remain active in politics or pursue any further role within his party following the loss. His comments, however, are likely to resonate with other legislators who supported Bill 7 and who may be assessing their own standing with constituents in its aftermath.

World.title: Human rights Advocate calls for unity
World.content:
Governance expert and human rights advocate Wesley Miyanda has called on Zambians to protect the country’s long standing culture of peaceful democratic transitions, urging political leaders and their supporters to place national unity above political interests.

Mr Miyanda said Zambia has enjoyed peace since attaining independence and has conducted elections that resulted in changes of government without bloodshed or widespread political violence.

Speaking in an interview with the media, the governance expert appealed to political actors, particularly those dissatisfied with electoral outcomes, to use established democratic and legal processes to address their grievances rather than resorting to actions that could threaten the country’s peace and stability.

“Petitions are very important and they are constitutional. No one can stop them. I think that is the best thing we should do. We need to follow the process and see how the issues are resolved at the end of the day,” said Mr Miyanda.

He cited Zambia’s history of political perseverance as an example of how electoral disputes and defeats can be handled within a democratic framework.

He noted that some political leaders had lost elections several times but continued to participate in the democratic process, reorganising and returning to contest subsequent elections without mobilising supporters to cause unrest.

Mr Miyanda said political leaders should consider the broader interests of the country rather than allowing political disagreements to divide citizens.

“We cannot afford to put this country on fire because of politics. We don’t have any other home apart from this home called Zambia,” he said.

Mr Miyanda urged both winners and losers of elections to demonstrate restraint, peace and unity, saying the responsibility to protect Zambia’s stability rests with every citizen.

He said Zambia should now focus on healing and reconciliation following political contestation and begin rebuilding trust among citizens.

Mr Miyanda further warned that political instability could undermine Zambia’s economic prospects by discouraging potential investors.

He argued that investment could help create jobs and business opportunities while contributing to efforts to address the rising cost of living.

Mr Miyanda called on Zambians to put aside personal attacks and political divisions and work collectively to move the country forward.

He said the responsibility of the current generation is to preserve the peace inherited from previous generations and leave behind a stronger and more united Zambia.

“We should put our heads together and forget about personal attacks. Let us become a picture of this country that we should move forward and even make it better than we found it,” said Miyanda.

World.title: GATBRO International launches solar competition
World.content:
GATBRO International has launched the Doom Win a Solar Competition that is aimed at helping community members to access solar products that protect them from malaria.

Speaking during the launch in Lusaka, GATBRO International Head of Marketing, Kalwa Hackett says that the campaign is aimed at rewarding consumers, while protecting homes.

Ms Hacket said that consumers will have a weekly chance to win power banks and shopping vouchers.

“Every week, consumers can also win from 270 power banks and a share of the K200,000 worth of ShopRite vouchers,” she said.

“The campaign is a way of rewarding our consumers while helping families protect their homes.” She added.

And TIGER Brands International – Market Development Manager, Etienne Eksteen committed to enhancing people’s lives through the company’s Social Corporate Responsibility initiatives.

Mr Eksteen also commended ShopRite and other stakeholders for making the competition successful over the past two years.

World.title: LSUC gazetted as higher learning Institution
World.content:
Lusaka South University College (LSUC) has announced that it has been officially featured in the Government Gazette of Zambia, marking a historic milestone in the institution’s journey toward becoming a premier centre for higher learning and innovation.

The Government Gazette is the official legal publication of the Republic of Zambia.

Being gazetted, alongside accreditation by the Higher Education Authority (HEA), grants LSUC the legal mandate to award internationally recognised certificates and degrees, conduct high-level research, and provide expert consultancy and professional short-term training.

Speaking on behalf of the Board of Directors, Peter Chikubula noted that the recognition is a testament to the institution’s commitment to quality.

Mr Chikubala said the recognition is a demonstration of trust in the institution by the Government.

“Our official gazetting is more than just a legal formality, it is a seal of trust from the Government. It enables us to empower our students with qualifications that are respected world-over, ensuring they can compete in the global marketplace,” Mr Chikubula said.

He said over the years, LSUC, also registered under TEVETA, has been at the forefront of addressing national challenges through specialised skills training.

Mr Chikubala said the college has made a significant impact in the renewable energy sector, specifically in solar technology.

“By building local capacity during periods of national load shedding, LSUC has provided Zambians with hands-on skills necessary to achieve a sustainable energy mix and support the nation’s green energy goals,” he said.

Mr Chikubala emphasised that LSUC is dedicated to producing graduates who possess the practical skills required to transform and grow the Zambian business landscape.

World.title: Africa: All of Africa Today - August 25, 2026
World.content:
Two UN Peacekeepers Killed in South Sudan Ambush

Two UN peacekeepers have been killed and seven others injured after unidentified gunmen ambushed a UNMISS patrol in South Sudan's eastern Jonglei state. The injured include three peacekeepers, two national police officers and two civilian staff. UNMISS chief Anita Kiki Gbeho condemned the attack and called for a prompt investigation, warning that attacks on peacekeepers may constitute war crimes. The incident comes as renewed violence puts South Sudan's fragile peace process under increasing strain. The country remains one of the world's most dangerous places for aid workers, with at least 36 humanitarian workers killed since January.

Prince Harry Steps Down from African Parks Board

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Prince Harry has stepped down from the board of African Parks, an African wildlife charity he supported for 10 years. However, he remains a supporter of its conservation mission. His departure follows an independent investigation into allegations that rangers managed and funded by the organisation committed human rights abuses, including beatings, rape and torture, against indigenous people in Congo-Brazzaville. African Parks admitted the abuses last year and said it had since strengthened its safeguarding measures and governance. Harry's exit comes as he and Meghan prepare to relocate with their children from California to the UK.

Kagame Slams 'One-Sided' US Sanctions Over DR Congo Conflict

Rwandan President Paul Kagame has criticised US sanctions imposed over Rwanda's alleged involvement in the conflict in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo. He said that they add to existing problems without addressing the root causes of the crisis. The US sanctioned the Rwanda Defence Force and four senior commanders in March, accusing them of supporting AFC/M23. Kigali described the measures as one-sided. Kagame said international pressure should also address the role of the FDLR, the Congolese government and other actors, arguing that the conflict cannot be blamed solely on Rwanda. He said Rwanda would continue pursuing peace while taking measures it considers necessary to protect its security.

Former DP Gachagua Vows to Contest 2027 Presidential Election

Former Kenyan Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has said that his impeachment does not automatically prevent him from contesting the 2027 presidential election. Gachagua is challenging the decision in the Court of Appeal and potentially the Supreme Court. Gachagua argued that the High Court acknowledged his right to a fair hearing was violated. However, they still upheld his removal from office, which he called a constitutional "absurdity". Gachagua insists he remains a presidential contender, declaring that he is not a "kingmaker" but a potential candidate himself. He said that his opposition to President William Ruto is driven by concerns over governance rather than personal bitterness.

Close 

Tanzania Commission Begins Probe Into Election Violence

The Presidential Commission of Inquiry into the Individuals Involved in Violence and Violations of the Law during and after the October 2025 General Election has officially begun preparations to investigate those responsible. Commission chairperson retired Court of Appeal Judge Shaban Ali Lila said it will collect evidence from the public and other stakeholders. He said the commission would receive oral testimony, examine documents, and visit locations identified as connected to the incidents under investigation. The commission, established by President Samia Suluhu Hassan, will assess the evidence in accordance with Tanzanian laws and regulations.

US Seeks Wider UN Arms Embargo on Sudan

The United States has proposed expanding the UN arms embargo on Darfur to cover all of Sudan, as the country's civil war enters its fourth year. US Envoy Massad Boulos told the UN Security Council that weapons and financial support from outside powers were fuelling the conflict and proposed including drones and related technology under the embargo, as well as increasing monitoring. Sudan has backed a technical extension of the existing embargo but warned against measures that could weaken its army. Russia has expressed concerns about expanding the sanctions. The war between Sudan's army and the Rapid Support Forces has killed tens of thousands and displaced millions, with Darfur among the areas worst affected by violence.

World.title: South Africa: Businessman Seeks Bail in Trafficking Case - South African News Briefs - August 25, 2026
World.content:
KwaZulu-Natal Businessman Seeks Bail in Trafficking Case

A KwaZulu-Natal businessman accused of human trafficking and sexual exploitation is set to apply for bail at the Durban Magistrates Court, reports EWN. The 65-year-old, whose identity is protected by law, was arrested by the Hawks. He is accused of being the ringleader of a trafficking operation in which four women were allegedly lured from Johannesburg to Durban with promises of sales jobs before being forced into prostitution and pornography. His alleged accomplice, a 48-year-old man, is also expected in court. The businessman has also been linked to senior police officers and politicians through testimony at the Madlanga Commission.

Two Killed, 12 Injured in Eastern Cape Crash

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Two people have been killed and 12 others injured in a collision involving a car and a minibus taxi in Duncan Village in KuGompo City, Eastern Cape, reports SABC News. The crash occurred as the two vehicles were travelling in opposite directions. The provincial Transport Department has said that reckless and negligent driving is suspected to have contributed to the collision. The injured passengers were taken to Cecilia Makiwane and Frere hospitals, while a case of culpable homicide has been opened at Duncan Village SAPS.

Limpopo Lawyer, Cop Husband Seek Bail in R4m Fraud Case

A Limpopo lawyer and her Tshwane Metro Police officer husband are set to continue their bail application over allegations that they defrauded three deceased estates of more than R4 million, reports EWN. Charlotte Tibana, who runs a law firm in Polokwane, is accused of unlawfully transferring money from trust accounts. Acting as executor, while Peter "Gagash" Nonyane is alleged to have been involved in the fraud. The State is opposing bail and has expanded the allegations from an initial R1.75 million to more than R4 million. Tibana faces three counts of fraud and two of money laundering. Nonyane faces two counts each of fraud and money laundering. Both deny the allegations.

World.title: Kenya: Ruto Warns Opposition of Tough Political Contest
World.content:
Nairobi — President William Ruto has issued a warning to his political opponents, saying they will face a tough political contest.

Speaking during a public address in Narok North, Ruto said some people opposing his administration's programmes would be surprised by the political response.

"I can see there are some people whom we are going to give a very tough political battle, and they will be surprised, won't they?"

"I told them the other day, that even if they have been paid, even if they have been hired, even if you have been organised and sent to oppose housing, can't you use a little common sense to understand how you are going to oppose this housing programme? You come and tell us that you oppose housing because a chicken cannot climb a storey building," the President said.

The President accused sections of the opposition of mobilising people to reject government initiatives, including the Social Health Authority and affordable housing programme.

"I am telling my competitors, stop treating us like fools. You are telling us that we should go back to NHIF, which covered only eight million people, and abandon SHA, which covers 32 million people."

"Why are you testing our intelligence?

You are telling us to go back to NHIF, where you had to wait for three months before getting treatment, while with SHA, when you go and register that same day, you are already eligible to receive treatment that same day," the Head of State said.

World.title: Tanzania: Vice President Nchimbi Resigns
World.content:
Tanzania's Vice President Emmanuel Nchimbi has announced his decision to resign from office.

Nairobi — Tanzania's Vice President Emmanuel Nchimbi has announced his decision to resign from office on September 4, barely a month after he urged rights groups to "fight" for a new constitution.

Nchimbi announced Tuesday that he had written to President Suluhu informing her of his decision to retire from politics and public service and relinquish the Vice Presidency.

The announcement comes a week after local media reports on mounting pressure for the Vice President to resign, which prompted the suspension of a local media outlet.

Tanzania's Swahili Times confirmed Nchimbi's resignation on Tuesday, while the Vice President's Office did not share the resignation letter on its social media platforms.



Nchimbi cited President Samia Suluhu Hassan's desire for change as the reason for his decision.

He said he had promised Suluhu in August 2025 that he would assist her and Tanzania "to the best of my ability and with integrity," and would step aside whenever she felt the need for another Vice President.

"I am fully satisfied without a doubt that the Hon. President desires a change, so I have decided to fulfill my promise," he said.

His resignation will take effect on September 4 in accordance with Articles 50(2)(c) and 149(2) of Tanzania's Constitution.

AU declares Tanzania's election flawed and undemocratic

SADC declares Tanzania's election flawed after failing democracy test

The announcement comes about a month after Nchimbi made a strong call for Tanzanians to push for a new constitution during the opening of the 15th General Meeting of the Tanzania Human Rights Defenders Coalition (THRDC) in Dar es Salaam.

"If I were given the chance to tell Tanzanians just one thing, I would tell them: 'Fight to get a new constitution,"' Nchimbi said on July 24.

He said a new constitution based on national consensus was essential for strengthening human rights, good governance and democracy.

"Fight to get a constitution that has the agreement of all stakeholders, a constitution with consensus in the nation," he said, arguing that it should guide Tanzania for the next 50 years and protect citizens' rights.

Nchimbi said constitutional reform offered a foundation for addressing the various demands raised by Tanzanians and different groups.

"When you listen to many of the demands from different people, you find they have lined up many things all at once. You must choose the single major thing that can carry everything in the country. It is the Constitution," he said.

The constitutional reform process began in 2011 under former President Jakaya Kikwete but stalled in 2014 before a referendum could be held.

Close 

Suluhu has previously indicated that the process would be revived before 2030, while the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) pledged in its 2025 election manifesto to continue the process.

Nchimbi thanked Suluhu and CCM for their confidence in him and Tanzanians for their cooperation throughout his public service career.

He pledged to remain a "good citizen of Tanzania" after leaving office.

World.title: Uganda: Hundreds of Passengers Stranded As Taxi Crackdown Bites
World.content:
Kampala — Hundreds of passengers were left stranded across the Kampala metropolitan area on Monday as traffic police launched a crackdown on commuter taxis in dangerous mechanical condition. The operation, which began as early as 6:00 a.m., targeted dilapidated 14-seater taxis commonly known as "gganyegenya" operating in Kampala, Wakiso and Mukono districts.

Police deployed heavily along major routes, including Gayaza Road, Jinja Road, the Northern Bypass at Busega, Namugongo, Kawempe and Hoima Road, stopping and impounding taxis found to be in dangerous mechanical condition. At Rubigi Police Station along Hoima Road, one of the busiest checkpoints, police impounded at least 40 taxis serving routes to Kakiri, Nansana-Gganda and Nansana-Nabweru, areas known for having large numbers of older taxis.

Passengers were ordered to disembark and find alternative transport, while the impounded vehicles were towed by police recovery trucks to the Nakawa parking yard, which has been gazetted by Kampala Capital City Authority for impounded vehicles. Tifu Nabapa, the Officer in Charge of Traffic at Rubigi Police Station, said some taxis were identified through visual inspection, while others were checked both inside and outside."Yes, it is easy to see that this vehicle is in dangerous mechanical condition. You only look at it outside and inside and tell people to get out. We're not arresting drivers; we're telling them to go back home. But most of them have parked their vehicles; they have not shown up," Nabapa said.

The crackdown was announced last Thursday by Minister of State for Works and Transport Fred Byamukama, who directed police to begin impounding taxis in dangerous mechanical condition from Monday. Byamukama said the operation covers the Kampala metropolitan area and is intended to remove old and poorly maintained taxis from the roads.



He said the government was specifically targeting vehicles that pose a danger to passengers and other road users. "These taxis are beyond repair. You find them loading people, but when you enter, the seats are torn and smell. Some are tied with superglue. The conductor is holding the door with superglue, the doors cannot lock, and the driver is using a steering wheel tied with ropes. When you look at the tyres, the people are moving at the mercy of God," Byamukama said.

He cited Katooke Road in Nansana, Gganda-Kyebando, Kalerwe-Gayaza, Nakawa-Luzira, Kakiri and Busunju as some of the routes where the taxis operate. Byamukama said some vehicles have boots tied with ropes and warned that such vehicles endanger both occupants and other road users. He also linked some old taxis to highway robberies, saying worn-out vehicles are sometimes abandoned by owners in garages and later sold by mechanics to desperate buyers.

At Gganda-Nansana, the crackdown disrupted the morning commute, with passengers who normally board 6:00 a.m. taxis to Kampala remaining stranded for hours. Joan Nabakooza, a market vendor, said she had spent more than three hours waiting for a taxi to the city. "I'm going back home, because most of the taxis on this road are very old. That is why none of them have shown up. They have stayed away because their colleagues are telling them that police in Rubigi are impounding every vehicle coming from this road," Nabakooza said.

Some taxi operators said they had been aware of the operation but were caught between complying with the directive and trying to earn a living. Joel Musasizi, a taxi driver from Wakiso whose vehicle was impounded at Rubigi, said his employer had instructed him to drive the vehicle empty to Kisenyi-Mengo for repairs. He said he nevertheless picked up stranded passengers along the way in an attempt to earn some money before being stopped at the checkpoint.

"I don't know what I will tell my boss, because he had warned me not to load people, but I wanted some money along the way for survival today. Things have not moved well for me," Musasizi said. He appealed to the government to give taxi operators more time to repair their vehicles. Muzamir Ndibo, Chairperson of Bwaise Taxi Park, welcomed the crackdown but questioned whether it would be enforced consistently. Ndibo alleged that some traffic officers allow drivers of unsafe taxis to continue operating after receiving bribes. "They get cash from the drivers who give them bribes.

Close 

They stop them on the road with worn-out tyres, sometimes with no side indicators, clearly in bad condition but with passengers on board. The driver gets out, gives 10,000 shillings to the officer, and he will gradually let him go and return with other passengers day by day," Ndibo alleged.

The operation is part of intensified road-safety enforcement by the Ministry of Works and Transport and traffic police. Other measures include impounding vehicles without valid inspection certificates, cracking down on overloading and reckless driving, and conducting mechanical spot checks at major taxi parks and highway entry points.

World.title: Nike x NFL Rivalries uniforms return for 2026 season with 8 new teams, including Lions and Texans

For the 2026 campaign, eight new teams continue the Nike x NFL Rivalries program through distinct uniform designs created for each participating team.

The teams include teams from the AFC South – the Houston Texans, Tennessee Titans, Jacksonville Jaguars, and Indianapolis Colts – and NFC North – the Chicago Bears, Minnesota Vikings and Green Bay Packers.

World.title: Sarah Spain says WNBA players need ‘real media,’ but that sounds more like league-approved PR
World.content:
Sarah Spain thinks the WNBA should steer its players toward what she calls "real media."

That’s a PR job. Not a journalism job.

MEGAN RAPINOE CALLS ON TRADITIONAL WNBA MEDIA TO BE REPLACED WITH THOSE WHO ‘UNDERSTAND QUEER CULTURE’

On a recent episode of her podcast, Spain said she wants the league to keep setting up relationships with "the real media" that covers the WNBA "in a fair way."

Her definition of fair is pretty clear. Players trust the outlet, the outlet helps build their brands and the WNBA helps make the relationship happen.

She’s laying out a league-approved list of "reporters" players are supposed to trust.

The people who don’t make it? Spain threw them in with "a rando" on the internet spreading "bulls---."

And, by the way, Spain’s already inside the system she wants the league to grow. Spain's podcast has recently featured Connecticut Sun assistant coach Roneeka Hodges, Golden State Valkyries guard Veronica Burton, Seattle Storm players Dominique Malonga and Awa Fam, WNBA legends Cheryl Swoopes and Ticha Penicheiro, and former WNBA president Donna Orender.

Spain has the access and she calls that fair coverage. Then she says the WNBA should help its players find more outlets like hers.

That's convenient, huh?

The WNBA has publicists, marketers, agents, sponsors and social media teams to build brands. It doesn't need to turn reporters into another arm of that operation.

The credential emails show what 'fair' can mean

Spain’s preferred media setup is already taking shape in the WNBA.

I know because the teams have put it in writing.

The Atlanta Dream denied an OutKick credential request for its Aug. 5 game against the Phoenix Mercury. In follow-up answers, the Dream said it had denied 14 applications, given priority to season credential holders and outlets that consistently cover the team, and considered "the tone of coverage."

Tone of coverage.

That has nothing to do with whether a reporter got facts wrong. It has everything to do with whether the team likes the way it is being covered.

WOMEN’S SPORTS MEDIA OUTLET BACKS TRANS ATHLETES, THEN AVOIDS QUESTIONS FROM REPORTER WHO DISAGREES

The other credential denials use different words, but the same record keeps pointing in one direction.

The Dallas Wings said priority went to outlets that regularly cover the Wings and WNBA. The Connecticut Sun cited "reputable media/wire services" and outlets with a record of covering the organization. The Las Vegas Aces said it would prioritize local outlets and organizations that regularly provide editorial coverage of the Aces and WNBA.

The Chicago Sky asked a Fox News reporter about his planned coverage, denied the request and said credentials were for media covering games "for basketball purposes."

Then Atlanta told us it weighs tone.

That’s the one that matters.

The WNBA can call the preferred outlets reputable. Spain can call them real media. But a credential decision based on tone is still a team deciding whether it likes the reporter doing the coverage.

The WNBA knows where to take the story it wants told

And the league just gave us another example.

When it wanted the public to know Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White were ineligible for the 2027 draft, the WNBA didn’t answer OutKick’s questions about the rule it used. Instead, unnamed league sources told Front Office Sports the men were ineligible and called their declarations "simply publicity stunts."

Front Office Sports printed the conclusion and the league’s framing. But it never told readers whether it asked the WNBA to define "woman," explain its eligibility standard or say how Freedom and White failed it. If it did ask, readers were never told the WNBA refused to answer.

That’s different from the treatment OutKick gets when we report something inconvenient for the league. Then Front Office Sports wants documentation, competing sources and a discussion about our motives.

Spain says the WNBA should steer players toward "real media" outlets they can trust. The league has already made clear which outlets it trusts: the ones that will carry its message without making it answer the question.

LEFT-WING SPORTS HOST SARAH SPAIN LAUNCHES DISGUSTING PERSONAL SMEAR OF SOPHIE CUNNINGHAM

USA Today columnist Christine Brennan asked DiJonai Carrington whether she intentionally poked Caitlin Clark in the eye during the 2024 WNBA playoffs. It was a question that had to be asked after an incident happened on the court, yet the WNBA Players’ Association responded by calling for Brennan to lose her access.

Spain has gone after Brennan, too. Earlier this summer, she called Brennan’s Caitlin Clark coverage a "dereliction of duties as a journalist" and questioned whether Brennan’s book promotion explained her singular focus on Clark.

In Spain’s version of "real media," the reporters who ask the wrong questions don't belong.

ZERO BS. JUST DAKICH. TAKE THE DON'T @ ME PODCAST ON THE ROAD. DOWNLOAD NOW!

Then Sophie Cunningham said "biological men" shouldn't compete in girls’ and women’s sports. Days later, the WNBA’s biggest players and Commissioner Cathy Engelbert were available all weekend in Chicago for All-Star festivities.

The questions should have been obvious to any reporter interested in doing their job.

Do you agree with Cunningham? Does the WNBA support female-only sports? What is the league’s policy on transgender eligibility?

The reporters with access didn’t ask.

Spain had access, too. She moderated a panel at the WNBA’s All-Star Media & Innovation Summit, hosted a live show, sat courtside at the game and later said she spoke with Paige Bueckers, Fever coach Stephanie White, Stephanie Dolson and Aliyah Boston.

Her All-Star recap had plenty about the parties, cookies, mascots and her baseline seat. It didn't include a single question about Cunningham’s comments, female-only sports or the WNBA’s transgender eligibility rules.

And when Fever coach Stephanie White read a prepared statement accusing unnamed people of hate, fear mongering and divisiveness, WNBA media elevated the rehearsed rant into an "important" moment instead of testing a single one of those claims.

World.title: Major brain changes that occur around age 50 could impact dementia risk
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

The brain may undergo a notable shift at midlife, as new research suggests that its protective immune cells begin to decline and are increasingly replaced by inflammatory cells at around age 50.

Researchers from the University of California, San Diego; New York Genome Center; and University of California, Irvine, found that these brain changes may help explain why aging increases the chances of neuroinflammation and neurodegenerative disease, including dementia.

The study analyzed postmortem tissue from the hippocampus – the portion of the brain that is responsible for learning and memory – in 40 neurologically healthy adults, ranging from 20 to 95 years of age.

THE 'AGE' OF YOUR BLOOD COULD PREDICT DEMENTIA RISK, NEW STUDY SUGGESTS

"The most striking change was that after about age 50, the brain’s resident immune cells, called microglia, appear to be increasingly replaced by immune cells that enter from the bloodstream," first author Nathan Zemke, Ph.D., principal investigator at the UC San Diego Center for Epigenomics, told Fox News Digital.

"Microglia normally protect the brain by clearing debris and responding to injury, but the incoming cells carry stronger inflammatory signals."

The researchers believe this shift may contribute to chronic inflammation linked to cognitive decline and neurodegenerative diseases, including Alzheimer’s.

They also noted the deterioration of cells involved in maintaining the blood-brain barrier – the protective filter that helps keep harmful substances out of the brain – as well as widespread changes in DNA and gene activity.

'LONGEVITY GENE' MAY PROTECT THE BRAIN FROM ALZHEIMER'S BY BOOSTING DNA REPAIR, STUDY FINDS

One of the most exciting implications of the study, according to Zemke, is that the replacement immune cells originate in the blood, which means they are more accessible than cells already deep inside the brain.

"It may eventually be possible to modify blood-derived immune cells so that they are more protective and less inflammatory when in the brain," he said. "That could provide an entirely new way to approach Alzheimer’s and other neurological diseases without having to directly manipulate cells within the central nervous system."

Although these findings are still in early stages, Zemke said, gaining a better understanding of why this immune-cell replacement happens – and why it happens earlier in some people than others – could lead to new strategies for preserving brain health during aging.

The study’s chief limitation is that it studied human brain tissue collected postmortem from different individuals across the adult lifespan, the researchers noted.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"That allows us to identify strong age-related patterns, but it cannot directly show how the same person’s brain changes over decades or prove that a particular cellular change causes cognitive decline or Alzheimer’s disease," Zemke said.

CLICK HERE TO 

"We also do not yet know what triggers the influx of blood-derived immune cells into the brain. Determining whether changes in the blood-brain barrier, inflammation, genetics, lifestyle or other factors initiate this process will be an important next step."

The researcher emphasized, however, that he would not recommend that people make any specific medical or lifestyle changes based on this study alone.

"These findings are primarily about understanding the biology of brain aging and identifying new directions for prevention and treatment," he said.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

The timing and extent of the brain changes varied considerably between individuals, suggesting that brain aging is not necessarily a fixed process that happens identically in everyone.

"The next challenge is to understand what drives that variation and whether some of those factors can be modified," Zemke added.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The study also included a small sample of just 40 people and examined tissue only from the hippocampus, meaning the findings may not reflect immune changes throughout the entire brain.

The study, which was funded by the National Institutes of Health, was published in the journal Science.

World.title: Smithsonian-linked museum in El-Sayed’s backyard puts America’s post-9/11 response on trial
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

DEARBORN, MI – Nearly 25 years after the Sept. 11 attacks, a Smithsonian affiliate in Michigan continues to use its 9/11 exhibits and anniversary programming to focus on discrimination and government actions in the attacks' aftermath, while giving less attention to the nearly 3,000 people killed that day, Fox News Digital found.

The Arab American National Museum (AANM) in Dearborn, Michigan, features an exhibit arguing that Arab Americans "suffered two-fold as a result of the tragic events of September 11th," both from the attacks themselves and from what the museum describes as unfair treatment by the U.S. government afterward. Since its founding, the museum has repeatedly hosted programs examining what it describes as discriminatory consequences of the U.S. response to 9/11.

Fox News Digital visited the museum earlier this month, reviewed its exhibits and gift shop, and examined years of anniversary programming and federal funding records.

The AANM has received hundreds of thousands of dollars in grant funding from the National Endowment for the Humanities and is also an affiliate of the Smithsonian Institution. The Smithsonian has been under intense scrutiny from conservative lawmakers in recent months for allegedly allowing political bias to influence its presentation of history.

TRUMP V. SMITHSONIAN: A TIMELINE OF HOW THE WHITE HOUSE FIGHT OVER 'WOKE' HISTORY UNFOLDED

One placard criticizes the government’s post-9/11 detention of immigrants investigated for possible terrorist links, noting that "virtually none were charged" in connection with terrorism.

"The Arab American community suffered two-fold as a result of the tragic events of September 11th. As with all Americans, they suffered the horror and grief. However, Arab Americans were unfairly held responsible, yet not a single Arab American was found guilty of any connection to September 11th," it reads.

On Sept. 11, 2001, 19 al Qaeda terrorists hijacked four passenger planes, crashing two into the World Trade Center and one into the Pentagon. Passengers and crew fought back aboard United Flight 93, the fourth plane, prompting the hijackers to crash the plane in Pennsylvania. The attacks killed 2,977 people and triggered the largest investigation in FBI history.

The museum placard also argues that Arabs faced harsher immigration enforcement after the attacks, saying some were "deported for minor visa violations or petty offenses which previously would have been overlooked."

HISTORIAN BLASTS SMITHSONIAN'S ACTIVISM SHIFT AFTER FIRST VISIT IN OVER A DECADE: 'COMPLETELY DIFFERENT PLACE'

In the 11 months after the attacks, immigration authorities detained 762 noncitizens on immigration charges in connection with the FBI’s terrorism investigation, including for overstaying visas or entering the country illegally, according to a Justice Department inspector general report. The watchdog found that some detainees with no terrorism ties were treated harshly and held under unnecessarily restrictive conditions.

Public opinion also showed a more complicated picture of the post-9/11 backlash. President George W. Bush publicly urged Americans not to blame Muslims for the attacks, and polling later suggested attitudes toward Muslim Americans actually improved in the immediate aftermath. The share of Americans who viewed Muslim Americans favorably rose from 45% in March 2001 to 59% in November, two months after the attacks, according to the Pew Research Center.

Beyond its permanent exhibit, AANM has repeatedly used programming around the 9/11 anniversary to examine discrimination and law-enforcement policies affecting Arab and Muslim communities.

The museum holds a "solidarity" town hall each year, where criticism of the American reaction to 9/11 is often the focus. The online description of the event does not mention the deaths connected to the attacks themselves, but rather "offers a safe space for communities to reflect and engage in dialogue about the harmful prejudices that Arab and Muslim (and anyone perceived to be Arab or Muslim) individuals face on both an individual and systemic level."

One such town hall in 2018 examined "how communities of color have been targeted through the frame of national security and profiled as violent threats."

A year later, the AANM’s annual town, which received support from the National Endowment for the Arts, criticized how "institutions and communities of color have been infiltrated" by law enforcement as well as how leaders of those groups have been "targeted" following 9/11.

SMITHSONIAN AMERICA 250 EXHIBIT FEATURES 3X MORE LIBERAL ITEMS THAN CONSERVATIVE ONES

The AANM was founded in 2005, partially in response to the increased scrutiny directed at the Arab American community following the attack on the World Trade Center. In addition to receiving well over half a million dollars in funding from the NEH over its lifetime to support its exhibits and educational programming, the museum also benefited from a $385,000 grant from the Department of Housing and Urban Development which helped it expand its physical footprint in 2013. It received further HUD funding, over half a million dollars, between 2017 and 2019 as well as at least $50,000 from the State Department between 2016 and 2017, according to annual reports published by the museum.

Dearborn, where about 54.5% of residents are of Middle Eastern or North African descent, is a key political center in Michigan ahead of one of the country’s most competitive Senate races this year. Socialist-aligned Abdul El-Sayed, who is running for the Senate, drew strong support from the city earlier this month.

The museum’s focus extends beyond its criticism of the U.S. response to 9/11.

On Sept. 10 — the eve of the 25th anniversary of the attacks — the AANM is scheduled to host a screening of "Seeds for Liberation," a film that portrays Hamas’ Oct. 7 terrorist attack as part of a decades-long Palestinian "struggle" and places it within a broader history of "anti-imperialist and decolonial movements."

During Fox News Digital’s visit earlier this month, a section of the museum was dedicated to art criticizing Israel's alleged "occupation" of Palestinian land. One piece of art, the word "wall" presented in a stylized print, accuses the Israeli government of perpetuating a system of "apartheid."

The art installation broadly accuses Israel of targeting civilians in military operations, denying basic necessities to Palestinians and unjustly occupying land.

FORMER DEMOCRATIC STAFFERS, DEI LEADERS SHAPE SMITHSONIAN LEADERSHIP AMID POLITICAL FIRESTORM

One placard accompanying a sculpture states that Israel has killed more than 2,000 Palestinian children since Sept. 29, 2000, citing If Americans Knew (IAK).

The placard’s sourcing is itself controversial. Some pro-Palestinian organizations have distanced themselves from IAK over allegations of antisemitism and ties to White supremacists, allegations the group has disputed. IAK also operates a news site that has published articles rejecting the designation of Hamas as a terrorist organization.

Another placard attached to a sculpture pulls a quote from Defense of Children International Palestine (DCIP), which the Israeli government designated as a terrorist organization in 2021. DCIP and human rights groups have disputed the designation.

The museum gift shop also sells Palestinian-themed merchandise, including map-shaped magnets and key chains, coloring books promising to help children "explore Palestinian heritage" and keffiyehs.

IN CHARTS: A VISUAL BREAKDOWN OF THE SMITHSONIAN'S BILLION-DOLLAR TAXPAYER-FUNDED BUDGET

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The AANM, Smithsonian, NEA and NEH did not respond to requests for comment after being reached by Fox News Digital on Friday.

Smithsonian affiliates, like the AANM, are independently operated museums that maintain formal partnerships with the Smithsonian, providing them with access to artifact loans, educational resources and consultations from institutional experts.

In recent months, the Smithsonian has faced mounting pressure from Republican lawmakers and the president over allegations that its museums advance left-of-center ideological causes through their exhibits. Officials have threatened funding cuts against the institution if it does not root out what the Trump administration characterizes as anti-American bias.

The rise of GLP-1 weight-loss drugs could be changing more than what Americans put on their plates, as restaurants increasingly look to wellness drinks and other alternatives to traditional alcoholic beverages.

The National Restaurant Association's new 2026 Restaurant Beverage Trends report found growing interest in a wider range of drink choices, particularly among younger consumers, as restaurants experiment with everything from wellness and energy drinks to smoothies, lemonades and alcohol-free cocktails.

Chad Moutray, chief economist at the Washington, D.C.-based National Restaurant Association, told Fox News Digital that the growing use of GLP-1 medications is one of several health trends restaurant operators are watching.

MOVER OVER, APEROL: VIRAL ITALIAN SPRITZ ARRIVES IN US WITH EYE-CATCHING TWIST

The report, which was conducted by the National Restaurant Association and is based on surveys of consumers and restaurant operators across the country, found that health is already influencing some Americans' decisions about alcohol.

Among adults surveyed who said they don't drink alcohol, 25% cited health reasons. That figure climbed to 34% among Gen Z nondrinkers.

Several trends are converging as younger consumers become more health-conscious and GLP-1 medications become more widely used, Moutray said.

"I think you're seeing a lot younger folks who are, in general, wanting to be healthier. You have the Make America Healthy Again movement, which is also driving some of this trend," he said.

PROTEIN COFFEE IS EXPLODING IN POPULARITY AMONG ADULTS WORRIED ABOUT MUSCLE LOSS

"You have people drinking energy drinks and health drinks and all those things. And then you add to that the GLP-1 notion, where if you're taking one of those drugs and your appetite is more suppressed, you're not going to drink as much alcohol."

Restaurants are already preparing to broaden their drink selections.

Among limited-service restaurant operators, 24% said they planned to add new wellness drinks in 2026, while 26% planned to add energy drinks, 29% smoothies and 27% lemonades.

Just under half, 46%, planned to add new coffee offerings.

"I think as GLP-1s become less expensive as this year goes on and as we move into 2027, you're going to see restaurant operators continuing to look for alternatives that can be good menu options for consumers that might be taking those drugs," Moutray said.

Derek Brown, a hospitality consultant and founder of Drink Company, said he's also seeing GLP-1s contribute to a broader shift toward moderation.

"Yeah, there's no doubt that GLP-1s are having an effect on the way that people consume," Brown told Fox News Digital. "And it's part of a basket of things that's contributing to people moderating more often."

The drugs can affect people's appetites for both food and drinks, Brown said, potentially leading some customers to consume less alcohol or choose nonalcoholic alternatives.

"I think that's clearly part of this entire moderation trend that we're seeing that's just a part of it, but it's significant enough, so I think that's certainly a real thing," Brown said. "And I definitely think that bars and restaurants are starting to feel that."

The changing beverage landscape, however, doesn't necessarily mean younger Americans are abandoning alcohol.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Per the report, 71% of Gen Z adults and 74% of millennials surveyed said they drink alcohol either at home or at restaurants. Sixty percent of Gen Z adults and 68% of millennials said they drink alcohol at restaurants.

Moutray believes younger consumers are instead choosing from a broader portfolio of drinks.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

That broader selection could be increasingly important for restaurants. The report found that 87% of full-service operators and 80% of limited-service operators said beverages can be an important driver of customer traffic.

"It's driving traffic, it's getting people excited and it's, hopefully, also helping to improve overall profit margins," Moutray said.

World.title: Blue state's water failures could threaten food supplies across US, lawmaker warns
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

California's aging infrastructure is helping fuel a clean water crisis that could have ramifications across the country, a key House Republican warned.

Rep. Harriet Hageman, R-Wyo., accused California Gov. Gavin Newsom of playing politics with the management of the Colorado River, a major body of water that millions of people in the Western United States depend on. She's arguing that the Golden State's bloated bureaucracy and environmental regulations are making it more reliant on the Colorado River, thus stressing its supply and affecting the other six states through which it runs.

"The system is now becoming very, very stressed because California has not kept up with the infrastructure demands and needs of its citizens," Hageman told Fox News Digital. "Pinedale, Wyoming, may be a long way removed from Southern California, but when there are calls on the river and when there are demands that we reduce the amount of water that we are able to use in order to meet a demand downstream, that isn't fair."

California's water infrastructure has largely remained unchanged since the late 20th century, despite a ballooning population.

COLORADO SMALL TOWN ABANDONED AFTER ALL ELECTED OFFICIALS RESIGN, WATER CONCERNS GROW

Hageman argued that California's growing need paired with a lack of new infrastructure is hurting the agricultural sector in areas that rely on the Colorado River — which could have ripple effects beyond the West.

TRUMP CAN PROTECT CALIFORNIA AVOCADO FARMERS AND TAKE A BITE OUT OF MEXICAN CARTELS, TOO

"California could grow almost all the food we need in the United States, but they've really decimated their Ag industry because they've taken irrigation water away from their Ag industry to try to meet municipal demand and industrial demand elsewhere. So really it's just, it's a whole parade of bad decisions that are being made," she said.

"Food independence is a national security issue. We do not want to become food dependent on Mexico or Central America or bringing all of our food in from other countries. We have the resources to grow healthy, high-quality food right here while also protecting our environment."

Environmental groups like Tell the Dam Truth have opposed new dam builds in California, arguing they contribute to climate change while harming biodiversity.

"With its strong environmental laws, regulations, and policies, California has the opportunity to not only stop new dam construction, but also decommission dams to restore the biodiversity and carbon sequestration currently inundated in river valleys across the state," the group's website states.

Groups like the Sierra Club have also opposed desalination, an alternative water source that would require California to convert its abundant saltwater into a usable product.

But Hageman said that opposition was misguided.

"They're very backwards people. I kind of look at them like flat-Earthers. They're very backwards people in the way that they approach things. They ignore the fact that humans are also part of the natural environment, and they ignore the benefits of what we can create by building this much-needed infrastructure," she said.

The Colorado River's Upper Basin runs through Colorado, Wyoming, New Mexico and Utah. The Lower Basin runs through California, Arizona and Nevada.

TRUMP TO SHRINK 2 UTAH NATIONAL MONUMENTS BY 90%

It has faced growing problems, in part due to climate change and increased dependence, prompting discussions about whether the seven aforementioned states could update their existing water-sharing agreement.

A failure to do so thus far has prompted the Trump administration to step in and force steep cuts to the Lower Basin states for the next two years.

NEWSOM, WALZ URGE CONGRESS TO BLOCK ANTI-CLIMATE BILL IN THEIR ‘WOKE’ CRUSADE

Newsom praised the plan while pointing out California has reduced its use in recent years, but said it was only a "short-term" solution.

"This is a necessary step to protect a river that 40 million Americans depend on, at a time when climate change is driving a regional water crisis that makes every drop of water count. California continues to lead the way forward, growing our economy while cutting our Colorado River water use to the lowest level since 1949," he said of the Trump administration order. "Any long-term solution must share responsibility fairly across all seven states in recognition of the new reality of the Colorado River."

California also recently made plans for a new reservoir project, projected to cost $6.8 billion, which is expected to be completed in the mid-2030s. The state is also investing in new groundwater infrastructure and other initiatives to expand availability of the critical resource.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A spokesperson for the California Natural Resources Agency re-emphasized the state's reduced dependency on the Colorado River when reached by Fox News Digital.

"California’s Colorado River use is at its lowest since 1949 – and our urban water agencies have reduced their demand for imports by 50% since 2000. Even with that, we continue to invest billions of dollars to increase water supply as we face changing conditions driven by climate change," the spokesperson said.

"Suggesting we move the world’s fourth largest economy entirely to desalinated water is a deeply unserious proposal that ignores the underlying issues facing all users of the Colorado River. All Basin states must share the responsibility of caring for the Colorado River for generations to come – and that means real conservation from all seven states."

World.title: Supreme Court hands preliminary win to Trump on mail-in ballots executive order
World.content:
WASHINGTON — The Supreme Court handed an initial win to the Trump administration Monday in its effort to implement an executive order aimed at limiting who can receive mail-in ballots ahead of the 2026 midterm elections.

At issue are provisions that seek to create a federal list of eligible voters and order the U.S. Postal Service to deliver ballots only to those people.

The justices, divided 6-3 along ideological lines with conservatives in the majority, lifted an injunction a Massachusetts-based judge imposed in June that prevented key aspects of the executive order from going into effect this year in California and 22 other states that had challenged it.

The court also granted a similar application filed by Alabama and 11 other states.

The White House praised the court’s ruling, calling the executive order’s provisions “commonsense measures.”

“This Administration will continue to lawfully enact the agenda President Trump was elected on — which includes the safety and security of our elections,” White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said in a statement.

U.S. Postal Service headquarters in Washington. Erin Scott / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

Parts of the same executive order are blocked nationwide because of a ruling the same judge issued later in a different case, but the Supreme Court decision is likely to apply to that ruling, too.

That means the administration may, at least in the short term, be able to implement the executive order, but the legal battle is far from over.

“This decision is a painful setback, but it will not be the final word,” New York Attorney General Letitia James, who was among those who challenged the proposal, said in a statement.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, said Monday night that his state will launch a new challenge to the Trump administration’s policy on mail-in voting.

“Following today’s SCOTUS ruling, California WILL SUE again to BLOCK Trump’s attack on mail-in voting!” Newsom said on X. “Every eligible voter gets a mail-in ballot here — and we’ll fight to keep it that way.”

President Donald Trump has frequently railed against the widespread use of mail-in ballots as part of his broader complaints, offered without evidence, that the election system is plagued with fraud.

His efforts to encourage Congress to pass his SAVE America Act legislation that would impose new voting restrictions nationwide, including proof of citizenship to register to vote and voter ID, have so far failed.

Election workers process mail-in ballots at San Francisco County's election operations facility at City Hall in San Francisco in June. David Paul Morris / Bloomberg via Getty Images file

The Supreme Court decision is provisional, focusing only on the argument that U.S. District Judge Indira Talwani acted prematurely in preventing the provisions from being implemented in the 23 states before federal agencies had even drawn up plans for how to implement the executive order.

“The court’s disposition of this application does not mean that any measure taken by the Government to implement the order will necessarily be lawful. On that score, time will tell,” the court said in an unsigned ruling.

The decision leaves the door open to judges’ intervening later, especially with regard to any restrictions imposed for the coming midterm elections. On Friday, while the case was pending, the Postal Service issued its final regulation that would enforce parts of the executive order.

The dissenters were the three liberal justices on the conservative-majority court.

“Today’s decision does not address whether the President’s attempts to interfere with states’ administration of the November 2026 elections are lawful. Nor does it suggest that the Executive Branch has any constitutional or statutory authority to implement the President’s directives. Instead, today’s decision merely postpones adjudication of those challenges,” Justice Sonia Sotomayor wrote.

In a separate dissent, Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson accused the majority of “taking its eye off the ball” by focusing on a technical legal argument instead of what she views as the larger goal of the Trump administration: “to secure our imprimatur for its effort to foment chaos ahead of the November elections.”

The Trump administration told the Supreme Court the new regulations did not go as far as the executive order anticipated, saying the Postal Service “will not refuse to transmit ballots” even if senders are not on a state list of registered voters.

The Supreme Court decision is in line with one in a related case by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit that rejected a separate attempt by Democrats to block the executive order.

Lower courts declined to put the Massachusetts ruling on hold, leading the administration to turn to the Supreme Court.

Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote in the filing that it was premature for courts to rule on the issue, as neither the Postal Service nor other agencies have determined how they will implement the executive order. It would be a tall order for the chronically underfunded Postal Service, with just months to go before Election Day.

World.title: What to watch in today’s primaries and Scott Bessent threatens new sanctions on Iran: Morning Rundown
World.content:
South Carolina voters will choose the Republican candidate in the race to replace the late Sen. Lindsey Graham. The Trump administration plans its largest mass visa revocation in history. And how Penn State students reacted to a massive drug ring bust that made national news.

Here’s what to know today.

South Carolina offers the next major test of Trump’s influence

President Donald Trump helps Sen. Darline Graham off the stage during a campaign rally in Myrtle Beach, S.C., on Aug. 21. Saul Loeb / AFP via Getty Images

President Donald Trump quickly threw his weight behind Sen. Darline Graham when she announced her bid to run for a full term after the sudden death of her late brother, Sen. Lindsey Graham. But her candidacy has faced skepticism, particularly after a misstep at a debate last week. Now, the president’s influence faces its next test this election season.

The Republican Senate runoff today in South Carolina between Graham and Rep. Ralph Norman will show whether a Trump endorsement is still an important factor in Republican contests. Norman is a staunch conservative who has painted Graham as the “establishment” pick, and some Trump supporters are wary about Graham’s lack of experience.

Trump’s influence also faces a test in the Oklahoma GOP primary for governor. State Attorney General Gentner Drummond has touted his closeness to the president, even though Trump backed his opponent, former state Sen. Mike Mazzei. Trump has since panned Drummond as a “fake Republican.”

The Oklahoma race has become particularly brutal and personal. Fighting between the two candidates over accusations about their fitness for office led to the two men releasing drug tests in recent days.

Here are the other primary races to watch.

NBC News’ chief data analyst Steve Kornacki takes a closer look at a potentially decisive South Carolina district in The Data Dive, a new subscriber-exclusive newsletter on the numbers, trends and data shaping the biggest stories heading into the midterms. Read today’s edition here.

More politics news:

The Supreme Court handed an initial win to the Trump administration in its effort to implement an executive order aimed at limiting who can receive mail-in ballots before the midterm elections.

For subscribers: On the campaign trail, Trump branded himself as the “fertilization president” and promised to make IVF free. What happened?

Bessent threatens new sanctions on Iran in follow up to ‘economic D-Day’ threat

00:39 Bessent pressures countries to cut economic ties with Iran 00:00 00:00

The U.S. took steps aimed at further isolating Iran after Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent threatened an “economic D-Day” against the Islamic Republic. Bessent said yesterday that his department is sanctioning nearly 60 corporations, individuals and vessels that it says enables the Iranian regime’s “recklessness.” Bessent said Trump has been making phone calls to world leaders requesting that they stop trading with the Iranian regime. Earlier yesterday, the United Arab Emirates said it will end all trade relations with Iran.

While Iranian leaders downplayed the threat, experts said the success of Bessent’s announcement will hinge on whether the country’s most powerful trading partners — China, India and Russia — decide the U.S. threats are credible.

More on the reaction to Bessent’s announcement.

Related coverage:

Canadian leaders traded barbs with Trump over the new wave of tariffs imposed by the U.S., with Ontario Premier Doug Ford saying “everything is on the table” in terms of retaliation.

U.S. prepares for mass visa revocation

The State Department is expected to announce in the coming weeks the revocation of business and tourism visas issued between 2016 and 2026 whose holders have sought asylum or are now seeking asylum, according to State Department documents obtained by the Associated Press and two U.S. officials. The move to revoke so-called B1 visas — which are generally used for business trips — and B2 visas — are generally issued for tourism, family visits or medical care — could affect up to 200,000 foreigners and would be the largest single mass revocation of visas in U.S. history.

The revocations would not necessarily result in the holders’ immediate deportation, and it would likely face legal challenges.

Here’s what else to know.

Staff Pick: The reaction at Penn State to an alleged drug ring

The Old Main building at Penn State University in State College, Pa. Islam Daghestani / iStockPhoto via Getty Images file

When prosecutors announced that 14 people had been charged in what authorities described as a highly profitable cocaine-trafficking ring centered on two Penn State fraternities, the allegations quickly made national headlines and became the butt of online fodder. But when I went to State College, Pennsylvania to see how the news was reverberating on campus, I found something unexpected: Students barely seemed to care.

For two days, I knocked on fraternity and sorority doors and talked to students about the alleged scheme. Of those who did stop to chat, most said they didn’t know the defendants, hadn’t heard about the alleged operation before the arrests, or didn’t think it was that big of a deal.

My story captures the striking disconnect between the seriousness of the allegations and the decidedly muted reaction on campus, even as it has endured years of national scrutiny and Greek life-related scandals. — Matt Lavietes, breaking news reporter

World.title: Multiple dead, including children, in Montana shooting and house fire
World.content:
Multiple people, including children, died when a gunman opened fire at a Billings, Montana, home that was then set alight, authorities said Monday.

Police characterized the incident Sunday evening near the city’s West End neighborhood as a family disturbance. The gunman died of a self-inflicted gunshot, NBC affiliate KULR of Billings reported.

Interim Yellowstone County Sheriff Kent O’Donnell said at a news conference Monday that “multiple adults and multiple juveniles” died at the residence.

The dead have been identified, he said, but the number of those killed, their names and their ages will not be released for now.

“Because of the fire and obviously water that goes to suppress that fire, it’s going to slow our investigation of the crime scene recovery of evidence,” he said. “So we ask for patience as we complete this investigation.”

A possible motive was not available Monday.

Billings police and county sheriff’s deputies were dispatched to the shooting in the 300 block of White Star Circle at 6:01 p.m. Sunday, Billings police said on Facebook. O’Donnell said gunshots could be heard during the 911 call.

Officers and deputies reached the scene in roughly 10 minutes and at that point heard gunfire from the back of the residence, the police department said.

Three minutes later, the home was fully engulfed in flames, it said.

Video from the scene showed law enforcement officers taking cover behind patrol SUVs on the street near the home as a small tactical team behind a handheld shield moved toward the structure.

Firefighters were dispatched but may have faced water access issues and fewer fire hydrants than might be ideal, officials said.

“The delay in limited access presented significant challenges, fire conditions continued to worsen, and the residents ultimately became ... consumed by fire,” Billings Fire Chief Matt Hoppel said at Monday’s news conference.

The origin of the blaze was also under investigation.

Billings Police Sgt. Jeff Stovall said in a statement Monday that some information was being withheld “to protect the integrity of the ongoing investigation.”

“There are details we simply cannot release at this time,” he said.

World.title: ‘Getting no help’: Thousands in Gary, Indiana, still without power nearly 2 weeks after storms
World.content:
GARY, Ind. — The power outages caused by storms that roared through the region nearly two weeks ago have one resident of this Rust Belt city literally gasping for air.

Joetta Walker, who is 73 and has asthma, uses a nebulizer to help her breathe. But right now it’s a useless piece of machinery, and she has had to rely on an inhaler to survive.

“I have a nebulizer where I need to take breathing treatments,” Walker said in an interview at her sweltering home. “I can’t do that without the electricity.”

Lifelong Gary, Ind., resident Joetta Walker, 73, holds her nebulizer. Selina Guevara / NBC News

Walker said the inhaler doesn’t give her the same level of relief.

“I wheeze,” Walker said and demonstrated. “You hear it now because I get too hot.”

No other place in Indiana has suffered more as a result of those Aug. 11 storms than this mostly Black city on the southern tip of Lake Michigan, best known as the hometown of Michael Jackson and the Jackson 5.

As of Monday, more than 8,600 customers were still waiting for their power to be restored, most of them in Gary, the Northern Indiana Public Service Co. (NIPSCO) reported on its website.

Mayor Eddie Melton said he spoke with President Donald Trump and told him “explicitly that we needed help, that we needed resources.”

Melton said he asked Trump to sign an executive order “and move this thing forward so folks can start getting back to work and we start restoring Gary back to normal.”

“He said that he was going to do all that he can,” Melton said.

Melton said he also met with Republican Sen. Jim Banks. He hopes power for residents will be fully restored by Tuesday.

“I believe a good chunk of that will be restored today, and hopefully 100% will be restored tomorrow,” he said.

Melton’s hopeful forecast came a day after he ripped NIPSCO for failing to completely restore electricity to his city.

“Twelve days is too long for families to be without power,” he said Sunday in an address posted on the city’s Facebook page. “I have made it clear the current pace of restoration is unacceptable.”

Tree Care workers from Michigan remove a tree from the front of a home in Gary on Thursday after it was toppled during a recent storm. Scott Olson / Getty Images

In an email Monday, NIPSCO, the Merrillville, Indiana-based utility provider that supplies natural gas and electricity to over 1.3 million residential and commercial customers across the northern third of the state, said it’s “focused on safely restoring power to all customers in every affected community.”

On its website, it said it expects to restore power to all of its customers in Gary by Tuesday.

Walker said that can’t happen too soon. She said she has been relying on her nieces to bring her food and charge up her cellphone twice a day. She said she has $750 worth of pork chops, spiral hams and other foods rotting in her nonfunctioning freezer and refrigerator.

“All gone, gone,” she said.

At night, Walker said, she gets around the house by candlelight.

Walker stands in front of her empty fridge, where, she says, more than $700 worth of food has spoiled. Selina Guevara / NBC News

“I feel hurt ... because I feel like they can do better than this,” she said of the power company. “But I also understand how much damage was done, and I also understand the workers have to be tired.”

Another Gary resident, Dion Thomas, 40, said Monday was the first time he’d seen power crews in his neighborhood. But they seemed to be struggling to turn the electricity back on.

“Some people’s stuff was coming on, then it went back out,” he said.

In the meantime, people have been heading to parks to cook whatever food they have left over charcoal and eat it before it spoils, said Thomas, a father of three.

“It’s been crazy,” he said.

Since the power went out, there has been a spate of generator thefts in his neighborhood, said Calvin Boone, 44, a father of four.

“The kids running around, they stealing people’s generators right now,” Boone said. “I think about the older people, the health for them.”

Boone said that everybody has been feeling hot and miserable and that some have taken to sleeping in their cars with the engines on and the air conditioners blasting.

“We ain’t getting no help,” he said.

Channie Weaver got her power back overnight. But it was too late to save the food in her fridge. She said she’d gone shopping right before the storms hit and estimates she lost $300 worth of provisions.

“All the food is gone. We about to go out and get something out to eat,” said Weaver, 50.

Channie Weaver, 50, of Gary. Selina Guevara / NBC News

Weaver said she lives with her 22-year-old daughter, Desaray Weaver, and her granddaughters, Raelynn, 2, and Riley, 1.

“Man, it’s been rough,” Weaver said. “Being hot in the house, no air conditioning, plus my daughter — she’s pregnant. But it’s definitely been rough.”

Weaver and other Gary residents said in interviews that they can’t help but wonder whether the reason their city’s power is getting restored last is that it’s a mostly Black city.

“I feel like we at the bottom before everybody else,” she said.

Shaquille Brewster and Selina Guevara reported from Gary and Corky Siemaszko from New York City.

World.title: Why some Trump supporters aren’t sold on Darline Graham: From the Politics Desk
World.content:
Welcome to From the Politics Desk, a daily newsletter that brings you the NBC News Politics team’s latest reporting and analysis from the White House, Capitol Hill and the campaign trail.

In today’s edition, Sahil Kapur digs into a key challenge for Sen. Darline Graham ahead of the South Carolina runoff. Plus, Allan Smith breaks down the shifting political landscape around data centers.

Sign up to receive this newsletter in your inbox every weekday here.

— Adam Wollner

⚖️ Breaking news: The Supreme Court handed an initial win to the Trump administration in its effort to implement an executive order aimed at limiting who can receive mail-in ballots ahead of the midterms. Read more →

Why some Trump supporters aren’t sold on Darline Graham

Analysis by Sahil Kapur

MYRTLE BEACH, S.C. — On Friday, a South Carolina Republican voter named Roger showed up to a Donald Trump and Darline Graham rally wearing a “DARK MAGA” T-shirt. He arrived early and waited hours to see the president speak.

But Trump’s endorsement wasn’t enough to convince him to vote for Graham in Tuesday’s high-stakes GOP runoff. Graham’s recent debate performance affected his perceptions after she said that “national security is not my thing” when asked if Taiwan and the South China Sea are U.S. national security issues.

“Her people should have briefed her a little bit more,” he said. “Foreign policy is something that — you’re going to come in as a new senator, as a rookie, you’re gonna have to learn that.”

Glenda Clinkscales, who said she “loves Trump” and was “excited” to see him, didn’t harbor the same feelings for Graham. Like Roger, she was undecided.

“Some good answers and some not so good answers,” she said when asked what she made of Graham’s debate performance. “I’m not so sure about her right now.”

The hesitation by the two Trump supporters casts a cloud over Graham’s prospects for a six-year term as she faces five-term Rep. Ralph Norman, R-S.C.

Another voter, Daniel Musick of Myrtle Beach, labeled Trump “the best president we’ve ever had.” He had made up his mind for Norman even before watching Trump and Graham at the rally.

“It’s just that she’s untested. I don’t know enough about her,” he said, adding that “part of the reason” for his opposition to Graham is her debate moment. “Her answer on foreign affairs, when it came to China and Taiwan — it was really unclear that she knew her foreign policy, and to me that was the biggest issue.”

Norman has sought to capitalize on her debate blunder, but it’s not clear he is on the path to victory. Norman is 73, at a time when age is an issue for voters, and has been accused by Graham’s team of being insufficiently loyal to Trump as a member of the House Freedom Caucus that seeks to push his agenda to the right.

Graham, 62, has defended her debate moment by saying voters in South Carolina aren’t asking her about China and Taiwan.

“Now the critics say I shouldn’t run for the Senate. They say I’m not a politician. You know what I say? Guilty as charged,” Graham said at Friday’s rally with Trump. “And by the way, President Trump had never served in an elected office before, and I think he’s done a damn good job.”

Trump, for his part, said Graham was just “being honest” in the debate.

“I mean, she’s going to do what the military wants, and really what the president wants,” Trump told reporters Friday before the rally.

To other GOP voters who attended Friday’s event, Trump’s support was enough.

“Honestly, I don’t know as much about the platforms there, but if Trump supports her, I do too,” said Lynn Spivey, who was wearing a Darline Graham sticker.

Patrick Maguire contributed.

📱Related: MAGA Inc., the super PAC tied to Trump, has spent $830,000 on text messages and voter phone calls to boost Graham, Bridget Bowman reports.

Republicans wrestle with data center backlash as Trump promotes the benefits

By Allan Smith

As recently as last month, Republicans in some of this fall’s biggest races publicly expressed skepticism about the growing backlash to data center development.

A lot has changed since then. On Thursday, former Rep. Mike Rogers, the GOP nominee for Senate in Michigan, announced support for a one-year moratorium on data center development. In Wisconsin and Pennsylvania, Republican nominees for governor cut ads hitting their Democratic rivals for being too open to the projects.

Earlier this month, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who had welcomed the developments to his state and faces re-election this fall, ordered an audit of data center projects in the state before any more can advance. And in Ohio, GOP gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy released a plan stating that any future data center built in the state must pay the electricity bills and property taxes for nearby residents, adding that he will sign an executive order pausing development until such a plan is enacted into law.

Meanwhile, the National Republican Senatorial Committee wrote a memo last week for data center industry leaders detailing how in Ohio’s Senate race, the issue is single-handedly tearing down Republican Sen. Jon Husted as his Democratic rival, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, spends millions on anti-data center ads.

Data centers are one of the few issues in American politics that don’t fall along neat ideological lines. Both parties are rapidly trying to figure out what approach works best for them at the national, state and local levels. Democrats, including some who previously offered the industry a warm embrace, are similarly positioning to be seen as champions for data center accountability and tightly regulated growth as progressives angle for state and federal moratoriums on their development.

But the challenge is equally, if not more, daunting for Republicans, who have worked to build stronger relationships with tech leaders after they gravitated to President Donald Trump during his last presidential bid. And they’re campaigning as Trump himself has promoted the benefits of data center development needed to power the growth of AI.
