According to federal data at the time, the guidance said, African-American students represented just 15% of students overall but 35% of students suspended once and 44% of students suspended more than once. (NPR has reported that this trend actually begins in preschool.)

An American Psychological Association task force found no evidence that these disparities reflected differences in student behavior; instead, the APA said they "may be due to lack of teacher preparation in classroom management, lack of training in culturally competent practices, or racial stereotypes."

Reflecting on why she sent that 2014 memo, Catherine Lhamon, who ran OCR under Presidents Obama and Biden, tells NPR, given our nation's history, not looking carefully at school discipline rates through the lens of race would have been an abdication.

"The very first desegregation agreements that [OCR] was created by Congress to enforce included requirements that discriminatory discipline practices end," Lhamon says. These practices, she says, are "a feature of discrimination. And it's something that we have seen persist in schools over decades."

And so, as head of the department's civil rights enforcement unit, Lhamon warned school leaders that these disparities were not acceptable and "give rise to concerns that schools may be engaging in racial discrimination that violates the Federal civil rights laws."

In other words, they needed to look hard at their data to see if the numbers revealed meaningful racial disparities. If so, they could be investigated by the U.S. government.

Schools got the message.

In the years after that 2014 guidance, NPR reported that many school districts mounted a dramatic shift away from suspension and expulsion and toward the use of policies that kept students in school, including restorative justice, which emphasizes dialogue and mediation over punishment.

By 2018, NPR reported that the share of students suspended at least once had dropped from 5.6% to 4.7%, with Hispanic students seeing a 30% drop. Black students and students with disabilities also saw big drops, though suspension rates for both groups remained high.

Sponsor Message

Enforcement of this policy continued even into the first Trump administration.

In late 2018, OCR reached an agreement with Wake County Public School System in North Carolina after finding that, among other things, Black students being disciplined for their first offense were more likely to be suspended than similarly situated white students.

The backlash

After the 2014 guidance, conservative critics accused Lhamon of heavy-handedness, arguing that districts began going easy on disruptive, perhaps dangerous students out of a fear that any difference in their discipline rates between student groups would be considered discrimination.

In 2018, conservative commentator Max Eden, who would go on to work in the second Trump administration, wrote that "school districts must never again be presumed guilty and unable to prove their innocence, and kids should never again be put in danger because of statistics."

Eden argued that these relaxed discipline policies may also have made classrooms more disruptive.

In December 2018, a game of ping pong began: The first Trump administration issued new guidance formally rescinding Lhamon's.

In 2023, after returning to lead the Biden-era OCR, Lhamon again advised schools that they could be held accountable if their discipline data revealed concerning disparities.

But the backlash also continued, fueled by a COVID-driven spike in student misbehavior, which led to more classroom disruptions and stories of teachers feeling victimized by students.

Classroom discipline even became a talking point in the 2024 presidential campaign. The Republican platform pledged candidates "will support overhauling standards on school discipline [and] advocate for immediate suspension of violent students."

In April 2025, after Trump's return to the White House, he made good on that pledge and signed an executive order titled, "Reinstating Common Sense School Discipline Policies."

And finally, there's this month's guidance, signed by Kimberly Richey, the current head of OCR. In an interview with NPR, Richey says that, today, "classrooms are less safe, they are more disruptive, and that is all a fruit of this policy. And that's why we're ending it."

Sponsor Message

The new guidance

The latest guidance from the Trump administration argues that, under the previous policy, "schools ignored or covered up — rather than disciplined — student misconduct to avoid any purported racial disparity in discipline numbers that might catch the eye of the federal government. As a result, students who should have been suspended, expelled, or otherwise held accountable for dangerous or disruptive behavior remained in the classroom."

Richey argues the goal of OCR's previous approach was what she calls "racial balance": "To make sure that the number of African-American students [being disciplined], the number of Hispanic students, the number of white students, the number of Asian students — that it was equal across the board."

But, Richey says, this idea that any difference in discipline rates is a sign of discrimination — "that everything has to be equal and, if it's not, it's inherently discriminatory… That's false."

In the new guidance, Richey doesn't just warn schools against this kind of balancing. She advises schools that weighing discipline policies with any consideration of race, even if it's in the name of identifying and addressing disparities, is itself discriminatory and illegal.

As the new guidance puts it: "The consideration of race in student discipline is race discrimination."

Civil rights groups, including EdTrust, which focuses on education equity, reject this view.

"Schools must be able to examine who is being suspended, expelled, or referred to law enforcement, why those decisions are being made, and whether students are being treated differently for similar behavior," EdTrust's Eric Duncan said in a statement. "That is not preferential treatment. It is basic accountability to ensure all students are valued."

And Lhamon argues that by telling schools they cannot consider race, disparities won't go away. They'll simply become invisible to everyone except the students who are being hurt.

She says, this new guidance "is a scare tactic… designed to ensure that some of our kids in school will experience extraordinary harm."

Sponsor Message

Richey argues the opposite: This consideration of race isn't a tool of the law – it breaks the law.

"You cannot take race into account when you're disciplining students. It can't play a factor, and the racial balancing must end," Richey says.

The investigations

Fayetteville is one of two districts the department says it is investigating — the other is Milwaukee Public Schools. Little is known about why these two were singled out beyond what was included in the department's press release.

Of Milwaukee, the department release says, "education leaders derided facially neutral school policies as reflecting systemic 'whiteness,' seemingly encouraging school officials to consider race in disciplinary practices."

But, in response to a request for comment, a spokesperson for Milwaukee Public Schools said that the notice it had received from the Education Department didn't explain the reason for the investigation, and, "Once we receive more detail, we would be able to respond appropriately."

In Fayetteville, Superintendent Mulford, now in his fourth year running the district, says his team does review the district's discipline data. But, he adds, "we never talk about, 'Hey, go softer or harder on this particular group of people.' That doesn't even come into our language at all. So we preach consistency, the standard is the standard, everybody's held to the standard."

Mulford says he welcomes the department and its investigation. If it finds something, he says, "Great. Share it with us. If we're doing something wrong, we'll get it fixed."

But, if they're looking for inconsistency, Mulford says, he doubts they'll find it in Fayetteville.

World.title: At least 25% of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE, study finds
World.content:
At least 25% of former NFL players who died between 2016 and 2021 had CTE, study finds

toggle caption Patrick Smith/Getty Images

For years, as researchers have established a link between repeated impacts to the head and the degenerative brain disease known as CTE, one major question has loomed: Just how common is it — especially among high-risk groups, like professional football players?

A new study from researchers at Mass General Brigham, published Tuesday in the prominent medical journal The BMJ, seeks to establish a more accurate baseline of CTE prevalence among retired NFL players who have died. Of football players who appeared in at least one NFL game in their careers and who died between 2016 and 2021, the study found that a minimum of around 25% had CTE upon their death.

"We've known that this disease process can be caused by, in part, repeated traumatic brain injury. But we didn't know how common it was," said Dr. Daniel Daneshvar, the study's lead author.

Sponsor Message

Chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, is a degenerative brain disease that can only be diagnosed with a brain dissection after death. Because of that, most research about the disease has relied on brains donated to researchers by families or by individuals themselves, many of whom had seen or experienced symptoms, such as memory loss or major mood swings, that led them to believe they might have the disease.

That dynamic has long muddied the picture about the actual prevalence of CTE — especially for combat veterans exposed to traumatic brain injuries, or current and former elite-level athletes in contact sports like American football and ice hockey, where blows to the body and head are a regular occurrence.

Daneshvar and his colleagues drew on the large collection of samples at the UNITE Brain Bank at Boston University. The brains of more than 330 NFL players who died between the years of 2008 and 2021 have been donated to the bank. Of those, 93% have been diagnosed with CTE.

toggle caption Nick Cammett/Getty Images

To better understand what proportion of all NFL players that sample represents, the study's authors created a list of every player who had appeared in at least one NFL game since 1949. They referenced demographic data and obtained death certificates for all deceased players from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to create a denominator list of 1,712 players who died in the same time period. The researchers then narrowed the sample to those who had died between 2016 and 2021, when the proportion of players whose brains were donated for study was highest.

Sponsor Message

The prevalence estimate of 25% is at the "low end," Daneshvar said. The actual figure could be higher, the paper noted, pointing to a number of CTE diagnoses made outside of the brain bank sample, along with other suspected cases of CTE in former football players whose brains were not evaluated after death. Additionally, researchers wrote, an analysis of death certificates of football players who did not donate their brains revealed another 215 whose certificates listed a neurodegenerative disease as a cause of death.

At the extreme upper end, the study found that a maximum possible prevalence of CTE — if researchers assumed that every former football player had CTE except for the 20 whose brains had definitively been cleared of a diagnosis — was around 97%.

"The true rate of CTE at death in NFL players is somewhere in the middle," Daneshvar said.

In a statement to NPR, an NFL spokesperson said the league "continuously strives to make the game of football safer, including by implementing strategies to reduce concussions and head impacts."

"The NFL remains committed to ensuring that the NFL community has access to a robust — and expanding — set of resources to enhance their physical and mental wellbeing. We encourage former players to utilize these resources to identify and seek treatment when they are concerned about their health," the statement continued.

toggle caption Harry How/Getty Images

A secondary aim of the study was to examine the link between dementia and CTE. Because the disease cannot be diagnosed in living patients, the relationship between symptoms in life and a diagnosis after death is still fuzzy.

The study found a high correlation between dementia in life and a diagnosis of the most advanced stage of CTE, Stage IV, after death; more than 90% of Stage IV samples were also diagnosed with dementia by a clinician based on medical records and information obtained from loved ones.

Sponsor Message

But the link was far less clear between dementia and lower stages of CTE, or even those whose brains had been found to be free of the disease's characteristic buildups of tau protein. Some 40% of CTE-free samples were diagnosed with dementia.

That means that further research is needed to best help the thousands of current and former NFL players who are still living, said Rachel Grashow, a neuroepidemiologist at the Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health who was not involved in the study.

"If we're trying to think about how to practically apply this information to living former NFL players who've just left the league, or those who left a while ago and are starting to age, that part deserves further discussion," said Grashow, who studies football player health. "The next step in centering the experiences of the living former players is to encourage them to speak with their doctors and loved ones about any concerning symptoms."

Conditions like sleep apnea, high blood pressure and low testosterone — all of which are common among former NFL players and tied to prior head injury — can lead to symptoms commonly associated with CTE, she said, with one important difference: The former conditions are treatable, while CTE is not (for now).

"Our concern is that the public and kitchen table conversations around CTE are creating hopelessness in living former NFL players. And this hopelessness may discourage them from reaching out to their doctors and getting treated for conditions, like sleep apnea, that are causing worrisome symptoms," she said.

Dr. Randall Chesnut, a neurological surgeon at the University of Washington who was not involved with the research, said the paper is "significant."

toggle caption Steph Chambers/Getty Images

"It's really well done. It's a large population. It's well controlled within the limits of the statistical analysis that they can pull off on this," said Chesnut, an expert in brain- and spine-related sports injuries who also works as a concussion spotter in professional rugby matches.

Sponsor Message

Another caveat, Chesnut pointed out, was the average age of the cohort. Among the former players whose brains were donated, the mean age at death was around 66 years old, meaning most of their professional football careers took place before 2005, when CTE was first diagnosed in a former NFL player.

As scientific understanding of the relationship between repeated head trauma and neurodegenerative conditions has grown, the league has taken steps to improve player safety, such as banning dangerous plays, like traditional kickoffs and helmet-to-helmet tackles, and funding research of safer equipment.

"It was captured during a time when there was delayed recognition by the NFL that concussion was a big deal," Chesnut said. "So this may not represent the NFL in 2026."

Degenerative brain diseases can affect anyone, even those without a history of brain injury. Among Americans over the age of 55, the lifetime risk of eventually developing any form of dementia is 42%, one study published last year in the journal Nature Medicine found.

World.title: DHS conducted far-reaching surveillance during Minnesota ICE surge, court documents show
World.content:
DHS conducted far-reaching surveillance during Minnesota ICE surge, court documents show

toggle caption Jaida Grey Eagle for NPR

On a recent Sunday morning at Prince of Peace Lutheran Church in Roseville, Minn., Steve Sylvester, the interim pastor there, had an unusual announcement to make.

Standing at the altar, he told his mostly elderly congregation that the Department of Homeland Security had surveilled their church during the federal immigration enforcement surge that happened in the state last winter.

The revelation was part of a motion filed in federal court just a few days before the service, as part of an ongoing conspiracy case against ICE protesters.

According to government documents, an undercover DHS agent attended a meeting of ICE protesters at Prince of Peace in February. The agent captured the license plates of people there, and then compiled dossiers including their names, addresses, and information about their families and jobs, according to the motion.

Sponsor Message

"It feels weird. It feels like I'm living in 1950s Eastern Europe," Sylvester told NPR. "I don't know that it feels frightening or daunting. It just feels completely out of place and inappropriate."

He's far from the only person caught in the wide-reaching surveillance web spun by the federal government.

Surveillance at churches, schools and libraries

For months, the documents show, federal agents secretly made recordings of meetings held at churches, libraries, restaurants and schools around the Twin Cities. They infiltrated private group chats, sought the financial records of national labor unions, and gathered information on community members who had not been accused of any crimes.

"Quite honestly, it was breathtaking," says Rachel Levinson-Waldman, who directs the Liberty and National Security Program at the Brennan Center for Justice. "Just the scope of what was being revealed in terms of how deeply it had gone, how many government resources were being devoted to this."

toggle caption Jaida Grey Eagle for NPR

Cody Sanders, interim pastor at University Baptist Church in Minneapolis, says his first reaction was surprise, then anger, when he heard that an undercover agent wore a wire to a self-defense class held at his church this past May.

"I do imagine people will look over their shoulder a little more and wonder, 'Is there someone here who's trying to gather information?' Or when they see a strange car in the parking lot," Sanders says. "I hope we can resist the kind of suspicion that this is likely to generate."

Sponsor Message

Sergio Manancero manages La Doña Cerveceria, a brewery in Minneapolis where an undercover agent attended a meeting in January, according to court documents.

toggle caption Jaida Grey Eagle for NPR

"I would understand why they would send somebody to that meeting, considering it was open to anybody that wanted to come because they were probably trying to figure out whether or not protesters were going to do something more serious against their agents," Manancero says.

"Do I think the government spying on us in that way is maybe bad? Yes," he said. "Am I surprised that they did it? No."

Manancero says organizers at the event were planning a lawful ICE protest. In a way, he says, he finds it almost beneficial that DHS agents witnessed it firsthand to see that nothing suspicious was taking place.

During another meeting at a public library, an undercover agent allegedly told a person there that he worked in construction and could build items for more "direct action," and that he didn't mind going to jail.

Privacy and free speech concerns

Levinson-Waldman, of the Brennan Center, says the federal government has broad authority under the Fourth Amendment to gather information on people, though other laws do impose limitations. There isn't enough information yet to determine whether the surveillance in Minnesota was legal, she says.

toggle caption Jaida Grey Eagle for NPR

Regardless, Levinson-Waldman says, "Just because something's legal doesn't mean that it aligns with people's sense of what is ethical or what they're comfortable with having the government doing."

She says the tactics described in the documents seem to break from decades-long norms and guidelines. They remind her of COINTELPRO, the domestic counterintelligence program run by the FBI, which began in the 1950s and ended in the early 1970s.

As part of that operation, agents conducted intense surveillance on organizations it deemed subversive, including the Communist Party, the Black Panthers and civil rights leaders including Martin Luther King, Jr., and Malcolm X.

Sponsor Message

The abuses of that program, Levinson-Waldman says, led to a series of reforms, including tighter guidelines at the Justice Department on investigative techniques.

The government defended its actions in a court filing on Friday, saying it did not target the thousands of peaceful protesters in Minnesota.

Instead, it said it targeted the people who were ultimately charged in the conspiracy case. Prosecutors say they were planning activities not protected by the First Amendment, like setting up blockades at the federal building outside of Minneapolis that served as ICE headquarters during the surge.

According to the government, the surveillance conducted was "standard law enforcement practice."

Aaron Terr, director of public advocacy with the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, says the investigative tactics described in the court motion also raise First Amendment concerns, because this type of surveillance can also sweep up people engaged in perfectly lawful activity.

toggle caption John Moore/Getty Images

As part of its investigation, the documents show, DHS obtained the financial records for several nonprofits and labor unions, including the Service Employees International Union and the Communications Workers of America. In its response, prosecutors said requesting these records was "within the authority" of the agency.

"These reports raise the question of whether the government is investigating crimes or investigating political movements," Terr says. "When officials are infiltrating political meetings, recording protesters' license plates and examining years of financial activities by these mainstream advocacy groups, it raises the question, do they have actual evidence of criminal activity here?"

One government document presented to grand jurors shows a PowerPoint slide depicting a web of 18 organizations with the label "The Conspiracy." A DHS agent testified to the grand jury that it showed other organizations the defendants in the conspiracy case were affiliated with, according to the motion.

They included a local teacher's union, a bicycle repair shop, and the Minnesota affiliate of the AFL-CIO, a large federation of labor unions. In a statement, Minnesota AFL-CIO President Bernie Burnham said the government is "bringing back McCarthyism."

Sponsor Message

In its response to the court motion, the government said that it did not actually argue that the AFL-CIO or any other organizations shown in the web were part of the conspiracy.

Terr says the image communicates a troubling idea: Be careful who you associate with.

"The consequences of that are that many Americans may be afraid to attend a protest, support an advocacy organization, because they don't want to become the target of a government investigation," he says.

In a statement, DHS told NPR it does not comment on the existence or status of ongoing investigations. The agency directed NPR to the U.S. Attorney's Office for the District of Minnesota, which also declined to comment.

A hearing in the conspiracy case is set for this week.

World.title: How Canadian content on streaming platforms became a trade issue with the U.S.
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The fight between Canada and the United States on trade isn’t just about dairy, car parts and natural resources. It’s also about what appears on your Netflix homepage.

The Globe and Mail, citing a senior government source, reported Sunday that U.S. negotiators demanded Canada drop requirements for American streaming companies to promote Canadian content, including French-language content.

The federal Liberal government refused.

"We were not prepared to compromise on our sovereignty, the protection of the French language, and our culture,” Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a speech on Saturday after trade talks collapsed.

The demand is the latest in a years-long dispute involving the Canadian government on one side and American streaming giants and the U.S. government on the other. So how did we get here?

Stream Canadian

Ottawa has long required broadcasters to promote and support Canadian content (Cancon), all the way back to song quotas for AM radio stations.

In 1991, the government brought in the Broadcasting Act. The law states that "the Canadian broadcasting system shall be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians" and that the Canadian broadcasting system should "serve to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada."

But decades later, the rising popularity in Canada of streaming platforms such as Netflix, YouTube, Amazon Prime and Spotify raised questions about Cancon and broadcasting rules. Video and audio streaming services were not, for example, required to support and promote Cancon, but their TV and radio counterparts were.

Looking to address the imbalance, the former Trudeau government brought forward a bill in 2022 to update the Broadcasting Act, called the Online Streaming Act.

"Canadian broadcasters have invested in and introduced us to the incredible Canadian programs that so many of us love. We are updating our laws so online streamers have to contribute in a similar and equitable way,” a 2022 government news release said .

The legislation was controversial from the start, with the government and supporters saying it was a necessary evolution of Canada’s media laws in the digital age, while opponents expressed concerns that it was overreach and an attempt to regulate the internet.

American streamers and digital media companies opposed the legislation fiercely.

The bill passed with amendments and became law in April 2023, but the government delegated much of its interpretation — including how much money streamers would have to contribute to Cancon — to Canada's broadcast regulator, the Canadian Radio-television and Telecommunications Commission (CRTC).

But getting streaming companies to pay up has been a long and confusing saga.

In 2024, the CRTC decided that online streaming services with revenues of over $25 million would have to put five per cent of their Canadian revenues toward the Canadian broadcasting system, such as local radio and television news, and French-language and Indigenous content.

A sign for the CRTC is shown in Gatineau, Que., on April 22. The federal government ordered the broadcast regulator to implement the Online Streaming Act. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)

Big streaming companies such as Netflix and Disney Plus launched court challenges, and a Federal Court of Appeal judge said they would not have to make the payments until the court heard the case.

Despite this, in May of this year, the CRTC announced that it would increase the payments to 15 per cent of revenue for online broadcasters.

The U.S.-based Motion Picture Association (MPA), which represents companies like Netflix, Paramount Pictures, Prime Video, Walt Disney Studios and others, was not happy and even called the move a trade violation.

"The Motion Picture Association strongly condemns the CRTC’s decision to impose unprecedented, unnecessary, and discriminatory investment obligations on American streaming services operating in Canada," MPA said in a statement.

"This burdensome framework unfairly targets global streamers with requirements that directly violate Canada's obligations" under the Canada-United States-Mexico Agreement.

A few weeks later, the government directed the CRTC to rethink the increase. The government, including Carney, expressed concern that the levy would raise prices.

Ottawa also said it would issue a new policy directive to adjust how the CRTC is implementing the Online Streaming Act.

The MPA welcomed the move, while d ozens of Canadian cultural sector organizations asked the government to keep the requirement in place.

In a court document dated July 17, the attorney general’s office said the government intends to eliminate the payments entirely and replace them with taxpayer funding.

Earlier, in June 2025, the government abolished the digital services tax (DST), which required foreign and domestic large businesses to pay tax on some revenue earned from engaging online users in Canada. The government cited trade negotiations with the U.S. for the move.

Money isn't everything

But the current dispute might not be about funding at all.

The Online Streaming Act also requires online streaming services to make it easier for Canadians to see and access Canadian content on their platforms, including French- and Indigenous-language programming. The CRTC will start a consultation on how best to do that this fall.

Michael Geist, a law professor at the University of Ottawa and Canada Research Chair in Internet and E-commerce Law, writes on his website that the fact the government has backed down on payments while also saying Canadian culture is non-negotiable is telling.

The government appears to be "open to cutting mandated payments for culture and news, but not moving on the power to regulate how culture is distributed and promoted," he said in a post.

"If true, that represents a significant shift since the cultural sector has long viewed payments as a cornerstone of cultural policy."

WATCH | PM says he won't allow Canada to be a 'subsidiary' of the U.S.: Canada won't accept being 'subsidiary' of the U.S.: Carney | Duration 0:57 When asked by the Globe and Mail when Ottawa will come back to the table to hammer out a trade deal with Washington, Prime Minister Mark Carney said his delegation won’t accept attitudes that see Canada as a 'subsidiary' of the U.S. Carney's comments come after U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said Canada would come back to the table due to its dependence on the U.S. for security.

The Online Streaming Act isn’t the only law in American crosshairs.

Last year, the Quebec government introduced Bill 109, titled "An Act to affirm the cultural sovereignty of Québec and to enact the Act respecting the discoverability of French-language cultural content in the digital environment.” The bill forces streaming giants to add French-language content and make it more easily accessible to users. It became law in December 2025.

But why is the American government so invested in the issue that it could become a sticking point in trade negotiations?

Mariane Bourcheix-Laporte, a postdoctoral fellow in the communication studies and media arts department at McMaster University in Hamilton, said it could be about power.

"The Americans have had, since after World War II, a very strong cultural policy of pushing out American content into the world,” Bourcheix-Laporte, who has worked with the CRTC, said.

"This has been a strategy — a soft-power strategy — for the American government, in parallel to their military strategies and political alliances strategies."

World.title: 1 in 4 NFL players — or more — developed brain disease CTE, new study suggests
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

At least one in four former National Football League (NFL) players had evidence of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, or CTE, at the time of death, according to a new study from one of the U.S. research teams at the forefront of studying the devastating brain disease.

CTE — which can only be confirmed after death — is associated with repeated head trauma, often from contact sports. It can lead to debilitating symptoms ranging from severe memory loss and balance problems to major personality changes, including depression, aggression and thoughts of suicide.

A growing body of research has already shown exceptionally high rates of the disease in the donated brains of former NFL players. But researchers are quick to note that brain banks skew heavily toward people who experienced concerning symptoms during life and wanted their brains studied after death.

The new research, from Mass General Brigham, Boston University and the Concussion & CTE Foundation, aimed to estimate the prevalence of CTE among all NFL players.

"We were unfortunately both surprised but saddened to see that the minimum rate was so alarmingly high," said lead author Dr. Daniel Daneshvar, chair of Physical Medicine and Rehabilitation at Mass General Brigham and an associate professor at Harvard Medical School.

Nine in 10 donated brains had CTE

The researchers identified all former players who died between 2008 and 2021 — before the rise of soft-shell helmet additions that can reduce the severity of head impacts — including 235 who chose to donate their brains.

More than nine in 10 of the donated brains showed evidence of CTE, according to the paper published Tuesday in the British Medical Journal .

To account for the 878 players who did not donate their brains, researchers calculated a range of possible CTE prevalence. The most conservative estimate was about 25 per cent, assuming the confirmed cases among donors were the only instances of disease among the entire cohort of players.

The team says the true number likely falls somewhere in the middle.

Researchers watch real-time data coming in from an MRI scan on the brain of someone with suspected CTE. (Evan Mitsui/CBC)

Also striking, said Daneshvar, was that roughly six in 10 NFL brain donors with CTE met the clinical criteria for dementia.

"They had clinical impairment in their thinking and memory that was so severe they couldn't take care of their own activities of daily living," he explained. "Things like grooming themselves or feeding themselves, or managing their day-to-day activities — they couldn't do it because the pathology was so severe in their brain."

The more severe the CTE pathology was in someone's brain, Daneshvar added, the more likely they were to have dementia before death.

Efforts to protect athletes' brains

The findings were unsurprising to leading Canadian neuroscientist Dr. Charles Tator, a longtime brain injury researcher and outspoken advocate for safety measures in professional and amateur sports.

"If we're going to be faced with that degree of disability, I think it's another wake-up call that we have to pay more attention," said Tator, an emeritus scientist at the University Health Network's Krembil Brain Institute in Toronto.

The NFL, like other professional sports leagues, has made strides to better protect players, including its efforts to reduce dangerous tackles after kickoffs while allowing players to wear extra protective caps.

But Daneshvar said greater awareness of the risks is crucial, given mounting evidence that "the cumulative force to the head that someone experiences over their life has long-term consequences."

His research team said further studies should examine athletes who played more recently, and that prevention efforts should focus on reducing all sorts of repetitive head impacts that could drive CTE risk — not just concussions.

"How do we make common-sense decisions to protect our athletes' brains?" he said.

Dr. Charles Tator is photographed at Toronto Western Hospital in Toronto, in May 2023. (Alex Lupul/CBC)

Tator said those decisions need to start early, long before people enter the world of professional contact sports, to prevent people from having decades of repeated head injuries in football, rugby, hockey and beyond.

He cited the strict "remove-from-sport" protocols that are part of Ontario's concussion prevention legislation, dubbed Rowan's Law in memory of Rowan Stringer, an Ottawa high school rugby player who died after suffering multiple concussions.

"Now you might ask yourself, how come there isn't a similar law in other provinces of Canada — and there isn't," Tator continued.

"All provinces have done something about repetitive concussions, so it's not that they have no safeguards and no injury prevention programs, but they don't have what Ontario has, which is a law."

Former Canadian Football League (CFL) player Tim Fleiszer, who heads advocacy group Concussion Legacy Foundation, said it's important for minor sports leagues to reduce head impacts on developing brains, including those that don't typically result in obvious concussions.

"The biggest bang for the buck would be taking heading out of soccer for young children, particularly in practice, and following the lead of the United States and the U.K.," he said.

WATCH | Unlocking the mystery of how CTE destroys the brain: Unlocking the mystery of how CTE destroys the brain | Duration 11:22 Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy (CTE) is a devastating brain disease that ruins lives, but it can’t be diagnosed until after death. For The National, CBC’s Lauren Pelley gets an exclusive behind-the-scenes look at the Canadian research trying to change that.

Data never 'perfect' around CTE prevalence

The new findings on the possible prevalence of CTE among NFL players should "stir up some good discussion" heading into the football preseason, said cognitive neurologist and Sunnybrook Health Sciences Centre clinician Dr. Matthew Burke.

Still, he stressed the study is limited by its retrospective design and the inherent challenges of studying a condition that wasn't actually diagnosed during someone's life.

"A critic of a study like this would say that we have to take [these numbers] cautiously … but the data is never going to be absolutely perfect."

At the same time, Burke said the findings advance our understanding of CTE, which remains one of the most feared and high-profile brain diseases associated with the deaths of multiple well-known athletes — but one that's ultimately preventable.

WATCH | Hockey great Bobby Hull had CTE when he died: Hockey great Bobby Hull had CTE when he died, researchers find | Hanomansing Tonight | Duration 5:40 Bobby Hull, the Hall of Fame hockey player and two-time NHL MVP had chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE) when he died in 2023 at age 84, according to researchers at Boston University’s CTE Center. Hull had donated his brain to science to advance research on the disease.

Further study is needed to understand why some players with heavily impacted brains go on to develop dementia symptoms while others do not, Burke added, as researchers continue to untangle the mechanisms involved.

"On a surface level, it makes sense: Like, yeah, we shouldn't be hitting our heads over and over again and causing inflammation and damage," said Burke. "But I do still think our understanding of the pathophysiology is somewhat limited."

The study also hammers home an underlying challenge with CTE: People who suspect they have the condition can't receive a definitive diagnosis while they're still alive, meaning there is no treatment tailored specifically to CTE beyond supportive care for what can be a life-altering range of symptoms.

"We need to move conversations beyond just understanding this disease process towards curing it," Daneshvar said.

World.title: He sells golf trolleys, not cars. But he’s facing a $183K bill under a federal Chinese EV tariff
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The owner of a Pickering business which designs and sells electric golf trolleys says he’s being unfairly taxed at a rate intended for Chinese EVs. CBC’s Rochelle Raveendran spoke with Joseph McLuckie, who says his business is in jeopardy after he received a nearly $200,000 tax bill on a shipment of golf trolleys.

A Pickering, Ont., business owner who sells golf trolleys says he’s being unfairly taxed under a now-defunct federal tariff intended for Chinese EVs.

JPSM Golf designs and sells remote-controlled electric golf trolleys that carry players’ golf bags while they walk the course.

The company received a shipment of 330 trolleys from China in April 2025. At the time, the trolleys were subject to Canada’s standard 6.1 per cent import tariff, and the company paid just over $19,000.

But this past May, owner Joseph McLuckie received a letter from the Canadian Border Security Agency (CBSA), telling him the shipment had been reviewed and his trolleys had been assigned to a different tariff classification.

That reclassification meant the trolleys were subject to the China Surtax Order — a federal tariff that took effect in October 2024 and slapped a 100 per cent surtax on Chinese EVs, along with “electric and certain hybrid passenger automobiles, trucks, buses, and delivery vans."

McLuckie now must pay $182,883.95, including interest and GST.

The owner of JPSM Golf, which designs and sells electric golf trolleys, says he's being unfairly taxed at a rate intended for Chinese EVs. (JPSM Golf, Rafael Martins/Reuters)

“This has taken time off my life because of the stress and the sleepless nights … and just wondering what's going to happen next,” he said.

He said he’s at a loss as to why his golf trolleys are being included in a tariff that targeted Chinese EVs and intended to protect Canada’s auto industry.

“Let's go outside with one of my trolleys, and let's park next to an electric vehicle and let's ask the public: what do these two things have in common?” he said.

Unintended consequence of tariff, owner says

When the surtax order was announced in 2024, the government said in a news release the tariff was intended “to level the playing field for Canadian workers.”

An vehicle from Chinese automaker NIO pictured in Shanghai in March 2026. The federal government repealed the China Surtax Order the same month. (Lisa Xing/CBC)

In addition to EVs, the order also covered broader tariff classifications, including “motor vehicles for the transport of goods – other with only electric motor for propulsion.” That is the classification the CBSA applied to the trolleys in May, making them subject to the 100 per cent surtax.

Previously, the trolleys were classified under “motor vehicles for the transport of goods – other.”

The government repealed the China Surtax Order effective March 2026, but it still applies to shipments during the period that it was active, the Department of Finance confirmed in an email.

McLuckie said he believes the tariff was never intended to apply to products like his golf trolleys.

He said he doesn’t know how he’ll keep his business afloat with the new cost, and may need to consider job cuts for his six employees.

Wheelbarrows are considered vehicles: CBSA response

McLuckie is preparing to appeal the CBSA’s decision.

Prior to that process, JPSM Golf’s lawyer, Greg Kanargelidis, sent the CBSA a written submission, which argued in part that golf trolleys are not motor vehicles.

Vehicles don’t need to have a driver’s position, seat or carry passengers to be classified a vehicle, a CBSA senior trade compliance officer told JPSM Golf in a letter on July 7. (CBC)

In a response on July 7, the CBSA wrote the golf trolleys are "undoubtedly" considered motor vehicles, since they use an electric motor to move and transport goods.

Vehicles don’t need to have a driver’s position, seat or carry passengers to be classified a vehicle, wrote Juliana Leung, a senior trade compliance officer with the CBSA.

She added that traditional, non-electric wheelbarrows are also considered vehicles under the Canadian customs tariff .

The CBSA told CBC News in a statement that it couldn’t comment on specific cases.

The agency administers surtaxes “based on the legal wording of individual surtax order,” spokesperson Luke Reimer said in an email.

Over 180 requests for relief from order: feds

Alongside the CBSA appeal, McLuckie has also filed a remission request with the federal government. Remission orders provide full or partial relief from federal tax.

Kanargelidis said remissions are discretionary, meaning the Department of Finance has to agree that a remission is in the public interest.

Trade lawyer Greg Kanargelidis, who represents JPSM Golf, says the Department of Finance has to agree that a remission request is in the public interest. (Craig Chivers/CBC)

He said he believes the federal government has been dealing with an influx of remission applications due to tariffs.

The Department of Finance has received over 180 requests for remission since the China Surtax Order took effect, and has granted five remission orders, spokesperson Benoit Mayrand said in an email.

He said the department is currently assessing another 30 requests and expects to advance a sixth remission order this fall, but did not provide details on that order.

The government assesses each remission request in consultation with domestic producers “to determine whether the goods are in short supply in the Canadian market, cannot reasonably be sourced from non-Chinese suppliers, and whether other exceptional circumstances exist that adversely affect the Canadian economy,” he wrote.

World.title: Netanyahu warns of 'targeted strikes' if Hamas doesn't stop kites from flying toward Israel
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Israeli government is threatening to increase "targeted strikes" on Gaza unless Hamas takes action to prevent kites used by Palestinians, including children, from flying toward Israel.

In a statement posted to social media platform X on Sunday, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said that he and Defence Minister Israel Katz held a "situational assessment" on Sunday evening to discuss the “threat of drones, balloons and kites launched from the Gaza Strip toward Israel."

He said the meeting was also attended by Lt.-Gen. Eyal Zamir, chief of the general staff; the head of the National Security Council; and senior officials of the Israel Defence Forces (IDF).

Netanyahu went on to say that Israel was warning Hamas that if the launches did not cease immediately, "the IDF will act to increase targeted strikes against those responsible for the launches and will evacuate the population from areas used as launch sites for kites, drones, and balloons."

"Israel will not allow the Hamas terrorist organization or any other element in the Gaza Strip to threaten our communities again and compromise our citizen’s sense of security," he said.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defense Minister Israel Katz held a situational assessment this evening regarding the threat of drones, balloons and kites launched from the Gaza Strip toward Israel. The discussion was attended by Chief of the General Staff, Lt. Gen. Eyal… —IsraeliPM

But for Omar Halawa, 13, flying a kite by the shore in Khan Younis is his only reprieve during the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas, which governs the Gaza Strip.

"We fly kites so we can change our moods," he told CBC freelance videographer Mohamed El Saife. "There is nothing left in Gaza to make us happy."

Omar said he's been building kites himself, making the fringe on the sides as well as the tail. He said he's aware of the warnings Netanyahu has placed on those who fly them.

"We don't use any missiles, we are children," he said. "We don’t deal with Hamas, we want to live."

In the period before the Hamas-led Oct. 7, 2023, attack on southern Israel that sparked the war, Israel said burning kites and balloons were sent from Gaza, causing fires and other damage. Israeli officials now say several kites were found in a kibbutz near Gaza. No weapons or dangerous materials were attached.

Netanyahu's latest move comes as Israeli strikes and tank fire killed at least four people on Monday, including two children, hospital officials said, a week after a U.S. delegation asked Israel to draw down attacks.

The strikes hit the Bureij and Shati refugee camps, Khan Younis and a tent in Deir al-Balah. Two children, aged four and 10, were killed, along with two men.

The Oct. 7 attack on Israel killed some 1,200 people and saw 251 taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies. Israel’s retaliatory offensive in Gaza has killed more than 73,422 Palestinians, according to the enclave's Health Ministry, which says since a ceasefire took effect last October, Israeli airstrikes have killed at least 1,288 Palestinians.

A displaced Palestinian boy prepares a kite amid the ongoing conflict between Israel and Hamas, in Rafah, in the southern Gaza Strip, in February 2024. (Ibraheem Abu Mustafa/Reuters)

In a post on the Telegram messaging platform, Hamas said Netanyahu's statements about children flying kites "confirm a premeditated intention to continue the aggression and proceed with the plans of displacement and genocide."

The group said the recent strikes by Israel were a "further escalation in committing brutal crimes" against Palestinians and a "blatant disregard" of international law.

It also demanded that the Trump administration and mediators condemn Israel's actions and compel it to "adhere to the roadmap leading to a genuine ceasefire in Gaza."

Omar said he's now afraid to fly kites in case a strike happens because of him, and "everyone would be killed around me.... I don’t want to die, there is no security."

His mother, Yasmin Halawa, 38, said her son lost everything and can't afford to also lose his kite. "He lost his school, his soccer game, his swimming," she said. "So he decided to make a kite."

Halawa said she's worried that more bans will come down on children's activities because of security issues raised by Israel.

As the sun set, the children continued flying their kites, this time near their tents rather than on the shore of the Mediterranean.

World.title: What Trump's tariffs mean for AI, video games, cellphones
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

From cellphones to gaming consoles and artificial intelligence infrastructure, experts say the escalating trade war between Canada and the United States will mean higher costs for consumers and businesses.

Canada exported more than $4 billion US worth of electronics equipment to the U.S. last year that would now be subject to U.S. President Donald Trump's new 50 per cent tariffs on a wide range of goods. Certain electrical boards and controllers represent the highest dollar value of any export category targeted by the new U.S. levies.

On Saturday, Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada would match the Trump administration's tariffs dollar for dollar.

Experts say higher prices are a virtual certainty, as the escalating trade dispute threatens businesses on both sides of the border.

Carol McGlogan is president and CEO of Electro-Federation Canada, an industry group representing more than 230 companies in Canada's electrical and automation sector.

"The 50 per cent tariffs are devastating," she said on Monday, adding that 90 per cent of her member's exports go to the U.S.

"Increases in pricing are going to increase the cost of homes, schools, [and] buildings," McGlogan added.

"We know that we need to double the size of the [electricity] grid between now and 2050 … with the tariffs going both ways, we have just increased the cost of that for everyone, and that ultimately comes out of the taxpayers pockets."

Evan Light, an associate professor at the University of Toronto, says items like gaming consoles and cell phones have been rising in prices for some time now due to chip shortages and supply chain issues. He predicts the recent escalation in the Canada-U.S. trade war will make these items even pricier.

WATCH | Where to buy Canadian: ‘Buy Canadian’ website sees traffic surge 300% after U.S. trade talks collapse | Duration 4:41 Traffic to Canadian e-commerce marketplace Common Goods has surged 300 per cent since Canada-U.S. trade talks broke down, according to owner Valerie Crisp. She says the response shows continued interest in buying Canadian, even as consumers navigate the complexities of the new tariffs.

"In the short term, I think it's going to be pretty terrible for everybody," he said. "I think we'll see a lot of costs being passed on."

Ottawa-based Kinaxis makes software that companies use to manage their supply chains. Chief product officer Andrew Bell says many clients are using the company's programs to evaluate new suppliers.

"While the tariffs may initially start by being applied to supply chains, that's not where it stops. It ultimately stops at the person who is consuming or buying the product," he said.

Will tariffs slow AI adoption?

Bloomberg News recently reported that Nvidia, one of the world's most profitable companies, has warned its customers to expect an up to 15 per cent price bump for its prized artificial intelligence chips.

"Supply chain challenges, whether they be tariffs or other disruptions, can limit or constrain … supply. The result is an increased cost for those components," Bell said. "That is what we are seeing, and companies like Nvidia are seeing."

University of Toronto professor Light wonders if the trend towards higher prices could ultimately slow AI adoption and deployment.

"It almost gives us an opportunity to gut-check whether or not we want to buy full on into the AI space as much as we have, given that the expense will be multiplied in the U.S. and in Canada," he said.

World.title: Hayden Panettiere's death may be inspiring celebrities to protect child actors in Hollywood
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Several former child actors are speaking out following the death of Hayden Penettiere, saying there's a lesson Hollywood needs to take from it: young actors need better protections.

Over the past week, former child actors including Anna Paquin and Melissa Gilbert, have been sharing their own challenges with balancing fame and mental health, describing how vulnerable they felt while working at a young age, and sharing ideas to bring change to the industry.

Panettiere died earlier this month at age 36. While the cause of her death is still unknown, it has revived discussions about her struggles with mental health and substance abuse, which she detailed in her memoir This Is Me: A Reckoning, released in May this year. She isn't the only recently deceased former child actor to have faced such issues.

In June, actor Daveigh Chase, who voiced Lilo in Disney's 2002 animated feature Lilo & Stitch, died at 35, of complications from AIDS and polychronic substance abuse, according to the Los Angeles County Medical Examiner. In the days after her death, her father confirmed to media that she had been homeless.

In February last year, Harriet the Spy and Buffy the Vampire Slayer actor Michelle Trachtenberg died as a result of complications from diabetes. She also underwent a liver transplant in the months before her death at age 39.

Paquin, a Canadian-born actor who has been acting since she was 11-years-old when she won the Academy Award for best supporting actress for The Piano, said in a post on Instagram last weekend that their untimely deaths are no coincidence.

She wrote that children on sets are prematurely sexualized, and many of these "female, child 'stars' have profoundly sad lives and untimely ends."

The systems in place to protect these young actors may look good on paper, Paquin said, but her experience was they weren't as protective as they should have been.

Naming the problem

Gilbert, who worked as a child actor on the series Little House on the Prairie starting in 1974, wrote about the deaths of the former child actors on her Substack saying, "w hen three of us die so close together, something is very, very wrong. "

She said that child actors are expected to deliver without question, no matter what, lest they seem difficult, something she suggested makes them prone to exploitation.

Melissa Gilbert, who starred in Little House on the Prairie, wrote in an essay on her Substack newsletter that child actors are expected to do their jobs without question lest they seem difficult, which she says can make them prone to exploitation. (Valery Hache/AFP/Getty Images, NBC Television/Getty Images)

"These young professionals are children, and we should make sure they are allowed to be children. They should be allowed to say 'no'. Not push through physical or emotional pain. Not be made to support their entire families. And most certainly not to be followed everywhere they go by cameras, phones and prying, exploitive eyes," wrote Gilbert.

Her comments come as her husband, actor Timothy Busfield, is currently awaiting trial on charges of child sex abuse that are tied to his work as a director on the set of the TV series The Cleaning Lady, which ran from 2022 to 2025. Gilbert has defended Busfield, who denies the allegations.

The public is just starting to understand the cost of becoming famous at an early age, wrote Even Stevens actor Christy Carlson Romano in an opinion piece for Elle magazine last week.

She also highlighted how much the job can affect a young actor's self confidence, writing, "Kid actors have something major in common: rejection. We’re rejected from auditions more times before we’re 10 than most people accrue in 10 lifetimes … All before our frontal lobes have fully formed. Is it any wonder so many of us struggle with addiction?"

Carlson Romano — who started working at 12 and was acting in three Disney Channel projects simultaneously by the time she was 18 in 2002 — compared early fame to Chronic Traumatic Encephalopathy, or CTE, a progressive degenerative brain disease linked to repeated hits to the head.

"We now have language for youth sports: protocols, helmets, parents worried about concussions. But we have almost no language for what happens when stress, scrutiny, rejection, adult pressure, and the collapse of privacy become the architecture of a childhood," she wrote.

A new reckoning

The world of children's television was recently the subject of a 2024 Investigation Discovery documentary series called Quiet on Set: The Dark Side of Kids TV.

The series focused on working conditions at Nickelodeon, which former child actors and employees have alleged included sexual abuse, underpayment and a hostile work environment rife with misogyny.

Now, in the wake of such allegations and the recent deaths, veteran actors are publicly discussing ways to take matters into their own hands.

Paquin addressed part of her Instagram post to other child actors, asking them to contact her.

Actor Anna Paquin, who won the best supporting actress Oscar when she was just 11 for her role in The Piano, wrote about how child actors are treated in Hollywood in an Aug. 21, 2026, post to her Instagram account. (Leon Bennett/Getty Images, Tim Clary/AFP/Getty Images)

"I believe you and will stand by your side. You aren't alone," she wrote. "Let's have each other's backs. It might make public disclosure less terrifying."

Gilbert took Paquin's show of support as a call for former child actors to band together, writing that it was clear that no one else would act on their behalf.

" Our union has really been unable to do anything substantive about this," she wrote. "Sure, there’s a young performers committee, but it is essentially toothless, political and tends to get short shrift because there are always bigger fish to fry. They have handbooks and orientations but no real functioning, well-funded, far-reaching support group."

Gilbert, who served as president of the Screen Actors Guild (SAG) from 2001 to 2005, suggested that she and other former child actors should start their own group and meet with the head of networks.

In a statement provided to CBC News, a spokesperson for SAG-AFTRA disputed Gilbert's claim that the union hadn't taken meaningful action.

"The contracts negotiated by SAG-AFTRA for minors include comprehensive protections for young performers. Additionally, the union often improves these provisions," the statement said. "Additionally, the union recognizes the important role that educators, like the Studio Teacher members of IATSE Local 884, play in protecting minor performers."

Raquel Lee, a former child actor who appeared in the Quiet on Set documentary, and has spoken about her experience as a young Black actor working on Nickelodeon's The Amanda Show in the early 2000s, also weighed in.

"The fight continues" she wrote on her Instagram stories Sunday, sharing a quote fro m former actor and MeToo campaginer Rose McGowan regarding Panetierre's death.

Lee is also coming forward with her own allegations of abuse.

According to Variety magazine, Lee filed a lawsuit against Disney last Friday, alleging a former employee of the company raped her when she was 14 and working on the film The Poof Point. Variety notes that the lawsuit alleges the man, who was involved in the filming of the movie, "groomed her, sexually harassed and assaulted her during filming."

Disney has not responded to a request from CBC News for comment on the matter.

On her Instagram stories, Lee shared a photo of her younger self, writing "I will always fight for her! I am who I am today because SHE SURVIVED!"

World.title: What we know about how the Canada-U.S. trade talks fell apart
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said one of the main reasons he walked away from a deal with the Trump administration is because Washington demanded terms that would "destroy" big Canadian industries including the auto, steel and aluminum sectors.

He made the comment while facing calls from the Conservatives to reveal the details of the proposed deal that fell apart late Friday night.

"We did make some progress in recent weeks," Carney said on Monday in Lévis, Que. "In the end, that momentum reversed and we could not accept what the U.S. had offered, nor could we give what they asked."

U.S. Vice-President JD Vance offered a different version of events, accusing Canada of putting forward "a bunch of unreasonable last-minute demands" and urging Carney to "stop taking advantage of America."

While the federal government won't publicly reveal the details of the negotiations, Ontario Premier Doug Ford, who has been briefed on the talks, called it a "bad deal" and said he's glad Carney didn't sign.

Flavio Volpe, a member of Canada's advisory committee on this file and president of the Automotive Parts Manufacturers' Association, said after negotiators agreed in spirit to a potential deal, it was up to dozens of Canadian and American officials to write up the exact wording of an agreement.

When that "text started to crystalize," Volpe said, it didn't match what was discussed.

Here's what CBC News has learned happened behind closed doors.

Pickup trucks left out

CBC News has reported that before the deal's deadline, one of Trump's top deputies — U.S. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick — expressed dissatisfaction with what had been negotiated and pushed for the U.S. to do better.

Volpe said Lutnick has taken a hard line when it comes to Trump's objective to drain Canada of its vehicle production.

Carney said trade talks broke down with the U.S. in part because American negotiators changed the terms in the hours before the deadline to exclude medium- and heavy-duty trucks from tariff relief. (Chris Young/The Canadian Press)

American negotiators had initially agreed to drop the headline tariff on Canadian autos from 25 to 15 per cent, Volpe said. A source said American auto content would be exempt, reducing that tariff rate by up to half. (The sector had also been pushing for an exemption for Canadian-made auto content, which the U.S. didn't agree to, a source said.)

Then right before the deadline, the U.S. revealed it planned to exclude medium- and heavy-duty trucks. That move left out North America's most lucrative vehicles: pickup trucks.

Ford's F-Series pickups and the General Motors Silverado are made at Ontario plants and roughly 20,000 workers would have been severely impacted, Volpe said.

"The tariff was going to be so high in those places to not make that product viable," Volpe told CBC's The Current on Monday.

Carney called that exclusion a "big change" to the terms.

Sovereignty threats

In the final hours of talks, the Americans also tried to restrict Canada's ability to strike trade deals with other countries, Carney said.

WATCH | Unifor president says Trump is attacking Canadian manufacturing: Trump is trying to ‘destroy the manufacturing base of Canada’: Unifor president | Duration 10:13 Amid the aftermath of last-minute trade talks breaking down, Unifor national president Lana Payne says the Trump administration is purposely targeting Canada’s manufacturing sector.

That move would have been a direct hit to the prime minister's strategy to become less reliant on the U.S. and diversify trade.

"So the idea that the United States would have a word to say in the sovereign decision of Canada to enter into a free trade agreement with another reliable trading partner, obviously wasn't something that we were prepared to consider," Canada-U.S. Trade Minister Dominic LeBlanc told CBC's Power and Politics on Monday.

WATCH | LeBlanc on trade talks: Canada won't 'rush back to Washington' unless there's a 'viable' deal: LeBlanc | Duration 17:38 What would it take to get back to trade talks? Power & Politics asks the person leading Canada's negotiations, Minister for Canada-U.S. Trade Dominic LeBlanc.

The U.S. also wanted Canada to apply sectoral tariffs, primarily on steel and aluminum, to its trading partners. Countries that have a free trade deal with Canada would face tariffs on imports above 2025 levels, a source said.

Carney said he was only prepared to align with the U.S. on sectoral tariffs if they benefited Canada.

"That's us deciding to do something that's in our joint interests as opposed to being told to do something or being restricted to doing something else," he said.

Steel, aluminum, lumber

In the end, the prime minister also said there "wasn't enough movement" on American tariff relief for steel, aluminum and derivative products.

Sources said the U.S. had planned to reduce its 50 per cent tariffs on Canadian steel and aluminum to 25 per cent. Derivative products would have been subject to tariff rate quotas, a source said.

WATCH | Ford says Carney walked away from a 'bad deal': Ford says he's glad Canada didn't sign 'bad deal' with U.S. | Duration 2:11 Ontario Premier Doug Ford said he heard feedback from the province's steel and auto sectors over the past few days that the U.S. government had put forth a bad trade deal and gave Prime Minister Mark Carney credit for standing up for Canada in a 'very complicated' situation.

Washington was also talking about dropping a 10 per cent Section 232 tariff on Canadian softwood lumber by Sept. 1, but existing countervailing and anti-dumping duties would remain, industry sources said.

Culture

Carney said the Americans also pushed against the Canadian requirements for bilingual product labelling.

U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer dismissed the labelling claim on CNBC, calling it a "funny, fake story."

Carney fired back on Monday saying it's a fact.

He called the labelling issue an American irritant and said in the final hours of negotiations, the Americans took issue with Canadian rules that ensure French-language content is easy to find on streaming platforms like Netflix.

LeBlanc said it was the "cumulative total of a series of things" that surfaced near the end of talks that made Carney decide the agreement in front of them wasn't in the best interest of Canada.

Concessions Canada was willing to make

If the U.S. had agreed to "substantially" lower the tariffs hitting Canadian industries hard, Carney said he was willing to:

Drop Canada's retaliatory tariffs on American steel, aluminum and autos.

Encourage provinces and territories to return American alcohol to the shelves.

Carney asked premiers to end procurement policies that exclude U.S. companies from bidding on projects as a retaliatory measure against American tariffs, Nova Scotia Premier Tim Houston said.

Ottawa was also prepared to adjust dairy import licenses, giving licenses directly to retailers, an industry source said. The move could have made it easier to sell U.S. milk and cheese in Canadian stores, helping the Americans fill their entire duty-free trade quota under CUSMA.

WATCH | Trump lashes out after Canada suspends talks: Trump slams Canada over failed trade deal, but Republicans split over tariffs | Duration 2:36 In his first response to the failed Canada-U.S. trade deal, President Donald Trump blamed Canada and accused it of wanting 'the benefits of being a State, without being one.' But some Republicans think hitting Canada with new tariffs is a mistake.

The prime minister was elected on a promise to stand up to U.S. President Donald Trump and has promised he wouldn't sign a bad deal.

If he hadn't walked away, it would have been up to Carney to sell it to Canadians at a time when polling shows there isn't a lot of support for concessions and key figures were warning against what was on the table.

Manitoba Premier Wab Kinew said he thought Canada could push for a better deal.

Former Trudeau-era deputy prime minister and finance minister Chrystia Freeland told Bloomberg News a "bad outcome" would be Canada accepting a deal with permanent sectoral tariffs.

Canada's former chief negotiator during Trump's first administration, Steve Verheul, also warned, sources said , that Canada would be giving up most of its leverage before even entering CUSMA talks.

WATCH | Manitoba premier wants Canada to fight: Canada 'should be prepared to duke it out for 2 years' with U.S.: Kinew | Duration 2:39 Premier Wab Kinew says Manitoba is '100 per cent behind' Prime Minister Mark Carney's direction to retaliate against the new U.S. 50 per cent tariffs on almost $30 billion of Canadian goods. He noted U.S. President Donald Trump has two years left in office, and then 'hopefully sanity will return to America.'

Asked about the criticism, LeBlanc said Carney has been clear that the American tariffs are a violation of the CUSMA agreement Trump signed himself. But he said it wasn't "realistic in those sectors to get to zero tariffs in the short term" because the U.S. is tariffing all of its trading partners.

Angus Reid Institute president Shachi Kurl said on Monday that her polling shows 76 per cent of Canadians say it was the right decision for Carney to walk away.

"Almost seven in 10 Canadians tell us the prime minister showed strength by making the decision that he did," Kurl told Power and Politics. "It's a pretty strong endorsement."

LeBlanc says he's not going to rush back to the table unless it's clear from the U.S. that there's an offer "that puts us in an economically viable position" when it comes to steel, aluminum, autos and forest products.

World.title: De la Espriella calls for “iron fist” against crime in Colombia
World.content:
Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella called on the security forces to impose the law “like a giant with an iron fist, the iron fist of the State.”

During a meeting with commanders of the security forces, De la Espriella stressed that security “is the cornerstone of our government and the most forceful government policy.”

The president urged the security forces to confront crime with an iron fist and stressed that “our soldiers and police officers have the full and unconditional support of this government. Never again will they be mistreated or forced to bow down to crime.”

Here we must act like a giant with an iron fist—the iron fist of the state. And that ability to convey a sense of unity is what has a psychological impact on crime and sends a clear message to citizens: we are here to protect you, to look out for you, but also to enforce the law. President Abelardo de la Espriella

De la Espriella called to erase the distinction between organized crime and illegal armed groups, and “treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups,” claiming they are interconnected.

We have to stop treating these criminals differently. We must treat them all under a single designation, which is that of terrorist groups, because the criminal pyramid we have in Colombia—whose base is drug trafficking, followed by illegal mining, extortion, and smuggling—is all perfectly interconnected. The foundation of all crime and the primary source of all forms of violence is drug trafficking. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“When it comes to fighting crime, there are no differences—neither in the state’s actions nor in its response and certainly not in the categorization” that allowed peace talks with groups like the FARC and ELN, according to the president.

“That is over in this administration. They are all terrorists, and we are going to treat them as such, no matter what happens,” said De la Espriella.

World.title: De la Espriella claims 123,700 barrels stolen monthly from Colombia’s state oil company
World.content:
Oil thieves from north Colombia would be stealing at least 123,700 barrel of gasoline, diesel and naphtha, a month, claimed President Abelardo de la Espriella.

According to De la Espriella, the theft of the refined oil products that wee imported or produced by state-owned oil company Ecopetrol “is utterly alarming, and demands an immediate and forceful response from the State.”

Every month, approximately 123,700 barrels of refined products—gasoline, diesel, and naphtha—imported or produced by Ecopetrol would be stolen. This would occur solely on a 14-inch pipeline that connects Pozos Colorados, in Santa Marta, to the interior of the country, and the losses are concentrated mainly in Cesar and Magdalena. President Abelardo de la Espriella

“We would be talking about more than 1.5 million barrels a year, with losses exceeding $500,000 million for Ecopetrol and, therefore, for the nation,” the president said in a post on social media platform X.

De la Espriella added that “these fuels are used as raw materials in the illicit processing of cocaine” by illegal armed groups that operate in the country’s periphery.

If we confirm that a large portion of this fuel is being used to power cocaine production facilities, then we are not only dealing with a massive theft from Ecopetrol: we are dealing with a criminal network that may be linking the theft of hydrocarbons to drug trafficking and the financing of armed terrorist organizations. President Abelardo de la Espriella

The president ordered a “joint operation” of the military, police, prosecution and administrative authorities “to comprehensively combat this criminal economy” led by Defense Minister Jorge Eduardo Mora.

“I want results and periodic report on progress,” said De la Espriella.

Organized crime and illegal armed groups have been involved in fuel theft for decades.

World.content:

World.title: Colombia expands disaster region in 2nd emergency decree
World.content:
Colombia’s government drastically expanded the region affected by the August 10 earthquake in a second decree declaring an economic emergency.

According to the decree, President Abelardo de la Espriella declared the emergency in 15 of the country’s 32 provinces “for a period of thirty (30) calendar days, in order to conjure the crisis and prevent the spread of the disaster’s effects.”

“The territorial scope includes all municipalities listed in UNGRD Situational Report No. 36 and any additional municipalities where direct damage from the August 10, 2026 earthquake is specifically demonstrated,” said the decree.

The emergency decree declared a State of Exception, which allows the government to “adopt, through legislative decrees, all additional necessary measures and budgetary/credit operations to address the crisis” in the emergency region.

According to the decree, the government is considering the following extraordinary measures to respond to the disaster that left more than $9.5 billion in damages.

Tax, credit, and budgetary flexibility to direct new resources to disaster recovery.

Expedited public credit operations bypassing lengthy CONPES/DNP approvals.

Use of the Royalty Savings and Stabilization Fund (FAE) resources as repayable loans.

Expanding the “Works for Taxes” (Obras por Impuestos) mechanism to affected municipalities.

Direct management and monetization of seized assets administered by SAE/FRISCO to fund emergency shelters and humanitarian relief.

Authorizing financial cooperatives to temporarily extend credit and savings services to non-members affected by the disaster.

Streamlining judicial operations, education delivery (remote/alternative spaces), school feeding programs (PAE), housing subsidies, telecommunications repairs, and labor support transfers.

Previously, De la Espriella announced a “Miracle Fund,” which would be used to channel donations from the private sector and international partners.

Since then, Colombia’s elite donated COP1.6 trillion ($526 million) of the $30 billion the government believes it needs for reconstruction.

World.title: Colombia’s government publishes “white paper” on corruption by Petro
World.content:
The government of Colombia’s President Abelardo de la Espriella gave Prosecutor General Luz Adriana Camargo a white paper with more than 80 complaints over alleged corruption by the previous government.

The 135-page “Book of Truth that was presented by De la Espriella, contained “the result of the work carried out under the coordination of Vice President José Manuel Restrepo during the transition weeks between the presidential election and August 7” when he took office.

De la Espriella suspended the transition process on July 7 after Petro said he refused to recognize the president as his legitimate successor.

Consequently, the book contains mainly political criticisms of the previous “regime” and no evidence of misdeeds that hadn’t been picked by the Comptroller General’s Office, which monitors public spending.

This white paper, my fellow Colombians, does not intend to replace, far less anticipate, judicial investigations or the outcome of actions taken by prosecutors, inspectors, and comptrollers. The book actually represents something simpler and, at the same time, more serious, monumental, and decisive: the fulfillment of my duty as Head of State. I am fulfilling the responsibility that falls upon me by gathering available information and not allowing the facts recorded here in the book I have just delivered to be buried by silence and impunity.
