The move comes amid concerns about the health and safety of the animals, which remain under the care of Mexico’s environmental authority following the closure of the dolphinarium in October last year after videos surfaced of the dolphins displaying extreme distress.

Profepa stated that the nine dolphins – two females and seven males – are in delicate clinical condition, meaning their transfer cannot be immediate and each animal will require an individual protocol.

Since May, Profepa has been working to medically stabilize the dolphins through veterinary checkups, laboratory tests and monitoring of their behavior, feeding and response to treatment, the agency told Mongabay.

However, activist groups in defense of animal rights, including Veeleaf and Tide Breakers, have shared images and videos criticizing the care of the nine dolphins that remain in captivity. Reportedly, the dolphins are in small pools where they can barely move, are fed smaller portions of food than required and spend all their time in the sun, with no shade.

The future of these dolphins is tied to a reform that sought to transform the operations of dolphinariums in Mexico.

In July 2025, the Mexican Senate unanimously approved a nationwide ban on dolphin and other marine mammal shows, as well as the breeding of marine mammals in captivity except for conservation purposes.

The new regulations mandate the transfer of cetaceans to marine pens, or fenced-off ocean enclosures that slowly reintroduce the dolphins to their natural habitat, and limit interactions with those already under human care, prohibiting practices that could compromise their well-being.

However, the regulations needed to establish the application criteria have not been published yet; hence, the nine dolphins remain in the same pools where they have spent a good part of their lives.

The organization Empty the Tanks is demanding that the dolphins be temporarily transferred to existing marine pools at the Dolphin Discovery facilities in Isla Mujeres and Chankanaab, Cozumel. “We are not asking that they be released into the ocean. We are asking for a responsible, feasible measure backed by scientific evidence: that they be allowed to live in a much more natural environment while receiving the care they need,” the organization said in a statement.

According to a statement by Profepa, “All the decisions that have been made aim to ensure the best possible well-being of the dolphins, to help them survive in the best way possible and to alleviate their suffering.”

“We know that moving them to a semi-open enclosure at sea would be an improvement, but first we must guarantee that this move does not cost them their lives,” the statement continues.

With reports from Infobae, Por Esto! and Reportur

World.title: Aura farming battles make their debut in Mexico
World.content:
With a nod to the “You got served” hip-hop dance battle craze of two decades ago, kids and young adults in Mexico have begun to stage “aura farming” battles in public squares across the country.

What the heck is aura farming, you ask? Fair question …

Aura farming is a viral internet slang trend that describes doing intentional, effortless things to look confident or charismatic. Gen Alpha and Gen Z use the term to describe doing something to improve your “vibe,” your style or your perceived social status, without seeming like you’re trying too hard.

It even warrants a definition in Merriam-Webster: “the act of doing something to look cool, impressive, stylish, etc., especially — and importantly — without trying too hard.”

The concept grew on TikTok and Instagram, combining the video game concept of “farming” (carrying out repetitive actions for points), before dancing was attached to it, eventually evolving into physical “aura battles” in parks and streets across Latin America.

In Mexico City, three notorious aura farming battles took place last week: on Friday at the esplanade of the Palace of Fine Arts in Mexico City; on Saturday at the Monument to the Revolution; and on Sunday in the Condesa neighborhood (where there was even a prize of 3,000 pesos, or US $177).

The craze has reached beyond the capital, too.

Aura battles have recently been staged in Juárez Park in Xalapa, the capital of Veracruz, and children as young as six years old participated in a competition in Torreón, Coahuila.

Compiten en Concurso para "Farmear Aura" en Veracruz

Watch this video on YouTube

The “battles” attract massive crowds who watch participants compete symbolically with poses, dances, gestures and meme references to demonstrate who has more “aura.”

A winner is determined by crowd reaction (the volume of cheers, applause, laughter) and by the general impact made during the face-off. Essentially, the social presence displayed is “scored” like an imaginary video game.

Unfortunately, the events also have their detractors. The municipal council of Ignacio de la Llave, Veracruz, officially prohibited aura battles in public parks, arguing that it was not due to the theme or content of the competition, but rather “a strict matter of administrative procedures and regulations for public spaces.”

CNN traces the origin of aura farming to 2024 and said it gained international attention last year through viral videos of 11-year-old Indonesian Rayyan Arkan Dikha dancing at the front of a boat in a traditional rowing competition. Social media users commented on the high levels of “aura” the boy possessed and it took off from there.

The trend has become particularly popular in Latin America: A “championship” was staged at the University of Costa Rica in San Juan on Aug. 18 and several tournaments were organized in São Paulo, Brazil, this summer.

With reports from CNN, LatinUS, Infobae and Telediario

World.title: Nine Painters From One Rio Studio Show for Free
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Rio de Janeiro · Art

Key Facts — On show Nine painters from the Ateliê Oruniyá studio in Tijuca are showing drawings and oil paintings at the Centro Cultural dos Correios in central Rio.

— Free entry The show runs to 10 October, Tuesday to Saturday from noon to 7pm. There are ramps and a lift.

— Seven years The group grew out of weekly Monday evenings at the studio. Students followed their life-drawing teacher there from the federal university in 2017, according to the exhibition’s organisers.

— The market Curator Ayla de Oliveira says the group feared there was no market for figurative painting, then found buyers who wanted exactly that.

— Curator and artist Ayla de Oliveira chose the show and exhibits in it. That is ordinary practice for a collective, and worth saying out loud.

— The venue Correios halted its Rio exhibition programme in June, after a first-quarter loss of R$3.1 billion and a full-year 2025 loss of R$8.5 billion, then restarted it without announcement.

A studio in Tijuca, seven years of Monday evenings, and a bet that Brazilian collectors would buy figurative painting after all.

Nine Painters From One Rio Studio Show for Free. (Photo internet reproduction)

01 It started with a life-drawing class

In 2017, the exhibition’s organisers say, a group of students at the Escola de Belas Artes, the fine arts school of Rio’s federal university, were taking a class in drawing from a live model. Their teacher was the painter Nelson Macedo, described in the exhibition material as a life-drawing teacher at the school.

Some of them started going to his studio in Tijuca, a residential district in Rio’s north, where another painter, Ana Moura, also taught. What began as extra practice turned into a standing appointment.

From 2017 they met there on Monday evenings, for about seven years by the organisers’ count. They drew and painted, and they talked about film, poetry, folk art and the history of their own trade.

The studio is called Ateliê Oruniyá. Nine of the painters who passed through it are now hanging work together in a public exhibition hall in central Rio.

02 The part that concerns anyone who buys art

The show’s curator, Ayla de Oliveira, is one of the nine. She is a painter born in 1997, represented by the Mitre Galeria in Belo Horizonte, and she has shown at this same venue before.

Her account of the group’s early years is the most useful thing in the exhibition material. “There was a certain fear that there would be no space in the market for our work, because it was more figurative painting,” she says.

“When I entered the art market, I began to see, and to show the others, that there were indeed people interested in getting to know painting, and that there was space for this line of enquiry.”

Take that as one painter’s memory rather than as market history, because the record is less dramatic than the fear. The art historian Emerson Dionísio told Correio Braziliense in 2021 that figurative painting “never stopped existing” and, though it met discrimination in many markets, “never stopped selling and winning over the public.”

The one hard number available is older than it looks. The Brazilian art market grew 21% in 2023 against 2022, according to the country’s contemporary art association, and no comparable reading has been published since.

For a collector in Rio the practical reading is this. A studio group with no gallery machinery behind it can put nine figurative painters into a large public exhibition hall, which is a cheaper route to visibility than a commercial gallery.

03 What is on the walls

Drawings and oil paintings, figurative throughout. The subjects are domestic and Brazilian rather than grand.

Ayla de Oliveira shows Oferenda para Oxum na cachoeirinha, an offering to Oxum — the Yoruba orixá of rivers and fresh water, brought to Brazil by enslaved West Africans and venerated here in Candomblé and, later, in Umbanda — at a small waterfall. Maria Victória Santos shows Feira, a street market.

Nelson Macedo, the teacher the whole thing grew from, shows Lavadeira, a washerwoman. The full list of the nine painters is on the Correios cultural centre’s own listing.

The title, Inefável Presença, points at what a picture holds that a caption cannot. It translates roughly as “ineffable presence”.

04 The building nearly went dark this year

There is a second story here that the exhibition’s publicity does not mention, and it matters more to this newspaper’s readers than the paintings do.

In late June, Correios — the Brazilian post office — suspended its entire forward exhibition calendar in Rio. Artists, curators and production teams were notified the previous week; there was no public announcement.

Correios gave the reason as resource optimisation. The timing followed a first-quarter loss of R$3.1 billion, about US$600 million, which was 82% worse than the same quarter of 2025.

The company closed 2025 with a full-year loss of R$8.5 billion and negative net equity. Shows already installed were allowed to run to 4 July; after that, nothing, with no date given for a restart.

Separately, the government auctioned the old Correios headquarters at Rua Primeiro de Março 64 on 30 July, opening at R$47.8 million. That is a different building from the cultural centre, which stands around the corner and was not part of the sale.

No public statement reversing the suspension has appeared. What has appeared is programming: six exhibitions now run at the Rio centre through August and October, and three of them, including this one, opened together in the same week.

So the calendar is running again. A visitor should still treat the opening hours as worth a telephone call, because a venue that cancelled a season by internal memo can do it again the same way.

05 Worth the trip?

Yes, with one adjustment. Go on a weekday afternoon, because the centre closes Sunday and Monday, and combine it.

This is one of three shows that opened together that week, and one of six running now. The building itself, an eclectic 1922 building on Rua Visconde de Itaboraí, is worth the walk from Praça XV on its own.

Service Exhibition Inefável Presença — nine painters of the Ateliê Oruniyá, curated by Ayla de Oliveira Venue Centro Cultural dos Correios, Rua Visconde de Itaboraí 20, Centro, Rio de Janeiro Runs to 10 October 2026. The venue lists public visiting from 20 August; the press release gives 19 August as the opening Hours Tuesday to Saturday, 12pm to 7pm. Closed Sunday and Monday Entry Free, no age restriction Access Ramps and a lift, per the exhibition press material. Telephone to confirm if step-free access decides the trip Also on Two further shows opened the same evening, Matéria Familiar and Reencantar a Terra

Frequently Asked Questions

How much does it cost?

Nothing. Entry to the Centro Cultural dos Correios is free and there is no age restriction.

When is it open?

Tuesday to Saturday, noon to 7pm, until 10 October 2026. It is closed on Sundays and Mondays, so do not plan a weekend afternoon around it.

Is the work for sale?

The Correios cultural centre is a public exhibition space rather than a commercial gallery, and no prices have been published. Ask at the desk if you want to buy.

What does the title mean?

Inefável Presença translates roughly as “ineffable presence”. The word inefável describes something that cannot be put fully into words.

Can I get in with a wheelchair?

The press material lists ramps and a lift, and the venue describes itself as adapted for wheelchair users. Telephone ahead if step-free access decides your trip.

World.title: Free Three-Day Food Festival Opens on Rio’s Lagoa
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

Rio de Janeiro · Culture

Key Facts — Three days The fourth Festival Harmonia runs Friday 28 to Sunday 30 August at Parque das Figueiras, on the Lagoa Rodrigo de Freitas.

— Free entry Nobody pays at the gate, though food at the gastronomic islands is sold. The organisers had still not published daily hours, dish prices or any booking process for the cooking classes on Monday.

— Toquinho The bossa nova songwriter plays on Friday with Camilla Faustino. Roberta Sá closes the festival on Sunday.

— Six biomes The kitchen programme is built around Brazil’s six great landscapes rather than around its states.

— Public money The Ministry of Culture presents the festival and Petrobras pays for it through the Programa Petrobras Cultural.

— Getting there Parque das Figueiras is at Avenida Borges de Medeiros 1426, about ten minutes on foot from Jardim de Alah metro station on Line 4.

Three days of free-entry food and music on the Lagoa, organised around Brazil’s six great landscapes — and one awkward gap in what the organisers have told anyone.

Free Three-Day Food Festival Opens on Rio’s Lagoa. (Photo internet reproduction)

01 Three days, free to enter, on the lake

The fourth Festival Harmonia brings fifteen chefs and seven music acts to the edge of the Lagoa from Friday, and it costs nothing to walk in.

The draw depends on who you are. For most foreign residents it is Toquinho, the guitarist and songwriter who was Vinícius de Moraes’s writing partner for a decade, and who plays free on Friday evening with Camilla Faustino.

For anyone who watches Brazilian television it is Erick Jacquin, the French chef from MasterChef Brasil, who is on the teaching roster. The organisers have not said which day he cooks.

02 What there actually is to do

The festival has four parts. Cooking classes with named chefs, tasting sessions, a set of ilhas gastronômicas where five cooks serve dishes made for the weekend, and a small producers’ market.

Entry is free but the plates are not. At the 2024 edition dishes on the islands ran from R$10 to R$48, about US$2 to US$9, and no 2026 prices have been published.

Around that sit music, art and workshops for children. Rafael Sperduto opens on Friday before Toquinho; Leoni and the Orquestra Petrobras Sinfônica take Saturday; Roberta Sá and Serjão Loroza close on Sunday, with DJ Jamal playing both weekend days.

The organisers expect about 25,000 people across the three days. That is a two-thirds jump on the 15,000 they forecast for the 2024 edition, so arrive early if you want to stand near a stage.

03 Sorted by biome, not by state

Brazilian food festivals normally sort themselves by state. Bahia does its thing, Minas does its thing, Rio Grande do Sul brings the meat.

This one sorts by biome instead: Amazônia, Caatinga, Cerrado, Mata Atlântica, Pampa and Pantanal. Six landscapes, not twenty-six states.

It is a small change with a real consequence. Cooking the Caatinga, the semi-arid scrubland of the northeast, forces a menu around what survives drought, which is a different conversation from cooking the cuisine of Ceará.

Whether the kitchens deliver on that idea is the thing worth going to find out. It is also the only part of this festival that is not simply a free concert with food stalls.

04 Who is paying, and why that is worth a line

The billing on the festival’s own site reads “Ministério da Cultura e Petrobras apresentam.” The Ministry of Culture is the presenting body, under Brazil’s cultural incentive rules, and Petrobras is the sponsor.

Programa Petrobras Cultural is the state-controlled oil company’s cultural arm. The 2024 edition of this festival was sponsored under Brazil’s cultural incentive law; the route used for 2026 has not been published.

Separately, Petrobras opened a R$270 million cultural funding round in July, about US$52 million and the largest in its history. Those projects only start in May 2027, so that money is not what is paying for this weekend.

So a free cultural weekend on the Lagoa is paid for by an oil producer the federal government controls. That is not a scandal and it is not a secret, but a reader standing in front of a free stage is entitled to know whose money built it.

Production is by Farm House, the Rio agency that also produced the 2024 edition.

05 What the organisers have not told anyone

This is where the preview stops being useful and starts being honest. Three of the four things a visitor needs are missing from every published source.

Opening hours. The festival website’s programme section says only “Novidades em breve” — news soon. No 2026 hours appear on the site, in the press material, or in the two Brazilian write-ups that exist.

The cooking classes. Nobody has published whether they cost anything, whether you must register, or how many places there are. For a festival whose main selling point is eleven named teaching chefs, that is a strange gap three days out.

Parking. No guidance at all, for an event expecting 25,000 people beside a lake with limited kerb space. Take the metro to Jardim de Alah and walk the ten minutes.

The festival’s Instagram, @umfestivalemharmonia, is the likeliest place for a late schedule. Check it on Thursday before you commit an afternoon.

Service Dates Friday 28 – Sunday 30 August 2026 Hours Not published by the organisers as of 25 August Venue Parque das Figueiras, Avenida Borges de Medeiros 1426, Lagoa, Rio de Janeiro Metro Jardim de Alah (Line 4), about a 10-minute walk Entry Free. Food at the gastronomic islands is sold separately; 2026 prices not published Friday Rafael Sperduto; Toquinho with Camilla Faustino Saturday Orquestra Petrobras Sinfônica; Leoni; DJ Jamal Sunday Roberta Sá; Serjão Loroza; DJ Jamal Access Ramps, accessible toilets, a platform for wheelchair users, Libras interpretation and audio description Online umfestivalemharmonia.com.br · Instagram @umfestivalemharmonia · [email protected]

Frequently Asked Questions

Do I need a ticket?

No. Entry to Festival Harmonia is free and there is no ticketing platform for the festival itself.

Is the food free as well?

No. Entry is free, but dishes at the gastronomic islands are sold. The 2024 edition charged between R$10 and R$48 a dish, roughly US$2 to US$9. Prices for 2026 have not been published.

Are the cooking classes free too?

That has not been published. The organisers named eleven teaching chefs but said nothing about cost, booking or how many places each class has. Ask on the festival’s Instagram before you build a day around one.

What time does it open?

The organisers had not published daily hours by Monday 25 August. The 2024 edition opened at 3pm on the Friday and noon at the weekend, but that was a different year and should not be relied on.

Which day does Toquinho play?

Friday 28 August, joined by Camilla Faustino. The start time has not been published.

Where exactly is Parque das Figueiras?

On the western side of the Lagoa, at Avenida Borges de Medeiros 1426, next to Parque dos Patins. The nearest metro is Jardim de Alah on Line 4. It is not the Cantagalo side of the lake.

Brazil · MINING

Key Facts — What happened USA Rare Earth agreed in April 2026 to buy Brazilian miner Serra Verde for about US$2.8 billion.

— How big Serra Verde operates Brazil’s only commercial rare earths mine, producing four key magnetic elements.

— Who pays The U.S. Department of War increased its backing by US$250 million to support the acquisition financing.

— The catch The deal still requires approval at a shareholder meeting on 28 August 2026.

— What comes next Closing is expected promptly after the shareholder vote, likely within this week.

— Broader context Vale is studying entry into lithium and rare earths, a minister said.

A US$2.8 billion deal could reshape Brazil rare earths supply, with closing expected within days.

USA Rare Earth, a U.S. company, plans to acquire Brazilian miner Serra Verde for about US$2.8 billion. The deal, backed by additional U.S. government funding, is expected to close within days, according to a Brazilian financial newspaper on 24 August 2026.

Rare-earth minerals. The US closed its financing deal for Brazil’s Serra Verde mine. (illustrative)

The Deal’s Core Structure

USA Rare Earth, listed on Nasdaq, signed a definitive agreement in April 2026 to buy 100% of Serra Verde Group. The implied equity value is about US$2.8 billion, making it a significant transaction for Brazil rare earths.

Serra Verde owns the Pela Ema ionic-clay rare earth mine and processing plant in Goiás state. This operation is currently the only rare earth mine in commercial operation in Brazil.

The mine produces mixed rare earth carbonate and all four magnetic rare earths: neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium. These elements are critical for electric vehicle motors and wind turbines.

A Brazilian financial daily reported on 24 August 2026 that USA Rare Earth completed its capitalization. The newspaper said the acquisition is expected to be finalized this week, with a special meeting set for Friday, 28 August.

Financing and U.S. Government Support

USA Rare Earth secured US$1.55 billion in financing to complete the Brazil rare earths acquisition. The package includes U.S. Department of War backing, which was increased by US$250 million, Valor reported on 24 August.

The U.S. government backing supports a special-purpose vehicle that will acquire Serra Verde’s production. This move is explicitly tied to securing non-Chinese supply of magnetic rare earths.

A 15-year offtake agreement already commits 100% of Serra Verde’s Phase 1 magnetic rare earth output to a special-purpose vehicle capitalized by U.S. government entities and private investors.

The U.S. market report on the same day confirmed the upsized financing package. It noted that USA Rare Earth expects to close the deal promptly after the August 28 shareholder meeting.

Strategic Importance of Brazil Rare Earths

Brazil holds the world’s second-largest reserves of rare earths, a fact highlighted by a special feature on 19 August 2026. This endowment has attracted significant foreign investment in recent years.

The country’s rare earths sector is small but geopolitically important, as nations seek alternatives to Chinese supply. Serra Verde’s production targets this exact strategic demand.

The acquisition represents a major vote of confidence in Brazil’s mining potential. It also positions Brazil as a key player in the global rare earths supply chain.

Brazil rare earths are not just about mining; they involve processing and refining capabilities. The Pela Ema plant is a rare example of fully integrated production in the Western Hemisphere.

Vale’s Potential Entry into Rare Earths

Brazil’s mines minister said he is absolutely certain Vale will look at rare earths. This statement aligns with contemporaneous reporting on the mining giant’s strategic review.

Vale is publicly studying entry into lithium and rare earths, with its CEO emphasizing the market’s importance. The company is evaluating opportunities in these critical minerals.

Separate coverage notes Vale is seeking exploration permits for rare-earth-bearing minerals in Espírito Santo. These minerals include monazite and cerium,.

Vale is studying lithium and rare earth exploration options, Brazilian finance media report.

Timeline and Regulatory Approvals

The April 2026 announcement said the deal was expected to close in Q3 2026, subject to regulatory approvals. As of 20 August, closing had not yet been publicly confirmed.

An August 21 policy analysis noted that USA Rare Earth anticipated completion by the end of August 2026. This timeline has held, with the shareholder meeting now scheduled for 28 August.

The Brazilian financial newspaper reported on 24 August that USA Rare Earth expects the acquisition to be finalized this week. This rapid timeline suggests that regulatory hurdles have been cleared.

The special shareholder meeting on Friday, 28 August, is the final internal step. After that vote, the deal can close promptly, according to U.S. market reports.

Market Reaction and Industry Impact

The deal’s announcement has drawn attention across the mining and metals industry. Analysts view this as a landmark transaction for Brazil rare earths.

The US$2.8 billion price tag reflects the strategic premium on rare earth assets outside China. Investors are betting on sustained demand for magnetic materials.

Industry observers see this as a catalyst for further investment in Brazil’s critical minerals sector. The deal could unlock development of other rare earth projects in the country.

The involvement of the U.S. government adds a geopolitical layer to the transaction. This marks one of the largest U.S. investments in Brazil’s mining sector in recent years.

Serra Verde’s Unique Position

Serra Verde is described as the only rare-earth mine currently in commercial operation in Brazil. This unique position gives it strategic importance in the global supply chain.

The Pela Ema mine uses ionic-clay technology, which is cost-effective and environmentally less damaging than hard-rock mining. This process allows for efficient extraction of heavy and light rare earths.

The plant produces all four magnetic rare earths needed for permanent magnets in clean energy technologies. This includes neodymium, praseodymium, dysprosium, and terbium.

Serra Verde’s output has been vital for companies seeking non-Chinese sources of these critical elements. The acquisition by USA Rare Earth ensures long-term offtake for U.S. industries.

Looking Ahead After Closing

Once the deal closes, USA Rare Earth will control Brazil’s only operating rare earths mine. This gives the U.S. company a direct foothold in South American supply.

The U.S. government’s offtake agreement ensures a stable market for Serra Verde’s production over five years. This guarantees revenue and supports further investment in capacity.

For Brazil, the deal strengthens its position as a key supplier of critical minerals to the West. It also raises questions about the country’s own industrial policy for rare earths.

The next steps involve integrating Serra Verde into USA Rare Earth’s broader operations. Investors will watch for any further developments in this fast-moving Brazil rare earths story.

Frequently Asked Questions

The price is separate from U.S. government financing support, which includes a US$250 million increase in Department of War backing. Who is selling the Brazilian rare earths mine? The seller is Serra Verde Group, owner of the Pela Ema mine in Goiás, Brazil. This is the only rare earths mine in commercial operation in Brazil currently. When will the deal close? The deal is expected to close within days, likely after a shareholder meeting on 28 August 2026. USA Rare Earth completed its capitalization on 24 August. Why is the U.S. government involved in this deal? The U.S. Department of War increased its backing by US$250 million. This supports securing non-Chinese supply of magnetic rare earths. Is Vale getting involved in rare earths? Brazil’s mines minister said he is absolutely certain Vale will look at rare earths. Vale is studying lithium and rare earths, seeking exploration permits in Espírito Santo.

World.title: Brazil’s BRB shareholders authorize lawsuits over Banco Master losses
World.content:

Brazil · BANKING

Key Facts — What happened Shareholders authorized BRB to pursue civil lawsuits against ex-managers for losses from Master and Reag deals.

— How big The approval came from a virtual meeting with 7,495 shareholders voting in favor and one abstention.

— The catch The vote only grants permission; it names no one as guilty and files no lawsuit.

— Who’s cited Former BRB president Paulo Henrique Costa appears already arrested in the probe.

— What next Federal police asked for 60 more days, hinting more BRB directors face scrutiny.

— Background Banco Master moved R$1.6 billion (US$310.6 million) through Reag-linked funds, some allegedly non-paying.

The bank’s investors cleared a legal path, but no one is accused yet.

BRB (Banco de Brasília) shareholders authorized the bank to sue former administrators over losses tied to the Banco Master and Reag Investimentos cases on 24 August 2026. The vote happened in an extraordinary general meeting, but it does not itself file a lawsuit or assign blame.

Brazil’s BRB shareholders authorize lawsuits over Banco Master losses. (Photo internet reproduction)

The Vote and Its Meaning

BRB shareholders approved authorizing the bank to sue former administrators over losses in the Banco Master and Reag Investimentos cases on 24 August 2026. The decision came during an extraordinary general meeting, known as an AGE, held virtually, as Sou Brasília reported.

The proposal passed by majority, with 7,495 shareholders voting in favor and only one abstention. This approval does not file any lawsuit; it simply gives the bank the corporate authorization required to pursue civil-liability actions under Brazilian company law.

BRB stressed that the vote does not pre-assign blame to any specific individuals. The authorization is meant to target ex-managers who are identified as responsible for the losses, according to O Globo’s 24 August report.

The meeting’s outcome is a procedural step, not a verdict. It clears the way for the bank’s leadership to decide whether to initiate legal proceedings against named former officials.

Who Are the Former Administrators

The reports mention two former BRB executives by name in connection with the case. Paulo Henrique Costa, a former BRB president, was already arrested in the investigation, according to G1 and O Globo.

Dario Oswaldo Garcia Júnior, cited by Sou Brasília, is a former executive financial and control director among the ex-managers mentioned. However, the shareholder vote itself does not name these individuals or declare them responsible.

The authorization broadly covers former administrators identified as responsible for losses in operations related to Master and Reag. The exact scope of who might be sued remains undefined until the bank decides on specific actions.

BRB has emphasized that the approval is not an accusation. The bank’s legal team will now evaluate evidence and determine which individuals, if any, face civil lawsuits.

The Banco Master and Reag Connection

Banco Master moved R$ 1.6 billion (US$ 310.6 million) through funds linked to Reag Investimentos, according to UOL’s 26 July 2026 report. Some of these transactions were allegedly non-paying or potentially fictitious, per the liquidator and federal authorities.

This flow of funds sits at the heart of the losses BRB shareholders now want to pursue. The case is tied to the broader Operação Compliance Zero investigation, which looks into corruption schemes involving Master-linked funds.

O Globo reported on 21 August that the federal police asked the Supreme Federal Court for 60 more days to investigate. The police said they found suspicions involving more BRB directors in the inquiry.

The Master/Reag ecosystem involved complex financial maneuvers that may have harmed BRB. Shareholders are seeking accountability for those who oversaw these transactions during their tenure.

What the Approval Allows BRB to Do

The approval authorizes BRB to file civil-liability lawsuits against former administrators under Brazilian company law. It does not automatically start litigation, nor does it guarantee any lawsuit will be filed.

BRB’s management now has the corporate mandate to pursue legal action if they see fit. This could include seeking compensation for the losses linked to the Banco Master and Reag cases.

The vote also signals shareholder support for holding former leaders accountable. It reflects growing pressure on the bank to recover funds and address the fallout from the investigation.

Legal experts say such authorizations are common steps before complex corporate lawsuits. They allow the bank to act without seeking fresh shareholder approval for each legal move.

The Broader Investigation

Operação Compliance Zero is a federal police investigation into corruption schemes involving Master funds, as reported by O Tempo on 6 August. The probe has already led to arrests and has widened to include former politicians and allies.

Federal police asked for an extension of the investigation by 60 days, indicating ongoing work. The Supreme Federal Court, or STF, must decide whether to grant this extension.

The investigation has found suspicions involving more BRB directors, according to O Globo’s 21 August report. This suggests the bank’s exposure to the Master affair may be broader than initially thought.

As the probe continues, more details may emerge about the extent of the losses. Shareholders are watching closely, as the outcome could affect the bank’s finances and reputation.

Financial Impact and Losses

The exact financial losses from the Banco Master and Reag cases have not been fully disclosed. However, the R$ 1.6 billion (US$ 310.6 million) moved through Reag funds gives a sense of scale.

BRB shareholders are seeking to recover losses through civil lawsuits against former managers. The bank has not published a specific figure for the damages it claims.

The vote to sue suggests the bank believes it has a credible case for financial harm. Legal action could aim to claw back funds lost in the allegedly fictitious transactions.

Investors and regulators alike are monitoring how BRB calculates its losses. The outcome of any lawsuit could set a precedent for similar cases in Brazil’s banking sector.

Reactions and Next Steps

The shareholder approval has been reported by O Globo and Sou Brasília on 24 August 2026. The bank has not issued a public statement beyond what was reported.

BRB now decides whether to file lawsuits against the named former administrators. This decision will likely come after legal review and further investigation.

The federal police’s request for more time could bring new evidence to light. If the STF grants the extension, the inquiry will continue for at least another 60 days.

For now, the focus remains on the bank’s internal legal preparations. Shareholders and the public await the next move in this unfolding case.

What This Means for Brazil’s Banking Sector

The BRB Banco Master case highlights risks in Brazil’s financial system, especially with fund-linked transactions. It shows how corporate governance failures can lead to significant losses.

Shareholder activism, as seen in the vote, may become more common in response to such scandals. Banks may face increased scrutiny from investors and regulators.

The case also underscores the role of civil lawsuits in deterring misconduct. If BRB succeeds, it could encourage other banks to pursue former managers for similar issues.

Brazil’s legal framework allows for such shareholder authorizations, which balance accountability and due process. The BRB Banco Master affair will be watched as a potential benchmark for future cases.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did BRB shareholders approve on 24 August 2026? They authorized BRB to sue former administrators over losses tied to Banco Master and Reag Investimentos. The vote does not file a lawsuit or assign blame. Who are the former BRB administrators mentioned in the investigation? Paulo Henrique Costa, a former BRB president, has been arrested, and Dario Oswaldo Garcia Júnior, a former finance director, is cited. The shareholder vote itself did not name them as guilty. How much money moved through Banco Master and Reag? UOL reported R$ 1.6 billion (US$ 310.6 million) moved through Reag-linked funds, some allegedly fictitious or non-paying. The exact losses to BRB have not been published. Does the approval mean lawsuits are already filed? No, it only gives BRB corporate authorization to sue. The bank must still decide to file civil actions and against whom. What is Operação Compliance Zero? It’s a federal police investigation into corruption schemes involving Master funds. The probe led to arrests and a request for 60 more days, with suspicions involving more BRB directors.

Brazil · BANKING

Key Facts — What happened Febraban president Isaac Sidney said banks exaggerated credit supply, contributing to household over-indebtedness.

— How big Household debt has risen alongside credit expansion, with unsecured credit quality deteriorating, Reuters reported on 24 August 2026.

— The catch Central bank chief Galípolo says credit growth naturally raises indebtedness, not just high interest rates.

— Who pays Brazilian households bear the burden through higher delinquency and costly unsecured lending.

— What comes next The central bank may consider prudential measures to address the type of credit being extended.

Sector admits exaggerating credit supply as household indebtedness and delinquency climb.

Brazil’s banking federation Febraban acknowledged that banks overdid credit offers and owe a mea culpa. Central bank chief Gabriel Galípolo argued that more credit, not interest rates alone, explains rising household indebtedness.

Brazil Banks Admit Credit Overreach, Owe Mea Culpa. (Photo internet reproduction)

Febraban’s mea culpa on credit supply

Febraban, Brazil’s banking federation, admitted on 24 August 2026 that banks overdid credit offers. Isaac Sidney, its president, said the sector needed to acknowledge exaggerated credit supply contributed to household over-indebtedness.

He noted that high interest rates for a prolonged period were another factor. His comments came as the industry gathered for the Febraban Tech event, where central bank chief Gabriel Galípolo also spoke, a major industry gathering.

Sidney’s statement signals a shift from previous positions that emphasized external factors. The sector now accepts part of the blame for rising delinquency rates.

This mea culpa is rare and significant for Brazil’s banking industry. It reflects growing pressure on lenders as household debt strains the economy.

Galípolo’s argument on credit and debt

Central bank chief Gabriel Galípolo argued that more credit, not interest rates alone, explains rising indebtedness. He spoke at the Febraban Tech event on Monday, 24 August 2026.

Galípolo said it is normal for indebtedness to rise when credit expands. He warned against celebrating credit growth while complaining that debt rose afterward.

His remarks challenge the narrative that high interest rates are the main culprit. He emphasized that credit volume and type matter more.

The central bank chief’s perspective aligns with data showing broader household leverage increased. He stressed the need to focus on the kind of credit being offered.

Concern over unsecured lending

Galípolo highlighted concern about costly, unsecured lending in Brazil. He said the debt gauge excluding mortgage financing had risen sharply.

This reinforces the central bank’s concern about the type of credit, not just its volume. Unsecured loans carry higher risk for borrowers and lenders alike.

Data from the central bank shows unsecured credit quality has deteriorated. This trend worries policymakers who fear a spike in defaults.

The focus on credit type suggests the central bank may target specific lending products. Galípolo’s comments signal a shift in regulatory attention.

Rising household debt in Brazil

Reuters reported on 24 August 2026 that household debt has been rising alongside credit expansion. Central bank data shows broader household leverage has increased recently.

This debt growth has been accompanied by deteriorating unsecured credit quality. The trend affects millions of Brazilian households.

High interest rates, though prolonged, are not the sole driver per Galípolo. Credit supply has expanded rapidly, pushing debt levels up.

The combination of more credit and economic pressure has left many families struggling. Delinquency rates have climbed, adding to systemic concerns.

Delinquency trends and bank response

Higher delinquency rates have prompted banks to reconsider their lending strategies. The admission reflects this growing awareness among lenders.

Banks now face a delicate balance between maintaining credit access and managing risk. The mea culpa suggests a willingness to tighten standards.

Delinquency has hit record levels in recent months, pressuring bank profits. Lenders are becoming more cautious in their credit offers.

This response may slow credit growth in coming months. The industry is recalibrating after a period of aggressive expansion.

Central bank’s policy outlook

Galípolo’s comments come as the central bank considers prudential measures on household debt. These could include stricter rules for unsecured lending.

The bank has already lowered interest rates to 14 percent in August 2026. But credit growth continues to pose challenges for inflation control.

Policymakers are studying measures to address the rise in household debt. The focus is on preventing financial instability while supporting growth.

Galípolo’s argument suggests rates alone won’t solve the debt problem. Targeted regulation may be needed to curb risky lending.

Economic implications for Brazil

Rising household debt has broader implications for Brazil’s economy. It affects consumer spending and financial stability.

The central bank’s concern about credit quality signals potential headwinds for growth. Lenders tightening standards could reduce consumption.

Febraban’s admission may lead to more responsible lending practices. This could help stabilize household finances over time.

However, the transition may be painful for borrowers used to easy credit. Brazil faces a period of adjustment as debt levels normalize.

What comes next for credit markets

Brazil’s credit markets are likely to see tighter conditions ahead. Banks may reduce offers of unsecured, high-cost loans.

The central bank could implement new prudential measures. These would aim to prevent further deterioration in credit quality.

The sector’s mea culpa sets the stage for industry-wide changes. Lenders will likely cooperate with regulators to address risks.

The outcome remains uncertain, but the conversation has changed. Credit growth is now seen as a risk to manage, not just a goal.

Central bank data shows broader leverage increased and unsecured credit quality deteriorated. What might happen next in Brazil’s credit market? World.content:

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Guyana · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened ExxonMobil Guyana used AI to identify four new exploration opportunities in the Stabroek Block.

— How big Sixty pre-service secondary school educators will start math and science training in August 2026.

— The catch The company has not confirmed if the four opportunities contain commercial hydrocarbons or disclosed locations.

— Who pays The teacher training is part of the company’s US$100 million, 10-year STEM Initiative.

— What comes next The two-year STELLAR program runs through the Cyril Potter College of Education, starting August 2026.

— When The AI findings were reported August 13; the teacher launch was August 24, 2026.

Two separate initiatives from the oil major: AI-powered exploration and STEM teacher training.

ExxonMobil Guyana made two separate announcements in August 2026. One involves AI identifying new oil opportunities, the other trains 60 teachers in STEM.

ExxonMobil is bringing AI tools to Guyanese classrooms as its offshore output grows. (illustrative)

AI finds new exploration opportunities

On August 13, 2026, World Oil reported that ExxonMobil Guyana used artificial intelligence to find four new exploration opportunities. The AI reviewed historical discoveries, drilling results, and subsurface data in the Stabroek Block.

The company applied deep learning, machine learning, and high-performance computing to improve exploration decisions. Advanced seismic imaging helped identify these four potential sites.

A related report from ExxonMobil’s Q2 2026 earnings call confirmed the models were trained on past discoveries. The work produced four new discovery opportunities, but details remain limited.

The operator has not confirmed whether these opportunities contain commercial hydrocarbons. The company also has not disclosed their exact locations or estimated volumes.

Teacher training program launched

On August 24, 2026, ExxonMobil Guyana announced the Guyana STEM Teacher Training program. The initiative is called Enhancing Learning, Leadership and Academic Rigour, or STELLAR.

Sixty pre-service secondary school educators from across Guyana will begin specialized math and science training. The program starts in August 2026 through the Cyril Potter College of Education.

STELLAR is a two-year initiative under the company’s larger STEM effort. It is part of the US$100 million, 10-year Guyana STEM Initiative.

The program aims to strengthen STEM teaching capacity nationwide. It also seeks to improve student outcomes in mathematics and science across Guyana.

AI technology explained simply

the company uses AI to analyze large amounts of geological data quickly. This helps the company decide where to drill for oil and gas.

The AI models learn from previous discoveries and drilling operations. They also study subsurface characterization to predict where oil might exist.

This approach speeds up exploration and reduces risks for the company. It also helps find opportunities that traditional methods might miss.

The four new opportunities are a result of this advanced technology. However, more work is needed to confirm their commercial value.

STEM training details for teachers

The 60 pre-service teachers will receive specialized training in mathematics and science. They will study at the Cyril Potter College of Education, starting in August 2026.

This training is designed for secondary school educators across Guyana. It aims to build strong teaching skills for the next generation of students.

The program is part of a long-term commitment by the company. The US$100 million, 10-year initiative supports STEM education nationwide.

By training 60 teachers, the program hopes to reach many more students. This effort aligns with Guyana’s growing need for skilled STEM graduates.

Separate announcements, same month

The AI exploration findings came first on August 13, 2026. The teacher training launch followed on August 24, 2026.

Both are the company initiatives but are not connected as one program. They address different needs in the country’s development.

The AI work focuses on offshore oil exploration in the Stabroek Block. The teacher training focuses on education and workforce development onshore.

These announcements show the company’s broad investments in the country. They cover both energy production and human capacity building.

What this means for Guyana

For Guyana, the AI exploration could lead to new oil discoveries. This would boost the country’s economy and energy exports.

The teacher training helps build a local workforce for future industries. It supports math and science education in secondary schools.

Both initiatives signal long-term confidence in Guyana by the company. The company made its first Stabroek Block discovery in 2015 and now has more than 30.

The country relies on oil revenues for economic growth. Education investment aims to prepare citizens for diverse opportunities.

The role of local institutions

The Cyril Potter College of Education will deliver the teacher training. This institution is key to Guyana’s teacher preparation system.

the company partners with the Cyril Potter College of Education to ensure training relevance. This collaboration helps meet the specific needs of Guyana’s classrooms.

For the AI work, the company uses its global technology expertise. The company brings advanced tools from its worldwide operations.

This ensures compliance with Guyana’s oil and gas laws.

Next steps for both initiatives

the company will continue evaluating the four AI-identified opportunities. The company needs to determine if they hold commercial reserves.

If promising, the company may drill test wells in the future. This process could take months or years to complete.

The STELLAR teacher training will run for two years until about 2028. The 60 teachers will graduate with enhanced STEM teaching skills.

the company may expand the program based on results. The company has committed to a 10-year STEM effort in the country.

Frequently Asked Questions

What did ExxonMobil Guyana announce in August 2026? ExxonMobil Guyana made two announcements: using AI to find four new exploration opportunities in the Stabroek Block, and launching the STELLAR program to train 60 pre-service teachers in STEM. How does the AI exploration work? The company uses deep learning, machine learning, and seismic imaging to analyze data from past discoveries. This identified four new exploration opportunities, but their commercial value is not yet confirmed. What is the STELLAR teacher program? STELLAR (Enhancing Learning, Leadership and Academic Rigour) is a two-year math and science training for 60 pre-service secondary teachers. It starts in August 2026 at the Cyril Potter College of Education. How much does ExxonMobil Guyana invest in education? The teacher training is part of a US$100 million, 10-year Guyana STEM Initiative. This broader program aims to strengthen STEM teaching and student outcomes across the country. World.title: Statkraft Chile Fills Los Lagos Reservoir, Eyes 2027 Start
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Chile · ENERGY

Key Facts — What happened Statkraft Chile filled the reservoir of the Los Lagos hydroelectric plant, a major construction milestone.

— How big 52 MW of installed capacity, with average annual generation of about 260 GWh, per Statkraft.

— Where The Los Lagos project sits in the Pilmaiquén River basin in Mapuche Williche territory in southern Chile.

— The catch Mapuche-Williche communities had already filed a complaint in Norway under the Transparency Act, citing the planned reservoir filling among their concerns.

— Who pays Statkraft estimated total investment at about US$200 million when it approved construction in 2019.

— What comes next Commercial operation is expected in 2027, pending final works and regulatory approvals.

A long-delayed hydropower project in Mapuche Williche territory reaches a key milestone.

Statkraft has filled the reservoir of its Los Lagos hydroelectric plant in the Pilmaiquén River basin in southern Chile. The company expects the plant to begin commercial operation in 2027.

Statkraft has started filling the Los Lagos reservoir in southern Chile. (illustrative)

A Key Milestone in a Long Wait

Statkraft has filled the reservoir of its Los Lagos hydroelectric plant, according to reporting in late August 2026. The filling marks a major step in a project that has become a symbol of permitting delays in Chile.

The plant sits in the Pilmaiquén River basin in southern Chile, an area of rich water resources. But the project took years to reach this stage due to complex environmental and regulatory processes.

Reservoir filling is typically one of the last steps before a hydroelectric plant can start generating power. For Los Lagos, this step signals that construction is nearing its end phase.

Statkraft Chile now expects the plant to begin commercial operation in 2027. This timeline depends on completing remaining works and passing final inspections.

The Project at a Glance

The Los Lagos hydroelectric plant is located in the Pilmaiquén River basin, which flows through southern Chile. The area is part of Mapuche Williche territory, giving the project cultural and social significance.

Statkraft says the run-of-river plant will have an installed capacity of 52 MW, with a 35-meter dam and a reservoir of about 192 hectares.

Hydroelectric projects use flowing water to spin turbines and generate electricity, providing a renewable energy source. The Los Lagos plant will contribute to Chile’s electricity grid once operational.

Chile has abundant rivers in its southern regions, making hydropower a natural fit for its energy mix. However, such projects often face scrutiny over their environmental and social impacts.

Why the Filling Drew Complaints

Mapuche-Williche communities had already filed a complaint in Norway under the Transparency Act, citing the planned reservoir filling among their human-rights concerns.

Communities argue that the project affects their territory and way of life, raising concerns about consultation and consent. The complaint highlights tensions between renewable energy development and indigenous rights.

Statkraft, as a Norwegian company, operates under national laws that require human-rights due diligence. The complaint tests whether those obligations extend to overseas projects like Los Lagos.

The outcome of the complaint could set a precedent for how Norwegian companies handle community relations abroad. It also shines a spotlight on Chile’s own permitting and consultation processes.

A Symbol of Permitting Delays

Public reporting tied to the complaint calls Los Lagos a symbol of permitting delays in Chile. The project’s long journey reflects broader challenges in getting energy infrastructure approved.

Chile has ambitious renewable energy targets, but projects often face years of studies, hearings, and red tape. The delays can deter investment and slow the transition to cleaner power.

Statkraft Chile has navigated these hurdles, but the process has not been smooth. The company had to meet strict environmental standards and engage with local communities step by step.

Now that the reservoir is filled, the project enters its final phase. Yet the permitting lessons from Los Lagos may inform how Chile approves future hydropower developments.

What Happens Next for the Plant

With the reservoir filled, Statkraft Chile will focus on commissioning the plant’s turbines and systems. This includes testing equipment and ensuring everything runs safely before power generation begins.

Commercial operation is expected in 2027, but the exact date may shift based on testing results. The company has not disclosed a specific month for the start of operations.

Once online, the plant will send electricity into Chile’s national grid, which serves millions of homes and businesses. Its output will depend on water flows and the plant’s installed capacity.

Statkraft lists the plant at 52 MW, designed to generate roughly 260 GWh per year.

The Broader Context in Chile

Chile is expanding its renewable energy portfolio, including solar, wind, and battery storage projects. Hydropower remains a key part of the mix, especially in the water-rich south.

In recent months, Chile has added significant solar and storage capacity, showing a shift toward diverse clean energy sources. But hydro projects like Los Lagos offer reliable, dispatchable power.

The permitting delays seen with Los Lagos could prompt Chile to streamline approval processes. Faster permits might encourage more investment in renewable energy infrastructure.

Balancing speed with environmental and social safeguards is a delicate act for regulators. Los Lagos serves as a case study in how those trade-offs play out in practice.

Statkraft’s Local Presence

Statkraft operates in Chile with a portfolio anchored by three operating hydropower plants totaling 263 MW, plus three wind projects of 110 MW. Los Lagos is the company’s newest hydro build.

The company has emphasized safety and sustainability in its Chilean operations, reporting several years without major accidents. This track record supports its reputation as a responsible operator.

Local engagement with communities has been a mixed experience, as the complaint shows. Statkraft Chile has committed to dialogue, but tensions remain in some areas.

Managing these relationships will be crucial as Statkraft Chile pursues growth in Latin America. The company also has wind projects in Peru, showing regional ambition.

Looking Ahead to 2027

The path to commercial operation in 2027 is now clearer after reservoir filling, but obstacles could still arise. Final testing, grid connections, and regulatory sign-offs all remain.

The company will provide updates as milestones are reached in the coming months. Investors and observers will watch closely for any changes to the schedule.

Successful completion of Los Lagos would mark a significant achievement for Statkraft Chile. It would also demonstrate that complex hydro projects can finally move forward in Chile.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the Los Lagos hydroelectric plant? The Los Lagos plant is a hydroelectric project by Statkraft Chile in the Pilmaiquén River basin in southern Chile. It is expected to start commercial operation in 2027. Why is the reservoir filling important? Reservoir filling is a critical milestone that allows the plant to eventually generate electricity. It signals that construction is nearly complete and testing can begin. What concerns have communities raised? Mapuche-Williche communities filed a complaint in Norway about Statkraft’s human-rights due diligence. They worry about impacts on their territory and have raised issues of consultation and consent. How much power will the plant generate? Statkraft lists the plant at 52 MW, designed to generate roughly 260 GWh per year. When will the plant start operating? Statkraft Chile expects commercial operation to begin in 2027. The exact date has not been specified and may depend on final testing and approvals.

World.title: Dominican Republic Growth to Outpace Latin America, ECLAC Says
World.content:
By subscribing you agree to our privacy policy . We never share your email.

The morning intel from across Latin America. Free.

Dominican Republic · ECONOMY

Key Facts — What happened ECLAC forecast the Dominican Republic economy to grow 4.0% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027.

— How big The projected 2026 rate is nearly double the 2.2% average for Latin America and the Caribbean.

— The catch The 4.4% Dominican Republic growth prediction for 2027 depends on global conditions and domestic reforms staying on track.

— Who pays Telecom regulator Indotel says 62% of the phone and data sector uses Chinese-made equipment, a strategic risk.

— What comes next The government must manage trade ties and digital infrastructure to meet the ECLAC forecast.

Regional forecasters see the Dominican economy expanding well above the Latin American average, while a telecom regulator warns about equipment reliance on China.

The Dominican Republic’s economy will grow 4.0% in 2026 and 4.4% in 2027, according to projections released by ECLAC on 20 August 2026. This paces well above the 2.2% regional average forecast for Latin America and the Caribbean this year.

Santo Domingo. ECLAC sees the Dominican Republic as one of the region’s fastest growers.

ECLAC Forecast in Detail

The Economic Commission for Latin America and the Caribbean, known as ECLAC, released its 2026 Economic Survey on 20 August. Revista Mercado reported on 24 August that the Dominican Republic will grow 4.0% this year and 4.4% next year.

These figures place the country among the fastest-growing economies in the region. The Latin America and Caribbean average is just 2.2% for 2026 and 2.5% for 2027, according to the same report.

The Dominican Republic’s forecast matches the broader Central America subregion, excluding Cuba and Haiti, which also projects 4.0% growth. This consistency suggests strong momentum in the subregion.

Órbita Informativa noted on 21 August that the Dominican Republic appears as a regional leader in ECLAC’s ranking. The country’s growth outlook reflects robust domestic demand and investment.

Why Growth Beats Regional Peers

Tourism, construction, and remittances anchor the strong Dominican Republic growth outlook from abroad. These sectors have remained resilient despite global inflationary pressures and tighter financial conditions.

The country benefits from stable macroeconomic policies and stable macroeconomic policies and inflation-targeting monetary management that attract foreign investors. ECLAC’s report highlights productive formalization as a key to sustaining this pace.

Government infrastructure spending and private consumption continue to drive economic activity in 2026. The central bank has managed inflation without stalling credit growth, supporting business expansion.

Regional comparison shows only Guatemala matching the Dominican Republic’s 4.0% projection for 2026. This puts the island nation in a select group of high performers in Latin America.

Telecom Sector’s China Dependence

Indotel, the Dominican Institute of Telecommunications, revealed that 62% of the telephone and data sector depends on Chinese brands. Revista Mercado reported this on 24 August 2026, citing the regulator’s assessment.

This dependence refers specifically to infrastructure and equipment used in networks, not just consumer devices. The revelation came amid debate over Viettel Global Investment’s entry into the Dominican market.

Viettel, a Vietnamese company, won rights to part of the radio spectrum through a recent tender. The regulator flagged this reliance as a ‘technological dominance’ issue in communications.

Indotel’s statement frames the 62% figure as a technological dominance issue. It underscores the challenge of diversifying suppliers while maintaining network costs and performance.

Viettel Entry Sparks Debate

The spectrum allocation to Viettel and Claro Dominicana became a political and regulatory flashpoint in August 2026. The decision aims to increase competition and improve digital infrastructure across the country.

Dominican Today reported on the Indotel award, noting it covers key radio frequencies for mobile services. This move could lower prices for consumers and expand coverage in rural areas.

However, the entry of a foreign player raises questions about national security and market control. Legislators have called for scrutiny of Viettel’s ownership and operational practices before full deployment.

The regulator defends the tender as transparent and aligned with international standards. It argues that more competition will reduce dependence on any single equipment vendor over time.

Fiscal Challenges and Tax Gaps

An IMF assessment flagged that the Dominican Republic could unlock up to 3% of GDP by closing compliance gaps in the ITBIS, the value-added tax. This finding comes from a report highlighted by Devdiscourse in August 2026.

Improving tax collection would provide funds for infrastructure and social programs without raising rates. The government has made digital payments a priority to increase transparency and reduce evasion.

The IMF recommends expanding the tax base and modernizing the tax administration. These steps could support the ECLAC growth forecast by funding productive investments.

Regional Economic Context

ECLAC’s survey shows Latin America and the Caribbean growing just 2.2% in 2026 and 2.5% in 2027. This represents a slowdown from previous years due to weak global trade and high interest rates.

The Dominican Republic’s 4.0% projection stands out against this sluggish backdrop. Panama, for example, is expected to grow 4.4% this year, slightly above the Dominican figure, per Prensa.com.

Central America, excluding Cuba and Haiti, is projected to expand 4.0% in 2026 and 4.2% in 2027. The Dominican Republic fits this dynamic subregional pattern, benefiting from trade and tourism.

ECLAC called for productive formalization to escape a low-growth trap, as noted by Times509. This means bringing informal businesses into the official economy to boost productivity and tax revenue.

Outlook for 2027 and Risks

The 4.4% Dominican Republic growth forecast for 2027 assumes continued stability in global demand and no major external shocks. Dominican Republic growth depends on tourism arrivals and remittances remaining strong.

Risks include potential trade disruptions, natural disasters, or a slowdown in the US economy. The US is the Dominican Republic’s largest trading partner and a major source of tourists.

Domestic challenges like energy costs and bureaucratic hurdles could temper investment. The government’s focus on infrastructure may mitigate some of these risks, analysts say.

ECLAC will likely revisit these projections in its next survey, adjusting for new data. For now, the outlook positions the Dominican Republic as a regional standout.

What This Means for Investors

Strong Dominican Republic growth makes the country an attractive destination for foreign direct investment. Sectors like telecommunications, tourism, and manufacturing may see increased capital inflows.

However, the heavy reliance on Chinese equipment in telecoms poses a reputational and security risk for investors. Companies may need to diversify suppliers to mitigate potential sanctions or supply-chain issues.

The tax compliance gap offers both a challenge and an opportunity for businesses. Firms that operate transparently could benefit from a more level playing field as enforcement improves.

Overall, these projections suggest a resilient economy with room to expand, but careful management is required. Investors should monitor policy shifts around technology and taxation closely.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is the projected Dominican Republic growth rate for 2026? ECLAC projects the Dominican Republic’s GDP will grow 4.0% in 2026. This outpaces the 2.2% average for Latin America and the Caribbean. How fast will the Dominican economy grow in 2027? The forecast for 2027 is 4.4% according to ECLAC. This marks a slight acceleration from the 2026 projection. Why is the Dominican Republic expected to grow faster than neighbors? Strong tourism, construction, and remittances drive the economy, along with stable policies. These factors attract investment and support consumer spending. What does Indotel say about Chinese brands in telecom? Indotel says 62% of the telephone and data sector depends on Chinese brands. The regulator raised this point during the debate over Viettel’s market entry. Is the 69.1% electronic-transfer revenue increase confirmed? No, that specific figure has not been confirmed by official sources. Available reports do not document any anti-crisis plan lifting electronic-transfer revenue by that amount.
