World.title: Dancing House Marks 30 Years With a Free Weekend of Dance in Prague
World.content:
Prague’s Dancing House will celebrate its 30th anniversary with a free two-day program of dance classes, performances and workshops on August 29 and 30.

Jiráskovo náměstí, next to the landmark on the Vltava embankment, will host a temporary stage and dance floor throughout the weekend.



The program will run from 11 a.m. to 7 p.m. on both Saturday and Sunday.

Visitors can join professional instructors for classes in bachata, street dance and Latin American dance. There will also be sessions for children, dance demonstrations and opportunities to meet and talk with instructors.

The event is open to all levels, with participants able to watch performances or take part in the classes.

Weekend program

The schedule is the same on both days until the evening finale.

11:00 a.m. – Opening

11:05 a.m. – Children’s dance class

11:50 a.m. – Talk with the instructor

12:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

12:05 p.m. – Bachata class

12:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

1:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

1:05 p.m. – Street dance class

1:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

2:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

2:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

2:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

3:00 p.m. – Hat Jazz performance

3:05 p.m. – Children’s dance class

3:50 p.m. – Talk with the instructor

4:00 p.m. – Bachata demonstration

4:05 p.m. – Bachata class

4:50 p.m. – Talk with bachata instructors

5:00 p.m. – Street dance demonstration

5:05 p.m. – Street dance class

5:50 p.m. – Talk with the street dance instructor

6:00 p.m. – Latin American dance demonstration

6:05 p.m. – Latin American dance class

6:50 p.m. – Talk with instructors

7:00 p.m. – Acrobatic performance

7:05 p.m. – Hula Hoops performance

The closing acrobatic performance will differ each day. Saturday will feature a handstand performance, while Sunday will bring Duo ReAct.

Admission is free. Organizers will also provide light refreshments.

Completed in 1996, the Dancing House is one of Prague’s best-known examples of modern architecture. It stands at the corner of Rašínovo nábřeží and Jiráskovo náměstí, overlooking the Vltava.

The building was designed by Croatian-Czech architect Vlado Milunić in collaboration with Canadian-American architect Frank Gehry. Its curved forms and leaning towers give the impression of a dancing couple, which inspired its Czech name, Tančící dům.

The building is also known by the nickname “Ginger and Fred,” referring to American dancers Ginger Rogers and Fred Astaire.

World.title: Bolt Launches App-Free Ride Kiosks in the Czech Republic
World.content:
Bolt has introduced self-service kiosks in the Czech Republic that allow customers to order a ride without a smartphone, mobile data or the Bolt app.

The first kiosk is now operating at Westfield Chodov in Prague. A second will open at Westfield Černý Most on September 1. The company says it plans to consider other high-traffic locations in the future.



The kiosks use TapBox technology and provide access to the same Bolt driver network, pricing and safety standards available through the app.

Customers can place an order directly at the screen, making the service available to people who do not use smartphones or cannot access their phones at the time.

Both shopping centres have also introduced dedicated parking spaces for Bolt drivers collecting passengers. Customers are directed to these designated areas rather than having to meet drivers at potentially unsafe stopping points such as bus stops.

How Bolt kiosks work

Ordering a ride takes several steps. Customers enter their destination, select a ride category and provide their phone number. The available categories are Standard, Comfort, Premium and XL.

Payment is made by card. Once the booking is completed, the kiosk prints a confirmation and sends an SMS containing the vehicle details, estimated arrival time and instructions for finding the driver.

The kiosks operate around the clock and support Czech, English, German, French and Ukrainian.

Each ride booked through a kiosk carries an additional CZK 25 fee.

Bolt says the system could also benefit drivers by connecting them with customers who might otherwise be unable to use the app. The company expects the kiosks to reduce waiting times between rides at busy shopping centres and create additional opportunities for drivers.

The Czech launch follows the introduction of similar kiosks in Slovakia earlier this summer, including at airports.

World.title: Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Cycle Routes but Cycling Numbers Barely Rise
World.content:
Prague is continuing to expand its cycling infrastructure, but the number of recorded bicycle journeys across the city has remained largely unchanged.

Automatic counters installed on major cycling routes recorded about 5.6 million passages in 2025, roughly 1 percent fewer than the previous year.

After adjusting for counter failures and temporary route closures, however, the Technical Road Administration (TSK) calculated a 0.4 percent increase in cycling traffic.



Prague Adds 18 Kilometers of Routes Away From Traffic

The city added 18 kilometers of two-way cycle paths and other cycling routes separated from motor traffic during the year. The total length of marked cycling routes increased by one kilometer to approximately 550 kilometers.

Routes separated from car traffic now account for 263 kilometers of the network, an increase of seven kilometers compared with the previous year.

TSK operates automatic counters at 31 locations on Prague’s main cycling routes. The devices use induction loops or radar to record cyclists and can determine their direction of travel.

The largest increase in two-way cycling routes came over the past year. Their combined length grew from 63 to 81 kilometers. These routes allow cyclists to travel in both directions on streets that are otherwise one-way for motor vehicles.

New two-way routes were added mainly in Prague 7 around Letná, in Prague 5 in Barrandov, and in Prague 6 around Na Petynce, Rozdělovská and Podbaba.

Modřany Remains Prague’s Busiest Cycling Route

The highest number of cyclists was recorded in Modřany, at the intersection of Vltavanů and U Kino streets. The counter registered 578,016 passages during the year.

Another 540,656 cycling journeys were recorded on Povltavská Street south of Troja Castle.

The largest year-on-year increase was recorded on the Barrandov Bridge, where cycling traffic rose following the completion of its more than two-year reconstruction.

World.title: Leading candidates for Hungary’s “almighty” National Asset Recovery and Protection Office have presented their programmes
World.content:
Hungary’s new National Asset Recovery and Asset Protection Office (NVVH) is tasked with protecting public assets, investigating suspected misuse of state property and helping recover unlawfully acquired public wealth. The relevant legistlation establishing the new body was accepted by the Parliament in July and the body’s head is to be chosen by the National Assembly this Friday. Then the institution’s charter will be accepted in September, so the work can begin.

Hungary’s “almighty” National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) is set to start its work soon, but first the Hungarian Parliament must choose its head. There are three top contestants whose hearing took place today in the Hungarian Parliament’s Justice ad Constitutional Affairs Committee.

Miklós Ligeti: no witch hunt

The accountability not pursued in 1990 must finally be achieved, Miklós Zoltán Ligeti, the legal director of Transparency International Hungary, told the justice and constitutional affairs committee of parliament on Tuesday during his hearing as a nominee for the head of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH). He added that while asset recovery and accountability must begin, the office itself must be established first.

Miklós Ligeti, one of the candidates for the post of the head of Hungary’s new National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Photo: MTI

NVVVH’s mandate will not be limited to the past 16 years. “It is not a NER-purging office,” he said, referring to the moniker “system of national cooperation” of the Orbán regime. A legal procedure cannot be turned into a witch hunt, he added. Ligeti emphasised that the new authority must cooperate with many other bodies in the fight against corruption. Without this, the entire process is doomed to fail, he said.

In response to a question, Ligeti stressed that the primary goal is to restore public trust in the state. On the risk of political retribution, he said he did not see why this office should be feared more than any other authority.

Anna Róza Unger: developing an immune system

The first six-year mandate of the leader of the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) will suffice to uncover “what happened in this country“, but the cases are not expected to end in binding sentences within that period, political scientist Anna Róza Unger said before parliament’s judicial and constitutional affairs committee on Tuesday.

Unger, who is vying for the position of head of the NVVH, said the mandate will be enough to launch the procedures “to bring everyone responsible, be it a big man or a small one, a city mouse or a country one, before the court.” This would go for “all who committed it, those who allowed [crimes] to be committed, and for Hungarian society to grasp and learn what had happened so it can never happen again,” she said.

The NVVH will work to map the system that created and operated corruption rather than to unveil concrete cases, she said, “so that the newly forming Hungarian democracy may develop an immune system which, after a period of consolidation, makes re-occurrence impossible,” Unger said.

Nicholas Sárvári: NVVH ‘must become rule of law’

Hungary’s Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) “should become an integral part of the rule of law“, Nicholas Sárvári, the Tisza Party’s nominee to head the new organisation, said in parliament’s judicial committee on Tuesday.

Péter Magyar’s government granted unprecedented powers for the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Photo: Facebook/TISZA Párt

Sárvári noted that the structure of the authority was defined by law, and said that as its head he would “find the right experts for each task“. The candidate suggested that the way public assets had been handled in Hungary in previous years was “unacceptable“, adding that he felt “ashamed as a Hungarian“. Restoring public trust and building transparency will be one of the main tasks of the new authority, he added.

If you missed – The Guardian: Hungary is ‘de-Orbánising’ at record speed

Former PM Orbán’s party does not take part in the procedure

The Hungarian Parliament is expected to elect NVVH’s leader on Friday and adopt its charter during the autumn session, with the authority expected to be set up later in the season.

Péter Magyar’s Tisza has supermajority in the Hungarian Parliamet, so it will depend only on their MPs who the head of the new body will be. Photo: Facebook/Forsthoffer Ágnes

The Hungarian Civil Liberties Union (TASZ), the Hungarian Helsinki Committee, the K-Monitor Public Benefit Association and the World Federation of Hungarians were represented at the meeting in a consultative capacity.

Former government party and main opposition party Fidesz and its ally, KDNP did not send their MPs to the hearing.

World.title: Hungary’s overpriced Covid ventilator mystery: Why thousands are still gathering dust in warehouses
World.content:
Anita Orbán, the foreign minister, has filed a criminal complaint concerning purchases related to ventilators purchased during the coronavirus pandemic under the previous Orbán government.

Brutal amount of money spent

The complaint concerns purchases made in March and April 2020, worth a total 300 billion forints (EUR 827m) by the previous foreign ministry led by Péter Szijjártó, Orbán said, adding that the purchases had been made outside the public procurement system.

The documents reviewed so far have raised “suspicion of embezzlement causing extreme damage and other crimes … suggesting the responsibility of top management” at the previous ministry, Orbán said, adding that the procurement had mostly targeted ventilators.

Former FM Szijjártó looking at a ventilator. Photo: Facebook/Szijjártó Péter

The ministry has established that its predecessor had “overpurchased“, buying too many equipment, while there was “a significant difference between purchase and producer prices”, she said.

Lack of staff was the bottleneck, not the number of vetilators

The minister noted that an invasive ventilator requires an ICU specialist, a qualified nurse, oxygen supply, and an ICU bed, which at the time of the pandemic limited the number of patients in intensive care to between 800-2,000. “The bottleneck was not the restricted number of ventilators … despite that fact, the decision makers considered the number of ventilators as an indicator of the full capacity,” she said, adding that “at the height of the epidemic only 2,500 ventilators had been sent to the hospitals, the vast majority of the stock is still in a warehouse.“

As for the purchase price of the equipment, the difference from the producer price was 13.4 billion forints in the case of six companies, she said. Quoting press reports, she said the average price of a ventilator was 17 million forints, while producers sold the same models between 1,000 and 5,000 US dollars (348,000-1.3m forints).

If you missed: The Hungarian government bought Chinese ventilators known to be dangerous

Szijjártó tried to hide important details

According to the minister, the previous ministry had left behind “incomplete documentation” but added that the original documents “could not be fully erased and a lot of them could be restored, which provided a better image of what happened.” She added that her ministry’s staff had managed to restore 130,000 files concerning the procurement.

According to information from the ministry, its predecessor had purchased 16,853 ventilators, protective gear, PCR tests, and medicines in spring 2020, under the previous government’s “special legal order” introduced at the beginning of the pandemic.

World.title: Previously unseen footage of Hungarian Gripen crash as minister reveals how disaster unfolded
World.content:
One of the Hungarian Defence Forces’ Gripen fighter jets crashed on the grounds of Szolnok military airfield on Monday after suffering a malfunction during a training mission. The pilot ejected from the aircraft. Romulusz Ruszin-Szendi, the Defence Minister and former Chief of the General Staff, has revealed fresh details of the incident, which could have resulted in an even more serious catastrophe and endangered further lives at the military airfield. He said the outcome depended on the experience and presence of mind of the 51-year-old pilot.

Gripens were practising high-speed interceptions

As we reported on Monday, the aircraft had been conducting high-speed interception drills in Hungarian airspace alongside another Gripen. After completing a second exercise, however, a fault warning appeared and the mission was abandoned. The two aircraft then headed for Szolnok, as the malfunctioning fighter could no longer safely return to its home base at Kecskemét.

Drones were used to search the burning wreck after the crash to determine whether firefighters were safe to start their work or not, considering the large amount of explosives the Gripen fighter jet was carrying during the exercise. Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

The pilot ejected during the landing, while firefighters arriving at the scene extinguished the blaze within minutes.

The aircraft was carrying air-to-air missiles and ammunition for its cannon, meaning the consequences could have been considerably worse had the pilot made an error. The cause of the crash remains under investigation, but Ruszin-Szendi gave important new details in an interview with Gábor Bochkor on Retro Radio’s morning programme.

‘All instruments went black’

Ruszin-Szendi said the Gripen was being flown by a 51-year-old pilot with more than 2,000 flying hours, including experience on international operations. The fighter pilot was in excellent physical condition but suffered spinal injuries in the crash and was undergoing surgery at the Honvéd Hospital.

The last Gripen accident took place in 2015 in Hungary. Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

According to the minister, the two aircraft had taken off from Kecskemét to practise high-speed interceptions. They successfully completed the first exercise and returned, but warnings began appearing in rapid succession at the end of the second interception. The cockpit instruments then went black.

Ruszin-Szendi said this made for an especially difficult situation because Gripens have no analogue instruments. In such circumstances, the pilot cannot read the aircraft’s speed or altitude from conventional dials, but must instead fly primarily by visual reference.

Aircraft began veering to the right

The situation was eased somewhat by the fact that radio contact between the two Gripens was not lost. With assistance from the accompanying aircraft, the malfunctioning fighter reached Szolnok airfield, where the pilot managed to land.

Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

The difficulties did not end there, however. The aircraft began veering to the right on the runway, and the pilot ejected only after realising that he could no longer regain control.

Ruszin-Szendi said the pilot had attempted until the final moment to save the fighter jet, estimated to be worth around 30 billion forints, while also putting his own life at risk.

The pilot risked his life to save the jet. Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

He added that ejection was no easy ordeal, as it could itself impose severe physical strain. A pilot may be subjected to forces of up to 15 to 20 G — 15 to 20 times the force of gravity — which is believed to have occurred in this case and may have contributed to the spinal injury.

If you missed – Polish bus driver speaks out after deadly Hungary crash: ‘No words can ease the families’ pain’

The injury may also have been worsened by the pilot landing on the concrete after ejecting.

Ruszin-Szendi visited the injured pilot in hospital. The airman was said to have been pleased that he could move all his limbs, and had already asked when he could return to flying duties.

Saab seeks answers over crash

The question now is how Hungary will replace the lost Gripen. Ruszin-Szendi said a decision could be made only once the investigation had established what happened.

Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

Swedish manufacturer Saab is also keen to determine the precise cause of the accident and is providing technical assistance to the inquiry. The minister said relations with the manufacturer were good, though negotiations over the price of a possible replacement aircraft would be a separate matter.

The minister made it clear that the Hungarian Defence Forces have the ability to protect NATO airspace despite the accident. He added that the Hungarian pilots were keen to fly again on the Gripen jets despite the ongoing investigation and the possible dangers. Photo: Anadolu/Robert Nemeti

The flight recorders have yet to be analysed, and there is still no definitive explanation for the crash.

World.title: How Hungary’s central bank squandered EUR 30.4 million in two years — inquiry concerning luxury project begins
World.content:
Built for almost EUR 55 million, closed after two years and now on sale for EUR 25 million: the Hungarian central bank’s luxury development on Lake Balaton. Those responsible for a development in Balatonakarattya, on which the Hungarian National Bank’s foundation spent almost EUR 55 million, may soon be identified, Ágnes Forsthoffer, Speaker of Parliament, said.

Lake Balaton ‘brought into’ luxury complex

The Tisza Party politician said that the central bank’s foundation had built an education and conference centre on the site of a former MÁV children’s holiday camp, describing it as a “sinkhole for public money”. Forsthoffer said that the project was a particularly striking example of how taxpayers’ money had previously been handled, MTI wrote.

She also noted that the luxury complex had operated for barely two years. The facility was available exclusively to MNB employees as a holiday venue before being closed on cost-cutting grounds. The property was subsequently put up for sale for EUR 25 million.

Forsthoffer highlighted another unusual feature of the scheme: she claimed that Lake Balaton itself had effectively been “brought into” the estate’s grounds, atv.hu wrote. The politician branded the arrangement “utterly outrageous”.

Inquiry into central bank project to begin

A parliamentary committee of inquiry into alleged abuses connected with the operation of the Hungarian National Bank is due to begin work on Wednesday. Forsthoffer said that its investigation could soon establish who was responsible for the Balatonakarattya project — and who benefited from Hungarian taxpayers’ money.

Parliament committee to start investigation in the issue soon. Photo: Facebook/TISZA Párt

World.title: Hungary to reclaim EUR 303 million as government moves to scrap controversial foundations
World.content:
The ministry of science and technology will recover a total HUF 110 billion (EUR 303 million) through the elimination of public interest asset management foundations (KEKVA), Zoltán Tanács, the minister, said on Facebook on Monday.

Tanács said his portfolio would take over the activities of the ZalaZONE and Élvonal foundations, adding that while the “redundant” foundations would be scrapped, the ministry would maintain their activities. He also added that scrapping the system would save the ministry an annual HUF 800 million.

According to Tanács, the two foundations have a combined HUF 62.5 billion on their accounts, while they also have assets worth nearly HUF 50 billion. “That is over HUF 110 billion – from now on in public funds,” the minister added.

Tanács said both Élvonal’s and ZalaZONE’s activities were crucial, the first focusing on the development of young talents and building world-class scientific teams and the latter having an automotive research and development infrastructure, which could provide a test environment for self-driving cars, drones and robots in future. “But all that does not require an unnecessarily expensive, not sufficiently transparent or controlled foundation model,” he added.

World.title: Hungarian FM Anita Orbán names new ambassadors: historians tapped for Paris and Warsaw
World.content:
Prominent historians and specialists are among the latest nominees for key ambassadorial and consular posts. Hungary’s Foreign Minister Anita Orbán has announced several new nominees for ambassadorial and consular positions, including historians selected for key posts in Paris and Warsaw.

Speaking on ATV’s Egyenes Beszéd on Monday evening, Orbán said the government had so far replaced 34 of Hungary’s 138 heads of mission since the change of government. She stressed that most of the new appointments were career diplomats, although several well-known experts from academia and other fields have also been selected.

Among the latest nominees are historian Balázs Ablonczy for Paris, election expert Mátyás Bódi for Barcelona, historian and Poland specialist Miklós Mitrovits for Warsaw, and China expert Tamás Hajba for Beijing.

Historian nominated for Paris

Ablonczy, a historian specialising in Hungarian-French relations, has been asked to serve as Hungary’s ambassador in Paris. He previously headed the Hungarian Institute in Paris between 2011 and 2015. Orbán described him as one of the country’s leading experts on Hungarian-French diplomatic relations, making his nomination one of the most notable among the latest appointments.

The Warsaw nomination has also gone to a historian. Mitrovits, a prominent Polish studies expert, currently teaches at a Polish university and has extensive experience researching Poland and Hungarian-Polish relations.

Election expert to become Barcelona consul general

One of the more unexpected names on the list is Mátyás Bódi, who became widely known in Hungary through his work on electoral geography. Orbán has asked Bódi to become Hungary’s consul general in Barcelona, although the nominees are currently at different stages of the appointment process.

The foreign minister said the government was seeking to select people with relevant professional expertise, language skills and knowledge of the countries and regions where they will serve. “These names also illustrate that we are trying to find the best person for every location,” Orbán said, highlighting professional preparedness and integrity alongside knowledge of the relevant language and bilateral relationship.

China post goes to an experienced China specialist

Tamás Hajba has been selected as Hungary’s next ambassador to Beijing. Unlike some of the other newly announced names, Hajba has a long career in diplomacy and international economic policy. He spent more than a decade working at Hungary’s Foreign Ministry before joining the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) in Paris, where he worked as a China specialist.

Orbán said the majority of the newly selected heads of mission were career diplomats, with Hajba among those appointments. She also said the government was trying to match diplomats to posts where their existing knowledge and experience could be put to the best use.

Why has Hungary recalled 34 ambassadors?

Orbán also addressed the government’s decision to recall 34 heads of mission since taking office. She rejected the idea that all of those diplomats had been recalled simply because they were associated with the previous Fidesz government. According to the minister, some were replaced because they had already spent an unusually long period in their posts.

Under previous governments, some ambassadors remained abroad for as long as 10 or even 12 years. Orbán argued that lengthy postings can create a diplomatic problem, as questions may eventually arise over whether a diplomat has become too closely embedded in the interests of the country where they serve.

The new government plans to restore a more traditional rotation system. Under the proposed arrangement, ambassadors and consuls general would spend four years on a foreign posting before returning to Hungary for at least one year.

World.title: Hungarian Gripen crash: Swedish Saab offers support as investigation begins
World.content:
The fighter jet that crashed near Szolnok on Monday was a single-seat Gripen C, not the latest E/F model. Saab says it will assist the Hungarian investigation, while the crash has also briefly affected the Swedish defence company’s share price.

Saab has confirmed that the Hungarian Gripen fighter jet that crashed near Szolnok on Monday was a single-seat Gripen C. The Hungarian pilot ejected from the aircraft and survived the crash. Hungarian authorities are responsible for investigating what caused the accident, while Saab says it will provide technical assistance to the investigation.

“Of course, Saab will assist in the investigation,” Mattias Rådström, the company’s press manager, told Swedish news agency Direkt.

Gripen developed a fault during a training flight

The aircraft was flying alongside another Gripen during a training exercise when a warning indicating a malfunction appeared in the cockpit. The training mission was aborted, and the two aircraft headed towards Szolnok, as the damaged fighter could reportedly no longer reach Kecskemét.

However, another incident occurred during the final stage of the landing. The pilot decided to eject, after which the aircraft left the runway area and caught fire.

The pilot survived the ejection and is currently reported to be in a stable condition.

Hungary’s air force has suspended Gripen training flights until the investigation is completed. The aircraft assigned to alert and operational duties continue to perform their missions. Investigators have already begun examining the crash site, while data from the fighter’s flight recorder – commonly known as its black box – could prove crucial in determining exactly what happened.

Could Hungary ground its Gripen fleet?

Saab has not announced a general flight ban for the Gripen following the accident. Asked whether the aircraft could potentially be grounded while the investigation is under way, Rådström said the company would have to return to the question if such a decision became necessary.

The crash leaves Hungary with 17 Gripen aircraft in service.

Saab said in June that it had completed deliveries under an additional agreement signed by Sweden’s Defence Materiel Administration (FMV) and Hungary’s Ministry of Defence in January 2024. Hungary had subsequently operated a total of 18 Gripen C/D aircraft: 16 single-seat Gripen C fighters and two two-seat Gripen D aircraft. Hungary has not purchased the newer Gripen E/F variant.

The Gripen is a single-engine, supersonic multirole fighter designed for missions including air combat, ground attack and reconnaissance.

Saab shares briefly fall after the crash

The accident also had a short-term impact on Saab’s shares on the Stockholm Stock Exchange, according to Világgazdaság. The stock initially reversed an earlier gain of around 0.8% and briefly fell by approximately 0.6% following reports of the Hungarian crash.

The shares subsequently recovered much of the lost ground. By around noon, Saab stock was up approximately 0.1% for the day.

World.title: The Guardian: Hungary is ‘de-Orbánising’ at record speed
World.content:
Péter Magyar’s government has launched Hungary’s most dramatic transformation since the fall of communism, according to a Guardian editorial – but concerns remain over constitutional moves targeting Fidesz politicians and the fate of more than EUR 10 billion in EU funds.

Hungary is undergoing its most far-reaching political transformation since the fall of communism in 1989, according to The Guardian, which says Péter Magyar’s government is dismantling Viktor Orbán’s 16-year political legacy at an “extraordinary pace”.

In an editorial published on Sunday, the British newspaper assessed Magyar’s first three months as prime minister, describing the changes as a “peaceful political revolution”.

The Guardian portrays Orbán’s former system as a “soft autocracy” that flourished on corruption and extended its influence across much of Hungarian society, from religion and culture to the media. Now, it argues, that system is being dismantled at remarkable speed.

New president and a shake-up of state media

One of the most significant developments highlighted by the newspaper is the appointment of András Baka as Hungary’s new president. Baka, a former president of Hungary’s Supreme Court, was removed from his judicial position during Orbán’s rule in a case that was later found to have violated his rights by the European Court of Human Rights.

His appointment stands in stark contrast to the departure of his predecessor, Tamás Sulyok. Magyar had accused Sulyok of effectively rubber-stamping the erosion of the rule of law, while a constitutional amendment brought his presidential term to an early end.

The Guardian also points to the return of news bulletins to Hungary’s main state television channel on 20 August, after a six-week suspension. The newspaper describes ending what Magyar has portrayed as overt political bias in state media as one of his key campaign promises. Magyar won April’s election despite an electoral system that the Guardian says was weighted in Orbán’s favour.

Make things easier with professional support in English. Explore Daily News Hungary’s Services in English and find the help you need.

Hungary goes after the legacy of corruption

The government’s efforts to dismantle corruption networks established during the previous administration have also been moving quickly, according to the editorial. The Guardian says well over EUR 100 billion in public funds, including billions in EU money, is believed to have been siphoned off during Orbán’s years in power.

Investigators have been given new powers to pursue allegedly misappropriated assets through Hungary’s newly established National Asset Recovery and Protection Office. Magyar has also confirmed Hungary’s participation in the European Public Prosecutor’s Office, a move intended to strengthen the protection of EU funds and the investigation of financial crimes.

The next major test could come as soon as this autumn. Brussels has given Hungary until the end of August to demonstrate that sufficient measures have been taken to tackle corruption. More than EUR 10 billion in frozen EU funding is at stake.

The Guardian considers it likely that the vast majority of the money will eventually be released, arguing that this would further cement the rapprochement between Hungary and the European Union after years of conflict.

Concerns over Fidesz and ‘revenge’

Despite its broadly positive assessment of the new government’s direction, The Guardian also raises concerns about some of Magyar’s methods. The newspaper points to constitutional manoeuvring aimed at preventing a number of Fidesz MPs from standing in future elections.

President Baka has himself warned against creating the impression that the new government is seeking revenge against Orbán’s supporters. The Guardian nevertheless argues that a root-and-branch effort to dismantle the former system was necessary, and notes that Magyar’s approach continues to receive strong public backing in opinion polls.

At the same time, the newspaper cautions that rebuilding Hungary as a “normal pluralist European democracy” will take time.

For now, it describes Magyar as a “one-man political whirlwind” at the head of what is effectively a national unity government, supported by voters from across the political spectrum.

From symbolic gestures to a political revolution

The Guardian also highlights the symbolic changes introduced by Magyar. In May, the new prime minister moved his office out of the Carmelite Monastery, the heavily guarded building used by Orbán during his premiership. The building has since been opened to the public.

“I was not elected simply to change the government, but to change the regime,” Magyar said shortly after taking office, the newspaper recalls.

Three months later, The Guardian argues, that symbolic break with the past has been accompanied by much more substantial changes.

World.title: “Seaside for Everyone” program aims to attract tourists to Romanian seaside in September
World.content:
The 49th edition of “Seaside for Everyone,” a well-known program that aims to attract tourists to the Romanian seaside through massive price cuts in accommodation, was announced on Tuesday, August 25, by the Federation of Associations of Romanian Tourism Employers (FPTR).

Initiated and coordinated by FPTR and supported through the participation of economic operators on the seaside, “Seaside for Everyone” advances holidays on the seaside at reduced rates for tourists.

The program takes place from September 1-30, 2026.

To date, 67 accommodation units from 10 resorts and tourist areas are enrolled. According to FPTR, a novelty of this year’s edition is the change in the list of participants. 24 of the units currently enrolled did not participate in the spring edition. Among them are units entering the program for the first time, as well as returning operators.

Moreover, compared with the spring edition, when the lowest rate communicated was RON 42/person/night, the current edition starts at RON 39/person/night for accommodation without meals, in Eforie Nord.

The minimum rates communicated by other participating units are RON 39 (EUR 7.43) in Eforie Nord, RON 65 (EUR 12.38) in Eforie Sud, RON 60 (EUR 11.43) in Costinești, RON 58 (EUR 11.05) in Neptun-Olimp, RON 74 (EUR 14.10) in Jupiter, RON 77 (EUR 14.67) in Saturn, RON 108 (EUR 20.57) in Mangalia, RON 80 (EUR 15.24) in Vama Veche, RON 69 (EUR 13.14) in Mamaia, and RON 65 (EUR 12.38) in Mamaia Nord.

The rates, the included services, and participation periods are established by each accommodation unit. Some offers are for accommodation, while others include breakfast or All Inclusive services. The packages can also be paid for with holiday vouchers, under the conditions accepted by each accommodation unit or travel agency.

Although the official period of the program is September 1–30, 2026, some units have submitted offers that continue into October. As such, tourists have more holiday options in the off-season, while operators can maintain their activity for a longer period.

The list of participating units, rates, validity periods and contact details is published on the official website of the Federation of Associations of Romanian Tourism Employers. The list is updated as FPTR receives new registrations.

World.title: Romanian MP Claudiu Năsui accepts nomination as Moldova’s economy minister
World.content:
Romanian lawmaker Claudiu Năsui accepted prime minister Vasile Tofan’s invitation to join the Moldovan government as minister of economic development and digitalization. The Save Romania Union (USR) deputy said the move would require him to resign from Romania’s Parliament.

“I have accepted the position of economy minister in the government of the Republic of Moldova,” Năsui announced on Facebook. He said he strongly agreed with Tofan’s vision of turning Moldova into “the most welcoming country for entrepreneurs.”

Claudiu Năsui said he would use his experience to support economic reforms, including the liberalization and privatization process started after the fall of communism. He also linked Moldova’s economic development to its efforts to join the European Union and strengthen ties with Romania.

“I chose to accept Mr. Tofan’s invitation to join the government of the Republic of Moldova, even though this step means giving up my mandate as a member of the Romanian Parliament and dedicating my experience to a new reform effort,” Năsui said.

“A more prosperous Moldovan economy also means a more prosperous Romanian economy as part of our shared European path,” he added.

Vasile Tofan announced that Claudiu Năsui would be proposed for the position of minister of economic development and digitalization, citing his economic education, private-sector experience, and previous involvement in government reforms.

Năsui studied economics at Paris Dauphine University and finance at Bocconi University. He has worked in the financial sector, including at PwC and Romanian bank BCR, and holds the Chartered Financial Analyst certification.

He was first elected to the Romanian Parliament in 2016 and served as Romania’s economy minister between 2020 and 2021. He also founded the Open Budget platform, which tracks public spending.

According to prime minister Tofan, Claudiu Năsui’s priorities in Moldova will include reducing bureaucracy, addressing problems at state-owned companies, cutting public expenditure, and removing obstacles faced by small and medium-sized enterprises.

“We need this type of energy at the Economy Ministry,” Vasile Tofan said. “We want the Economy Ministry to become one of the main drivers of state reform and economic growth.”

The Moldovan prime minister also announced that Eugeniu Osmochescu would be proposed as minister of agriculture and food industry. His responsibilities will include preparing Moldovan agriculture for EU accession and improving the sector’s competitiveness and resilience to climate change.

World.title: Romanian Cristian Mungiu’s Cannes winner Fjord draws over 150,000 viewers after French release
World.content:
Fjord, the latest film from Romanian director Cristian Mungiu, attracted more than 150,000 viewers shortly after opening in France on August 19. France is the first of more than 100 territories where the Palme d’Or-winning film is due to receive a theatrical release.

The film ranked first in box-office receipts during both its previews and its official opening day, when it was seen by 30,058 people, including 11,727 in Paris, according to a press release. By the end of its first weekend, it had drawn 140,346 viewers in cinemas, with the Paris audience accounting for 51,847 admissions.

Including preview screenings, Fjord reached a total audience of 151,121 across 270 cinemas. Its distribution is expanding to 290 screens this week.

“Based on the ratio between its first-day box-office revenue and final audience figures, Fjord could attract more than 800,000 viewers in France,” reads the announcement.

The film is distributed in France by Le Pacte, which has handled all of Cristian Mungiu’s films since 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days. The latter, which won the filmmaker his first Palme d’Or in 2007, attracted around 380,000 viewers in France.

The release figures place Fjord ahead of the opening-day performance of some other recent Palme d’Or winners. Jafar Panahi’s It Was Just an Accident, the 2025 winner, debuted with 20,000 viewers and eventually reached 700,000 admissions, while Sean Baker’s Anora opened at a level close to Fjord and finished with 654,000 viewers.

Cristian Mungiu’s film won the Palme d’Or at the Cannes Film Festival in May, along with the FIPRESCI Prize, the Citizenship Prize, the François Chalais Prize, and the Ecumenical Jury Prize.

Fjord was also shown to 43,440 viewers in Romania during a one-off screening on June 13. Distribution also began in French-speaking Switzerland in August, with releases scheduled for September in Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Greece, Italy, and Belgium.

Fjord tells the story of Lisbet and Mihai Gheorghiu, a married couple who move to a small village on a Norwegian fjord. They soon befriend their neighbors, the Halberg family, while the children of the two households grow close despite differences in upbringing and values. The cast includes Sebastian Stan, Renate Reinsve, Adrian Titieni, Alin Panc, Giulia Nahmany, and Ana Bodea.

World.title: Center-right European groups EPP, Renew ask EC to withhold PNRR funds to Romania over integrity law
World.content:
The leaders of the center-right European People’s Party (EPP) and Renew Europe, two of the most important groups in the European Parliament, publicly asked the European Commission on Monday, August 24, to withhold EUR 770 million in PNRR funds meant for Romania due to the “Fritz amendment.” Their plea concerns the retroactive application of a new integrity law that would invalidate the mandate of Timisoara mayor Dominic Fritz.

EPP president Manfred Weber and Renew group leader Valérie Hayer both signed a letter shared by POLITICO asking Commission president Ursula von der Leyen to make it clear that the money will not be granted unless Bucharest abandons plans to amend a law that could lead to Save Romania Union (USR) party leader Dominic Fritz being banned from holding the office of mayor.

Weber and Hayer also argued that retroactive application violates EU legislation and Romania’s Constitution and accused the Romanian Social Democrats of deliberately targeting Fritz. “Under the guise of fulfilling a reform milestone for the Recovery and Resilience Facility, the Romanian Parliament has introduced a measure that directly violates Union law and constitutes a serious setback for the rule of law in Romania,” they said in the letter.

"European taxpayers’ money must never become a blank check for political power games,” Hayer told POLITICO. Weber added that “if legislation is designed to remove a political opponent, and EU funds are used as leverage to enforce it, this is no longer just politics - it is a rule-of-law issue.”

In the letter, they also urged the Commission to send “a signal” before Romanian president Nicușor Dan promulgates the law and before the August 31 deadline for the reforms that would allow access to EU funds.

The Fritz amendment

Earlier this month, in a 5-3 vote, the Romanian Constitutional Court approved the so-called “Fritz Amendment,” introduced by the Social Democratic Party (PSD) into the law governing the National Integrity Agency (ANI). The same law is a PNRR milestone with EUR 770 million attached to it.

The controversial amendment stipulates that elected officials in office lose their mandate within 30 days if they receive a final decision of incompatibility or conflict of interest, even if this decision predates the new law. This means that the law would apply retroactively. In June, Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld a Timișoara Court of Appeal ruling that found Dominic Fritz in an administrative conflict of interest.

As such, under the amendment, Fritz is expected to lose his position as mayor of Timișoara within 30 days of the legislation entering into force. The USR leader announced that he will challenge the decision at the European Court of Human Rights, and argued that the measure applies to a past action, although the Romanian Constitution states that laws should apply only to the future.

On course for adoption

After it was declared constitutional, the amended law was returned to Parliament and was adopted by the Chamber of Deputies with the votes of PSD, the National Liberal Party (PNL), and the minority Hungarian party UDMR. It still has to pass the Senate on Wednesday, August 26, and then go to president Nicusor Dan, who previously criticized the same "Fritz amendment," for promulgation before becoming law.

The supporters of the amended bill said its adoption secures EU funding, despite the retroactive application.

"For those who vote to violate the rule of law for fear of losing money from the PNRR: I am sure the European Commission will not accept rewarding such an abusive monstrosity with European taxpayers’ money," Fritz said on Facebook, in reaction to the bill's passing of the Chamber of Deputies.

Since the CCR decision, Fritz was also reconfirmed as leader of USR, which is part of the Renew Europe group in the European Parliament.

World.title: Romania’s Patria Bank accelerates lending in Q2 2026, loan portfolio nears RON 3 billion
World.content:
Patria Bank (BVB: PBK), a major Romanian bank listed on the Regulated Market of the Bucharest Stock Exchange, ended the first half of 2026 with a total performing loan portfolio of nearly RON 3 billion, up approximately 12% compared to June 30, 2025.

According to the bank, the evolution was supported by the acceleration of commercial activity in the second quarter across both the legal entities and retail segments.

As of June 30, 2026, the portfolio of performing loans granted to legal entities reached RON 2.40 billion, up 9% compared to the end of 2025 and 13% compared to the same period of the previous year.

The volume of new loans granted to corporate clients accelerated significantly in the second quarter, reaching RON 466 million, 44% above the level recorded in Q2 2025 and 67% higher than in the first quarter of 2026. For the first half of the year as a whole, the volume of new loans granted to corporate clients reached RON 746 million, up 2% compared to the same period of the previous year.

“Our ambition is to become an increasingly relevant bank for the clients we serve and to turn every financing granted into a long-term relationship that evolves alongside their needs,” stated Valentin Vancea, General Manager of Patria Bank.

The Agro segment recorded the fastest growth in the first half of the year, with the performing loan portfolio reaching RON 523 million, 29% above the level recorded as of December 31, 2025. New loan sales in this segment reached RON 224 million, up 35% compared to H1 2025, driven by farmers’ seasonal working capital needs and interest in projects supported by European funds. At the same time, the Bank continued its diversification towards the financing of the food industry, where financing for clients advanced 67% compared to the first half of 2025.

The Micro segment portfolio reached RON 434 million, up 3% compared to the end of 2025. New loan sales in the first half of the year reached RON 114 million, below the high base recorded in the same period of the previous year. The bank expects activity in this segment to record a positive evolution in the coming quarters, supported by adjustments to the analysis flow for financing requirements.

Across the SME and Corporate segments, the performing loan portfolio increased by 4% compared to the end of 2025, reaching RON 1.44 billion. This evolution was mainly driven by the Corporate component, which advanced by 14% in the first six months of the year. The two segments generated new financing of RON 408 million, with a strong recovery in the second quarter.

In the retail segment, the total balance of performing retail loans reached RON 584 million at the end of June, up 9% compared to the same period of the previous year. Unsecured loans remained the main growth driver of the retail portfolio, advancing by 16% to RON 275 million. This evolution was supported by sustained demand for consumer loans and credit cards, as well as by the increasing share of sales generated through digital channels, including the Patria de Oriunde platform. The balance of secured loans also returned to growth, reaching RON 309 million, 3% above the level recorded as of June 30, 2025.

New retail loan sales reached RON 138 million in the first half of the year, up 8.5% compared to H1 2025. Of this volume, RON 80 million was granted in the second quarter, 19% above the same period of the previous year. Sales of secured loans increased by 32% in the first half of the year, reaching RON 29 million, while unsecured loans accounted for approximately 79% of the total volume of new retail loans, with sales of RON 109 million.

In terms of commercial financing, corporate commercial financing increased by 17% compared to the end of 2025 and by 31% compared to June 30, 2025, reaching RON 2.20 billion. Commercial financing related to the retail segment reached RON 2.25 billion, 8% above the level recorded one year earlier. Term deposits reached RON 1.91 billion, while the balance of current accounts increased to RON 338 million.

As of the same date, SAI Patria Asset Management had assets under management of RON 1.53 billion, up 78% compared to December 31, 2025 and 177% compared to June 30, 2025. The financial performance of the two entities is not included in Patria Bank’s individual financial results. After the end of the reporting period, on August 5, 2026, Patria Bank completed the sale to BRD Asset Management SAI of its 99.9944% shareholding in SAI Patria Asset Management. As a result, SAI Patria Asset Management is no longer a subsidiary of Patria Bank.

World.title: Romanian tech executives launch Outcome1.AI to develop ‘Digital Employees’ for European SMEs
World.content:
Romanian technology executives Bogdan Putinică and Alex Balint have launched Outcome1.AI, a startup developing AI-powered “Digital Employees” for small and medium-sized enterprises. Initially operating in Romania, the company plans to expand into Greece, Spain, and Poland.

Outcome1.AI’s platform allows SMEs to use Digital Employees for clearly defined business roles through a monthly subscription. Each AI system is assigned to one role, operates within established authority limits, and completes tasks or escalates them to a human employee when necessary.

The roles available at launch cover customer operations, finance and accounting, human resources, sales, IT, marketing, procurement, and data processing. Tasks can include responding to recurring customer requests, reconciling invoices, preparing HR documents, monitoring compliance requirements, qualifying sales leads, updating customer relationship management records, and triaging IT requests.

“An SME should be able to hire work capacity in the same way it hires a person for a role, with a predictable salary it can budget for - not license a tool and hope it can find someone to operate it,” said Outcome1.AI CEO and co-founder Bogdan Putinică, who previously led Microsoft’s operations in markets across Europe and Asia.

Putinică said the platform was designed to increase companies’ capacity while keeping decisions under human control. The startup presents Digital Employees as a way to cover work that existing teams cannot fully handle rather than replace current staff.

Outcome1.AI CTO and co-founder Alex Balint said reliability and safeguards were central to the platform’s development.

“An agent that sounds impressive in a demo and one you can trust with an invoice, a contract or a compliance decision are two entirely different things,” Balint said. “We built Outcome1.AI by tackling the technical challenge of combining Frontier AI capabilities with the safeguards a real company needs: accurate sources, clearly defined permissions, relevant context, evidence, and a clear escalation path.”

Alex Balint has more than 22 years of technology industry experience and has held positions at Microsoft, Amazon, and Stripe.

The company said its platform is SOC 2-compliant and certified under the ISO 9001 and ISO 27001 standards. It was designed to meet European data protection, security, and AI governance requirements, including the General Data Protection Regulation and the EU AI Act.

Outcome1.AI is supported by Microsoft for Startups, AWS Activate, NVIDIA Inception, and ElevenLabs Startups. The company said it is developing its own technology and intellectual property in Europe, with an architecture based on controlled access, traceable execution, role-specific permissions, and human oversight.

The launch comes as AI adoption among Romanian businesses remains at 5.2%, compared with an EU average of 20%, according to Eurostat data cited by the company. Meanwhile, 79% of Romanian employers report difficulties filling vacant positions, according to the ManpowerGroup 2026 Talent Shortage Survey.

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Bucharest Politehnica University completes modernization of largest campus in Romania
World.content:
Romania’s largest campus, operated by the Politehnica University in Bucharest, went through an extensive modernization process aimed at improving the quality of accommodation conditions, reducing energy consumption and developing more sustainable university infrastructure, according to a press release published on Monday, August 24.

The modernization, which started in July 2024 and is now complete, was split into two projects co-financed by the EU-backed National Recovery and Resilience Plan, or PNRR. The total investment neared RON 70 million.

The first investment, with a total value of RON 31.76 million, targeted the thermal rehabilitation of the P1–P6 dormitories, which have a total of 1,682 accommodation places. Through the works carried out, the project aimed to increase the energy performance of the six buildings by at least 50%, reducing energy consumption and contributing to better conditions for students living on campus.

The interventions targeted six buildings with a total gross built area of 32,711 square meters, as part of the university’s strategy to modernize infrastructure and transition toward a more energy-efficient campus.

In parallel, Politehnica Bucharest developed the accommodation infrastructure in the Regie area of the city by constructing a new student dormitory with 170 places, an investment with a total value of RON 38.21 million.

The new building has a gross built area of 5,901 square meters and is designed as an energy-efficient accommodation facility. The places are intended for students, with priority given to those from disadvantaged categories, with the social component and equitable access to education being central elements of the project.

Through the two investments, 1,852 accommodation places in the Regie Campus were modernized or newly created, while almost 38,600 square meters of student infrastructure were targeted by the transformation process.

The projects address both the need to improve students’ living conditions and European objectives regarding energy efficiency, sustainability and the green transition in education, according to the press release.

Both projects were implemented between July 19, 2024 and August 31, 2026, with funding through the National Recovery and Resilience Plan.

(Photo source: Universitatea POLITEHNICA din București on Facebook)

World.title: Literary Map launches in Iași next week
World.content:
The Literary Map (Harta Literarǎ) platform will launch in Iași, eastern Romania, on September 4 with a public discussion about how literature can change perceptions of the city. The program will continue on September 5 with a literary walking tour led by Iași-based writer and screenwriter Florin Lăzărescu.

The launch event will begin at 7 p.m. at Acaju Cafe and will feature Lăzărescu, Alecart representative Emil Munteanu, and translator and literary researcher Gabriela Vieru. Cultural journalist and translator Mircea Laslo will moderate the discussion.

Then, on September 5, starting at 11 a.m., Florin Lăzărescu will lead a roughly two-hour tour titled Something Happened to Me Around Here. The route will not be determined in advance but will develop through stories, memories, and contributions from participants.

“We are not visiting monuments or checking off tourist attractions. At most, we will pass by them,” Lăzărescu said. “We walk through Iași driven by stories, apparently heading nowhere. But stories always lead somewhere.”

Participation in the tour is free, but advance registration is required because places are limited. The starting point will be communicated to registered participants.

The Literary Map is an interactive digital platform documenting places featured in books, sites connected to literary history, and locations such as bookstores, libraries, and cafes. After launching in Bucharest and expanding to Brașov and Timișoara, the project is now adding Iași to its network of Romanian literary cities.

The Bucharest section currently includes more than 500 documented locations and over 1,500 connections to literary works and moments from the history of Romanian literature. The platform is available here.

(Photo source: press release)

World.title: Planned Amazon Warehouse in Czechia Faces Local Resistance, Again
World.content:
August deadline

Now being developed by investors Accolade and Garbe, the land of the Borsov Economic Development Zone I was purchased in 1998, with initial zoning plans banking on the construction of a large shopping centre.

This never materialised, and in 2020 developers received zoning approval for the construction of four smaller, separate industrial halls – two of which already have building permits – for a total built area of over 148,000 square metres. Now, the modalities have changed again.

Accolade and Garbe redesigned the entire project into a single, larger building (77,000 square metres in size, about 500 metres long and 15 metres high) specifically for a single tenant – Amazon – on an expected 20-year-lease agreement. About 2,500 people could be employed there, working on a two-shift rotation running almost non-stop from 06:30 to 04:30.

According to Borsov nad Vltavou’s mayor, Romana Rycova, the municipality was only informed about the change at the end of April. And in a video posted on August 13, Mayor Rycova stated that the municipal council must now approve the new variant by the end of August or the investors will redesign the project so they can bypass the municipality’s approval – despite an earlier promise made to residents to “wait as long as you need”.

Representatives for the investors tell BIRN that their earlier communication might have been misconstrued. “When we said that there would be no time pressure, we meant that we would not push municipal council members towards a particular decision or influence how they vote,” says Tomas Mile, project manager at Accolade.

“It did not mean that the project itself had no commercial timetable,” he says, adding that the municipality had been informed since late 2025 about the changes. Rather than a sudden change, Mile describes the new single-building option as “the gradual development of a new option in response to a specific requirement from a prospective tenant”.

Furthermore, he says that while “we understand the concerns raised by residents”, he makes the case that developers have shown goodwill and transparency over the past several months to explain the differences and varying impacts to local residents.

Amazon did not respond to BIRN’s requests for comment.

However, Horakova says she has attended all the public meetings held over the past several months and describes the communication there from developers as “misleading at best”.

Considering the new parameters of the project, she also believes that fresh independent studies should be conducted to upgrade now-outdated environmental impact studies and properly evaluate the impact of such a massive distribution centre on traffic, air-quality, noise pollution and local landscape preservation – just a few of the main concerns expressed by both residents and city officials over the past several months.

“We’ve found no evidence that these studies have been updated for the new design, including in the investor’s own newest technical documentation,” Horakova explains.

Echoing the thoughts of other locals, Horakova accuses the developers of “not being a trustworthy party”. Case in point, Veronika Zacha – who became Garbe’s senior manager for business development for Czechia after moving from Panattoni in 2022 – promised during an August town hall meeting: “We don’t want to pressure the municipality, we also understand that you need to familiarise yourself with all the information, so you have time.”

Yet shortly afterwards, city councillors received an SMS clarifying that developers expect a decision by the end of the month – or else they will move ahead with the four-hall format, according to information from iRozhlas.cz and other local outlets.

World.title: Across the Balkans, Foreign-Backed Luxury Developments Cause Local Anger
World.content:
Since Albania’s ‘Flamingo Revolution’ protests began in May, they have attracted worldwide attention and sparked debate within and outside the Balkans about high-profile investors’ mega-projects.

The protests began in response to the proposed luxury tourism projects on Albania’s Sazan Island and the Zvernec protected coastline. The 1.4 and 4.7 billion euro investments are being led by Affinity Partners, an investment firm run by Donald Trump’s son-in-law, Jared Kushner. Kushner and his wife Ivanka Trump first visited Albania in 2021 and announced plans for the development in 2024.

There has been much to anger locals about the projects, including comments Ivanka Trump made on a podcast where she referred to “discovering” Sazan Island and called the state-owned land a “private island”.

Another more substantive issue is that the Albanian government amended the laws on protected areas on February 22, 2024, allowing five-star hotels to be built inside protected areas. This occurred a month before Kushner’s Albanian projects were announced.

World.title: As Turkey Makes Peace, Kurdish Villagers Who Fled Conflict Contemplate Return
World.content:
“It was the biggest breaking point in my life,” said Aydin Kurdis, remembering the day he and his family left their village 32 years ago.

In the early 1990s, the village of Golord, known officially as Bostancik, was home to around 200 families. Its stone houses sat among hills covered with walnut and fruit trees. Villagers made a living raising livestock, while the orchards provided much of what families needed.

“Before we left the village, I didn't know what pain was. I didn't know what poverty was,” Kurdis said, sitting in front of the house where he was born and eating cucumbers just pulled from the garden down the slope on an August afternoon. “Life was hard on us after we moved to the city.”

Kurdis, 52, lives in Yuksekova, the largest district in Turkey’s southeastern Hakkari province, near the Iranian border. Golord is only a 45-minute drive away, but the final 10 kilometres are unpaved, with potholes dotting the dusty mountain road.

World.title: Experts Warn Proposed Limits on Serbian Officials Campaigning Will Be Ineffective
World.content:
Serbia’s parliament began a debate on amendments to the Law on the Prevention of Corruption on Monday – changes the government says will regulate political campaigning by public officials.

But the anti-corruption watchdog Transparency Serbia claims the measures are unlikely to be effective.

Transparency Serbia said the amendments “create the appearance that restrictions are being introduced, while in practice they will have virtually no effect”.

The watchdog pointed out that the OSCE’s Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) has identified campaigning by public officials as “a key element in blurring the line between the party and the state” in Serbia.

It noted that restrictions would apply only after the publication of electoral lists, and focus solely on the conduct of officials who have been nominated as candidates. As a result, the period before this remains unregulated.

It said this allows officials to use “pseudo-events” like school, hospital and construction site tours to campaign, as long as visits were arranged “before the elections were called”.

With advance notice of election dates, government candidates could schedule events “precisely for the period leading up to the elections, even though these events serve no purpose other than promotion.”

Serbia’s President Aleksandar Vucic has yet to name the precise date for early parliamentary elections, though he has said they will be held in October.

In the meantime, he has embarked on a prolific schedule of visits around the country. Videos from those events appear on media outlets and social networks, showing local people asking the president about infrastructure works and job opportunities. Vucic has also announced numerous giveaways for Serbian adults, alongside a range of subsidies.

This is precisely what Transparency Serbia has in mind with its definition of “promotional activity” by a public official. It says the draft amendments also fail to address ODIHR delivered recommendations on restricting “extraordinary spending by state institutions ahead of elections”.

The watchdog claims that this “helicopter money” – including various measures planned by the government, such as salary increases, lower medicine prices and one-off payments to various different sectors of society – will amount to almost one billion euros by the time the elections are held.

World.title: Translation Cutbacks Limit International Access to North Macedonia’s Literature
World.content:
For a small country of just under two million people, with a small language and an even smaller literary market, getting books translated and published abroad can be crucial to keeping its literature visible beyond its borders.

But for the past two years, Macedonian authors and publishers have had one fewer tool to help them do that. A government programme that provided grants to foreign publishers willing to translate and publish Macedonian books has been suspended since 2024.

The good news is that the Culture Ministry told BIRN there is a “real possibility” it will relaunch a redesigned translation programme later this year. But the bad news is how many excellent books have been denied a wider readership over the last two years.

The Ministry says it typically allocated between one to four million denars [16,000- 65,000 euros] a year for the programme. In 2024, around 84,000 euros was distributed through 31 contracts with foreign publishers. Foreign publishers interested in Macedonian literature could apply to North Macedonia’s Culture Ministry for funding to cover translation costs, reducing the financial risk of publishing authors who are largely unknown in their markets.

Without that incentive, publishers say, some potentially valuable translations simply do not happen. “Our success at international book fairs, such as Frankfurt, is diminished,” says Bojan Sazdov, editor-in-chief of the publishing house TRI and president of the Macedonian Association of Publishers.

“When there is interest in translating a Macedonian book, we can no longer point publishers to the programme as a way of obtaining funding for the translation.”

World.title: Hanging Out: Serbia’s Ruling Party Funfair is About Suppressing Voter Turnout
World.content:
Without Novi Sad’s EXIT Festival, this year’s summer entertainment in Serbia was provided by the ruling Progressive Party funfair.

After a long day visiting factories, inspecting schools, roadworks and parks, government ministers, advisers, and local authorities hung out with people under white tents.

The show included music, dancing, feasting, and live television broadcasts.

Just in the first 18 days of August, President Aleksandar Vucic made 64 live appearances on Serbian TV, according to the Centre for Research, Transparency and Accountability, CRTA.

Not quite a formal election campaign, if you ask Vucic. Something between a ‘presidential tour’ and a prequel to the actual election campaign that everyone expects in the autumn.

Such media domination is familiar to those who follow populism; party leaders skip formal institutions and speak directly to the people.

When this media takeover combines with the atmosphere of a village fair, people tend to ask private questions publicly. Here’s where the media literacy classes provided by Serbia’s tabloids begin paying off.

World.title: Seven Days: Ukrainian Recalls Captivity at Hands of Bosnian Serb
World.content:
Mykola said he spent most of his captivity in a forest pit between the villages of Shybene and Krasny Rih. He said his hands were tied and there were rats in the pit. When he killed one after it bit him, he said a soldier hit him in the head with a rifle butt. The soldier told him: “Kill another one and I’ll shoot you.”

Mykola said he saw other captives being tortured.

According to the Ukrainian Media Initiative for Human Rights, MIHR, which inspected the site, the pits were some 90 centimetres deep; those inside had to sit in water; they lost feeling in their legs; and they had to urinate and defecate in the same spot.

Lidiia Tarash, a journalist and head of the documentation department of MIHR, said the researchers were led to the site by Mykola. A dead body was found in one of the pits, as well as the remains of Russian military rations, fortifications and ammunition boxes.

MIHR identified five locations in the area where civilians were held and documented the capture of 43 individuals. Its findings helped lead to the indictment of Savicic. Multiple interlocutors said Serbs were among the Russian forces. Everyone named Savicic as being in charge, Tarash said.

In late May last year, the X account of Milorad Dodik, then the president of Bosnia’s predominantly Serb-populated Republika Srpska entity, published a photo of himself visiting the representative office of the Serbian Orthodox Church in Russia. Savicic was in the photo.

Britain imposed sanctions on him in November 2024.

Mykola said Savicic and his unit are the reason he still has trouble sleeping at night. His back was damaged during his captivity and he said he is haunted by the word ‘liberation’, which he heard over and over again from his captors.

“They kept saying: ‘We came to liberate you.’ But liberate me from what? From a normal life?”

Savicic’s trial is a matter of justice and responsibility, he said.

“None of them can say: ‘I was just following orders’ and to think they aren’t responsible for it,” Mykola told BIRN. “Someone gave you an order, but it was still your choice whether to execute it.”

World.title: August 25th 1991 – The Battle of Vukovar Begins
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – On August the 25th, 1991, the battle of Vukovar began, marking the start of one of the most devastating chapters of the Croatian War of Independence.

The most harrowing episode of the Homeland War began on this day in the eastern Croatian city of Vukovar when members of the JNA from the barracks in Vukovar joined Serbian paramilitary units. After doing so, they jointly launched an attack on both Borovo and Vukovar. Index writes that the siege lasted 87 days and transformed Vukovar into a symbol of Croatian resistance and heroism during the Homeland War.

the initial conflicts begin

Slobodan Milošević – NATO

After Croatia declared independence on the 25th of June 1991, local conflicts in eastern Slavonia had already begun. For centuries Vukovar had been a city where Croats, Serbs and Hungarians lived in peace, but the situation changed at the end of the 1980s with the rise of nationalism and the policies of Slobodan Milošević, who wanted to consolidate power in Belgrade.

On the 25th of August, the JNA left the barracks with six tanks that blocked the road towards Bogdanovci. The very next day a new attack on Borovo began that lasted the entire day. The firing briefly stopped, and already during the following night another offensive started. By the 30th of August, the clashes continued one after another, after which a short ceasefire occurred during which weapons were delivered to the Croats in Vukovar from Slavonski Brod, Vinkovci and Zagreb. At that time Mile Dedaković arrived in Vukovar and organised the army and defensive positions in the city.

the serbs wanted to go all the way to zagreb

The JNA commander in Vukovar was Života Panić, who wanted to capture Vukovar as quickly as possible in order to prevent further mobilisation of the Croatian army. The original JNA plan was to take Vukovar and Osijek, then occupy all of Slavonia so that the road towards Varaždin and Zagreb would be open. However, problems already appeared when fewer than two thousand Croatian soldiers withstood numerous JNA attacks in Vukovar.

The plan was not helped by the fact that only 13% of those fit for military service responded to the call-up. After news arrived of the large number of casualties in Vukovar, many soldiers deserted, and by the end of 1991 there were six thousand open court proceedings against deserters. The failure of mobilisation meant the cancellation of the grandiose conquest of the whole of continental Croatia, culminating with Zagreb.

the fall of vukovar and horrific crimes against humanity

Vukovar endured a three-month siege in which seven thousand projectiles fell daily. On the 18th of November the city fell, although only 10–15% of the buildings actually remained. The rest were entirely destroyed. The army entered the city and the expulsion of the non-Serb population and horrific war crimes and crimes against humanity began. Neighbours accused other neighbours of being a defender, informed on where families were located, and just a few days later more than 250 civilians were brutally killed at Ovčara in one single night.

The sight of the murder of hundreds of innocent civilians – Perun

The total number of victims is measured in the thousands of people, and there are probably other undiscovered mass graves containing those who disappeared during the war. The Serbian government under Aleksandar Vučić refuses to cooperate so that the remaining mysteries from the war can finally be resolved.

The city was returned to Croatia only in 1998 through peaceful reintegration, and the 18th of November is marked in Croatia as the Day of Remembrance of the Victims of the Homeland War. Vukovar has still not recovered from the war: today it has just over 25,000 inhabitants, while in the years before the war it was home to 45,000 people. As the largest Croatian port on the Danube, Vukovar was a busy centre of trade and transport.

Today. it is only a shadow of what it once was, and Croatian authorities from the 1990s until today have not invested enough in it. It was the fifth-largest city in the former Socialist Republic of Croatia, then larger even than Zadar, while today it is not ranked among the ten largest Croatian cities.
