World.title: Croatia is Full of Tourists, But “Coolcations” Are Increasingly Popular
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia remains full of tourists, but with horrifically hot temperatures now the norm, “coolcations” pose a serious threat to hotter countries as they become increasingly popular.

The director of the Croatian National Tourist Board, Kristjan Staničić, said that there are still more than a million tourists per day in Croatia and that August is so far at the level of last year’s results. Index reports that when speaking on HRT’s Dnevnik, Staničić said that Croatia is still at the peak of the tourist season, but he did not want to forecast what August would be like until the end. “For now I can say that August is at the level of last year’s figures,” he said.

“coolcations” are becoming more and more popular as people tire of overwhelming heat

Staničić also commented on a new tourist trend, the so-called “coolcation”, or the growing interest in cooler destinations in northern Europe. As he explained, because of ever higher summer temperatures and repeated heatwave cycles, many people are looking for places where July and August are more pleasant than on the Mediterranean and in southern Europe. He believes this trend will continue in the coming years and that the tourism sector must be prepared for it. He recalled that climate change has been affecting travellers’ decisions for a longer time, but considers that Croatia, thanks to its diverse offer, can respond to such changes as well.

As an example he mentioned Gorski kotar and Lika, where lower temperatures, quality accommodation, good gastronomy and contents linked to nature and active holidays can be found even during the summer.

inspectors clamp down on illegal rentals and s

Staničić also commented on the intensified work of the tourist inspection this season. Because of illegal operation, eight campsites, 23 holiday homes, 56 apartments, one smaller hotel and one hostel have been closed. He thanked the staff of the State Inspectorate and everyone involved in combating the black market. “Unfortunately, this is a phenomenon that is present and to which a response is needed,” he said. He added that cooperation of all institutions, tourist boards and competent services in the field is important, especially when there is knowledge of unregistered guests or facilities that provide services without being registered for it.

croatian tourism requires proper order

Staničić also spoke about the amendments to the Hospitality Activity Act, against which the Association “Save Small Family Renters” has submitted an objection to the European Commission. They object, among other things, to re-categorisation every decade, the need for co-owners’ consent in multi-apartment buildings, and the conditions for obtaining host status. Staničić expects the law primarily to help in combating the black market.

As one of the most important novelties he singled out the introduction of a registration number that every accommodation service provider will have to have if they want to advertise on global platforms. According to him, such a system should enable more effective control of both accommodation facilities and the online platforms on which they are advertised.

“Everyone has the right to turn to the European Commission,” Staničić said, adding that Croatia has taken over the European acquis which includes the introduction of a registration number. He assessed that this measure should be one of the key tools for combating the black market and “introducing order into Croatian tourism”.

World.title: Croatian Railway Ambitions Tie in With European Defence Efforts
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatian railway ambitions are closely linked with European defence efforts, as the country’s “decade of the railway” is still not really being felt on the ground by most.

Any reason for the renewal and development of the railway system in Croatia is very useful, including the security and defence one. But its civilian role remains primary. Index/Deutsche Welle/Igor Lasic reports that following two serious railway traffic incidents at the beginning of this month in Croatia, this mode of passenger and freight transport is once again a topic for the Croatian public.

Moreover, the general public has been reminded of the fact that Croatia is apparently currently in the middle of its “decade of the railway”. This is a state project for the development of this long-neglected mode of transport, with an investment of six billion euros for new tracks and vehicles. Yet despite years of reconstruction, the results are still not really visible on the ground, even though some concrete works have long been planned. The announced “railway renaissance” will therefore clearly still have to wait, and the recent traffic accidents have uncomfortably highlighted this uncertainty.

On top of everything, a new element has been included in the reasoning for the renewal of the Croatian railway sector, and that’s the wider European defence system. Europe is rapidly arming itself, and Croatia has also bought, among other things, more than 40 German Leopard 2 tanks. These, however, because of their exceptional weight, require equally exceptional railway transport capacities. All of this ultimately enters into the final calculation of the development project of the public company Croatian Railways. On the other hand, its relative urgency and the need for centralisation of the system somewhat remove the possibility of imminent privatisation of the sector, which until recently was quite realistic.

so long, privatisation

“Only through the security sphere and social cohesion around the issue of defence have we come to the conclusion that the railway must be managed by the state if we want an efficient system,” Ante Klečina, a railway expert and lecturer at the Department of Sustainable Mobility and Logistics of the University Sjever (North) in Koprivnica and Varaždin, told DW. He referred to the experience of some more developed European countries, such as Great Britain, whose experiments with railway privatisation ended rather ignominiously. Services became of poor quality and too expensive, the system failed in various aspects, and over time it was abandoned.

“First and foremost should be their functionality for civilian needs and, in fact, the organisation of civilisation,” Klečina continues, “which is relevant at every moment if we do not put that priority out of our minds. Whoever swears by the advantages of market mechanisms forgets that they are not developmentally suitable for large public systems, those that enable basic requirements.” In his opinion, the same applies to other elementary systems, e.g. healthcare, education and the judiciary, etc. The private sector, says Klečina, can be a supplement in certain segments, but the backbone must remain public.

“The reason is the necessity of central planning of such systems, as well as their primarily non-profit task, but also the need for enormous investments for which private individuals usually have neither the capacity nor the interest. Having seen this in practice, Europe has recently abandoned the idea of privatising railways, and the defence topic came afterwards as an additional reason,” considers Ante Klečina, formerly president of the Railway Alliance in the Republic of Croatia. He further notes that this mode of transport has no equal with regard to a series of key factors: above all overall cost-effectiveness, economic multiplier effects and environmental suitability.

central planning will always be needed

Socioeconomist Toni Prug, for his part, believes that behind the question of Croatian railways lies the general problem of political and scientific rejection of planning and public production as a relic of the past. That past concerns the period of socialism and Yugoslavia, and everything connected with it remained at the very least stigmatised after the war in Croatia. “In reality, however, all successful states are huge public production systems,” says Prug, “in which planning decides on the largest budgets within economies, on interventions whose importance for the population surpasses the importance of decisions that market actors make.”

This assistant professor at the Faculty of Humanities and Social Sciences of the University of Rijeka highlights the rule in business that when a market actor makes a mistake, i.e. when things go badly, competition replaces him. “And railways, like all other production systems of a public character that are physically fixed and have monopoly status, need to be carefully planned. Mistakes are much harder to correct. They are also managed differently, different parameters are optimised, a focus on profit does not help. It often cannot even be the goal; the goals are determined by the plan.” At the same time the question arises of whether the Republic of Croatia has the professional staff for designing and implementing this.

“private goals have prevailed over practicality”

“Our profession and managerial staff are educated through faculty and professional curricula that say almost nothing about why and how to produce systems and services of a public character, and why they are superior for certain needs,” Prug is convinced, adding that this knowledge still exists in some Croatian public systems, while in others it has collapsed and been left to spontaneity. In his assessment, the City of Zagreb represents a recent example in Croatia that planning can return and capacities be rebuilt. And on higher-quality, data- and analysis-based foundations, which does not concern the railway but can be a general model.

Toni Prug, who in his scientific work has dealt quite a bit with the topic of public sector management, finally conveyed to us the impression that Croatian Railways have so far been a kind of victim of the oil and automobile lobby. “Their private and profit goals have prevailed over the practicality, efficiency, safety and ecological superiority of modern railway systems,” he told DW. Such a hierarchy could change soon thanks to military priorities. But the future of the railway and of social development in general will certainly not be bright if its primarily civilian advantages remain somewhere beside the tracks.

World.title: Croatia Among European Record Holders for Firefighter Numbers
World.content:
August the 25th, 2026 – Croatia is among the European record holders when it comes to firefighter numbers as the overall number within Europe has fallen.

Poslovni reports that the total number of firefighters across the EU fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a year that was the worst in EU history in terms of burned area.

Croatia is among the European record holders for firefighter numbers, holding one of the highest shares of professional firefighters in employment in the entire EU. Back in 2025, they accounted for 0.43 percent of total employment, making Croatia second among the 22 EU Member States for which data has been made available. This places Croatia right behind Greece (0.47 percent), according to Euronews. The EU average was 0.18 percent. Portugal follows with 0.33 percent, while the lowest shares are recorded by the Netherlands (0.05), Austria (0.07) and Sweden (0.10 percent).

Across the entire EU there were around 372,400 professional firefighters. Germany had the most, 57,700, followed by France with 47,700 and Italy with 43,500. Next come Poland with 40,000 and Spain with 38,500; the four largest EU economies together account for 187,400 firefighters, or 50.3 percent of the total number. The overall figure in the Union fell from 390,600 in 2024 to 372,400 in 2025, a drop of 18,200 people in a single year that was the worst in EU history for burned areas. The European Trade Union Confederation and EPSU call this drop “reckless cuts” and note that Poland lost 9,000 and France lodt 4,100 firefighters.

Croatia doesn’t rank among the leaders in total numbers, but its share of total employment is among the highest. Eurostat data refers to professional firefighters, including forest firefighters, but not volunteer firefighters. The data also doesn’t show precisely how many professional firefighters are specialised specifically in fighting open-air fires.

The data comes at a time when Europe is facing an ever-growing fire risk. According to the European Forest Fire Information System (EFFIS) by the 13th of August, the figure had risen to 568,415 hectares from 1,647 fires. For comparison, 2025 was the most destructive season ever recorded in the EU, with 1,079,538 hectares burned in 25 of the 27 EU Member States.

For 2026 the EU has secured a fleet of 22 firefighting aircraft and five helicopters, and in the event of major fires member states can request additional firefighters and equipment through the European Civil Protection Mechanism. In addition, a record 777 firefighters from 14 European countries have been pre-positioned in Cyprus, Greece, Italy, France, Spain and Portugal. Croatia contributes two medium amphibious aircraft to the European fleet, and in 2026 the Commission is also opening a new regional firefighting base in Cyprus with capacity for six aircraft.

World.title: Zadar Was the Most Expensive Croatian City in July
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Zadar was the most expensive Croatian city of all in July, with strong economic growth very much being a double edged sword for the area.

Buying basic groceries has long been a negotiation with one’s own wallet for people in Croatia, but in July, the toughest conditions spilled over onto the area of Zadar County. The basic consumer basket for a four-member family here reached a record 498 euros, reports HRT. Morski writes that a basic daily trip to the shop or the market has become a source of stress for many, and citizens openly complain about the constant quiet price rises:

a previously bustling market sits almost empty

“Vegetables have become very expensive, they get used up quickly, you need a lot of them. Fruit is also very expensive and it seems to me that meat has gone up, fish has also gone up a lot,” says Zadar resident Katja. For pensioners, the situation is even more alarming. Every single purchase requires calculation and a search for discounts: “I really don’t go to the shops much. You buy where you can according to your wallet and that’s it, and yes it’s expensive, it’s definitely expensive, this isn’t for us pensioners, it’s abnormal,” is the honest assessment of Zorica, who lives on the Zagreb–Zadar route.

That consumer habits are changing and that people are buying significantly less than in previous years was confirmed to us by the sellers themselves. Zadar’s market, which in July should be bustling with local and foreign visitors, at times looks unusually empty.

Seller Rada briefly summarises the problem: “Everything is expensive, the shops too.” Her colleague Ilonka points out that even regular customers have thinned out their visits: “There are no customers. I normally have my own customers, but look, two people are walking through the market.”

the price of rapid expansion

How did it come about that Zadar took the top spot for the most expensive groceries? Experts explain that the answer lies in a specific economic effect of the rapid expansion of the regional economy.

Assoc. Prof. Dr. Jurica Bosna, Head of the Department of Economics at the University of Zadar, clarifies the background to this trend: “Nobody wants to have the most expensive basket of goods, but it still shows that the county is developing strongly, and this is an effect known in economics, when we grow faster than we perhaps should according to some optimal economic rates, then it’s unfortunately inevitable that inflation will develop and that the result will be like this,” he stated.

While macroeconomic indicators record the growth and development of the whole of Zadar County, for the general public, that statistic brings no comfort whatsoever. The vicious circle in which the economy advances strongly while prices rise in an unbridled way leaves the deepest mark on household budgets. Since wages and pensions do not come close to keeping pace, the consumer baskets of Zadar residents remain ever emptier.

World.title: Meet the Croatian Road Often Compared to the Legendary Route 66
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – There’s an incredibly scenic Croatian road frequently compared to the legendary Route 66 across the pond in the USA – and a drive along it is nothing less than breathtaking.

When someone mentions Route 66, most people immediately think of the endless American highway, old motels, neon signs and kilometres of asphalt running through some of the most famous landscapes of the United States. Few realise that Croatia has its own very interesting road with the same number in Croatia as well. It goes without saying that Croatia’s D66 doesn’t have thousands of kilometres or hold the status of an American icon, but because of the designation it carries and the landscapes it passes through, it resembles the US legend in many ways.

Putni kofer writes that it has been referred to many times as the Istrian version of Route 66 and presented it as a road that evokes old, nostalgic Istria. Today, the impressive D66 connects Pula, Labin and Vozilići with Opatija, and according to the official decision on the classification of public roads it is about 90 kilometres long. Still, if the goal is to find its most spectacular part, one should head towards the eastern coast of Istria, that is, towards Plomin.

the most impressive section begins at plomin

Plomin is an excellent place to start this short road trip. The old fortified little town sits on a hill above Plomin Bay, and right by the D66 there is also a rest area with a viewpoint. A few kilometres further on there is another spot from which the view opens towards the Kvarner Bay, Cres and Lošinj.

After that begins the stretch that makes it worth driving this road slowly. The asphalt winds under the slopes of Učka, the sea is almost constantly somewhere in sight, and on the other side of the Kvarner Cres appears. In certain places the road runs high enough above the coast that the view feels almost like from a large natural balcony. The greatest advantage of state road D66 is precisely that, over a relatively short distance, viewpoints, medieval places, steep coastline and well-known Kvarner resorts alternate.

the stunning Brseč, a town from 1102 towering above at 157 metres above the sea

SONY DSC

One of the places worth turning off the road for is Brseč. D66 reaches it after driving along the slopes of Učka, and the old part of the settlement is situated on a cliff 157 metres high above the expanse of Kvarner. The first written records of Brseč date back to 1102, although the area was inhabited much earlier. It is particularly interesting that the history of Brseč is also directly linked to the road that passes this way. The Tourist Board of Mošćenička Draga notes that the economic development of the place in the 19th century was spurred by the new road from Pula towards Plomin, then Brseč and Mošćenice and further towards Rijeka.

Today the medieval character of Brseč can still be felt in the narrow streets and passages of the old town core. From the cliff by the little church of St Magdalene one of the most beautiful views in the area opens up, while from the western entrance to the place Cres can be seen. Beneath the high rocks a completely different world is hidden. Between Brseč and Mošćenička Draga lie the beaches of Uboka and Jelenšćica, which can be reached on foot via paths that descend from the main road. The coastline in this area is extremely indented, with steep cliffs, tiny coves and stone fishermen’s cottages by the sea.

from ancient towns to well-known resorts

After Brseč the scenery changes again. D66 continues towards Mošćenička Draga, one of the best-known places at the foot of Učka. The road approaches the sea, and the high rocks gradually give way to beaches and a more built-up coastline. Mošćenička Draga developed from a fishing harbour, and today it is especially known for the long pebble beach of Sipar. Its pebbles were formed by the action of the stream that descends from the slopes of Učka and the sea that has shaped them over the years.

Just a few kilometres further on lies Medveja, another place along the D66 with a long pebble beach. After it comes Lovran, where the whole drive takes on a more elegant appearance. Instead of the almost wild coast around Brseč, old villas, gardens and houses appear along the road that recall the time when this part of the Kvarner became one of the favourite resorts of Central Europe.

just over 90 kilometres from pula to opatija

The entire D66 from Pula to Opatija is a little over 90 kilometres long, but for a panoramic outing the stretch from Plomin to Opatija is especially interesting. According to the kilometres listed on the EuroVelo 8 route, from the Plomin area to Opatija it is roughly thirty kilometres of driving.

That may not sound like much, but that is precisely the charm of this road. In a short drive one passes Plomin Bay, open views towards Cres and Lošinj, medieval Brseč, the steep slopes of Učka, Mošćenička Draga, Medveja, Lovran and finally Opatija. Although it forms part of the Croatian cycling route EuroVelo 8, this road should not be imagined as a lonely carriageway without cars. On the official route website traffic on certain sections is marked as moderate, and from Medveja towards Rijeka as heavy, so if you decide to cover it on four wheels, extra caution is recommended for cyclists.

World.title: Drniš Bypass Construction to Benefit Šibenik Port
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – The future Drniš bypass will greatly benefit the local economy, as well as Šibenik Port directly.

The construction of the second and third phases of the complex Drniš bypass project has begun, with the client being Hrvatske ceste (Croatian roads), and the contractor being the consortium of Texo Molior from Cavtat and CGP Slovenia.

Transport Minister Butković pointed out that after securing the financial structure and signing the contract, work on the project is now starting. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that he also noted that it is a technically complex intervention with a route that includes two overpasses, two viaducts and a bridge over the Čikola River. Speaking about the continuation of activities on the future Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, Minister Butković highlighted that the preparation of project documentation for the section from Drniš towards the Oklaj interchange is in an advanced stage.

a 34 million euro investment

After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, so the project is being gradually prepared for phased implementation. He also referred to the reconstruction of state roads DC56 and DC33, which connect the Drniš area with Split and Knin respectively, and whose total reconstruction value is around 34 million euros. After the design of that phase is completed, a tender is planned to be issued, gradually preparing the project for implementation.

“A tender has already been issued for one, the other is in preparation, so there will be a great deal of investment in road infrastructure here in the area of the town of Drniš and Šibenik-Knin County,” added Minister Butković. Šibenik-Knin County Prefect Paško Rakić stressed that the Drniš bypass is of great importance for the entire county, especially for the traffic connection of its hinterland, and that residents of the wider Drniš and Knin areas will use it.

“The Šibenik–Drniš–Knin expressway, as well as this bypass, is the backbone of Šibenik-Knin County in terms of traffic, and it is as important to us as the Pelješac Bridge,” emphasised Prefect Rakić. “This is historic for us,” emphasised Drniš Mayor Tomislav Dželalija, noting that generations of Drniš residents have waited decades for this project.

a massive development boost for the area

Expressing satisfaction that the works were ceremonially started today, he pointed out that the removal of transit traffic, along with increased traffic safety, will create additional preconditions for the expansion of the economic zone and the further development of the town. He added that the Government of the Republic of Croatia, through strong investments including road and railway infrastructure, is giving impetus to the town’s development, and thanked them for the projects being implemented in the Drniš area.

President of the Management Board of Hrvatske ceste Ivica Budimir emphasised that the project has a broader economic significance for Drniš, especially because of the direct connection of the industrial zone with the Šibenik port.

“After this road is constructed, the industrial zone in the entire Drniš area will develop significantly faster, better and to a higher quality, and become much more competitive,” emphasised Budimir. Speaking about the technical demands of the project, he added that almost ten percent of the route consists of viaducts, while the most significant structure is the large bridge over the Čikola River canyon, with a span of 220 metres, along with a series of other structures along the route.

World.title: Baćina Lakes – Meet Croatia’s Freshwater Phenomenon
World.content:
August the 24th, 2026 – Baćina Lakes are Croatia’s freshwater phenomenon, with water warmer than that in the sea and the ability to swim year-round.

If you’ve ever driven from Makarska down toward Dubrovnik, you’ll have passed by them. You probably glanced left for a second, spotted a blue patch amid the greenery, and continued on toward the sea. Yet there, just a few kilometres from Ploče, lies something no other Croatian town has: seven lakes within the boundaries of a single town. They are called the Baćina Lakes and bear names that sound like a list from an old book: Oćuša, Crniševo, Podgora, Sladinac, Šipak, Plitko Lake, and Vrbnik.

Putni kofer writes that six of them are interconnected by narrow passages, so you can paddle or boat from one into another, while Vrbnik, which is also the smallest, is completely separate from the rest. Together they cover about 138 hectares.

they’re warmer than the sea

The Baćina Lakes form a cryptodepression, meaning their surface is only slightly above sea level, while their bottoms lie deep below it. Although they are just a step from the sea and surrounded by permeable limestone, the lakes are freshwater. Some springs are nevertheless directly connected to the sea, so salt water appears in the deeper layers. In the Klokun area near Plitko Lake there is a spring that supplies drinking water to the town of Ploče and the surrounding area.

During the scorching summer, the water in the lakes is noticeably warmer than the sea, with tourist sources citing a difference of roughly three degrees. Because of this, the swimming season here starts earlier and ends later than on the coast. The best-known bathing spots are those near the Mindel spring, and the hidden coves and small beaches are reached by kayak, paddleboard, or traditional Neretva boat.

links with queen teuta

Legend has it that the Illyrian Queen Teuta adored this area, and the lakes are still called Teuta’s pearls. Historians, however, have their own evidence and explanations. Near Sladinac Lake the remains of the Roman settlement of Praetoria have been found, along with the remains of an early Christian basilica from the 6th century and a necropolis of stećci tombstones.

Around the lakes a walking and cycling path about 15 kilometres long has been arranged, with benches, springs, and information boards. In 2020 the Public Institution for Protected Natural Areas of Dubrovnik-Neretva County installed 19 educational boards about dragonflies, amphibians, reptiles, and birds. Near the Oćuša spring there is a bird-watching hide, and the lakes also contain three small islets, one of which is named the Island of Love. The entire area forms part of the Natura 2000 ecological network, within two zones of the Neretva Delta, as a habitat for strictly protected and endemic species.

a worthwhile stop off on a long drive south…

A visit to the Baćina Lakes is truly an experience you will remember for a lifetime. Walking the paths that wind right beside the lakes will reveal scenes covered in water lilies, the reflection of clouds mirrored on the still water, and the song of rare birds that creates an almost meditative atmosphere.

Here you can also swim in crystal-clear water that provides refreshment during the great heat, and a special experience comes when the sun sets and the whole landscape is immersed in golden and pink tones. Then the lakes take on an almost fairy-tale appearance. It is a perfect moment for a photograph, but also for simply enjoying the silence of nature.

In the heart of the summer season, a parking space at the viewpoint along the main road is almost impossible to find. Down by the lakes themselves, however, there are usually no crowds. Most travellers photograph the view and drive on, while those who go down to the water, sit in a boat, or cycle a loop are completely enchanted and, like us, probably think: “How is this place not far better known?”

World.title: Artist says giving up artworks to cover fraud loss hurts less than giving up studios
World.content:
In May, the Estonian Artists' Association (EKL) was defrauded of nearly €700,000. To cover part of the financial loss, works from the association's collection and newly donated pieces will be auctioned. EKL board member Jaanus Samma said it is less painful to give up artworks than the studios that belong to the association.

In addition to donated works, pieces from the association's collection will go under the hammer from October 8 to 10. They were mostly acquired from spring and fall exhibitions featuring well‑known Estonian artists.

"We decided to put part of the collection up for sale. Certainly not everything, and a very important part will remain. But when faced with the choice of selling a studio where artists work or a painting, it is less painful to give up the painting," Samma, a member of the art infrastructure council and the EKL board, said.

Rethinking the collection

"Our plan is not to enter the auction market. This will definitely be very different from classic fall auctions. We wanted the diversity of our association to be reflected in the auction. That is why all techniques and mediums are represented," Samma added.

"These decisions had to be made. In every bad situation, you have to look for something positive. On the positive side, this gave us a chance to rethink our collection. To understand what the focus is and what it could be in the future. That also made our choices easier, because we decided to keep all works that depict artistic life or where artists portray each other, their work, their studios," he said.

Graphic works with duplicate prints will also be sold. "We will sell one and keep the other. That does not hurt us as much. Fresh works donated by artists also play a major role. Even before the decision to hold an auction, some artists contacted us and wanted to donate. That is how the idea grew. There are well‑known names from different generations," Samma said.

Sales potential considered

The association does not yet dare to estimate how much money the auction will bring in. "We certainly do not expect to cover the entire lost amount. But even part of it would be a big help. When making the selection, we naturally thought about what might have sales potential, let's put it that way. What might be popular in a good sense, what fits the market context and what is collected," he explained.

On September 18, an exhibition will open in the ARS building in Tallinn for a couple of weeks, where people can view the works headed for auction. "I recommend coming not only to those who plan to buy something, because it will be a very diverse exhibition full of good art. The auction itself will take place online and bids can be made from home. In real life, these works are still quite different."

Samma said that in some ways the crisis has already passed. "All bills have been paid, life goes on, exhibitions are happening. The first shock is over and life has normalized. At the same time, the ax is still hanging overhead, because the association has taken out a loan and that loan must be repaid. In that sense, the crisis is still ongoing."

World.title: EDF: Attacks on Russian online store warehouses affecting situation on the front line
World.content:
Successful Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure and online retailers' warehouses have disrupted supplies to Russian forces and are affecting both daily life in Russia and the situation on the front, Lt. Col. Marten Suur said.

Successful Ukrainian drone strikes on Russia's oil infrastructure and warehouses belonging to online retailers are having a noticeable impact on, for example, fuel supplies to the Russian military and the availability of key electronic components, Suur said.

"The Russian army has priority when it comes to fuel supplies in Russia. But because the price of fuel on the black market has risen five- or sixfold compared with the spring, there is pressure at intermediate points in the logistics chain to steal it. As a result, less fuel reaches frontline units. Until now, fuel has been stolen before it reaches the army and the authorities have turned a blind eye to it. But now there is nothing left to steal, which makes logistics at lower levels considerably more difficult," Suur said.

Frontline units have also used fuel as a form of currency, selling or trading it to obtain supplies they lack, he added.

"That channel has now dried up. In addition, attacks on retail chains and warehouses belonging to Wildberries and Ozon have made all kinds of essential electronic equipment less readily available — drones, tablets, power banks and generators, all of which are badly needed at the front. We cannot speak of a major turning point, but we can speak of sand in the gears," Suur said.

Ukrainian forces have also successfully attacked Russian space centers, which in turn reduces Russian forces' ability to carry out long-range strikes and use drones in attacks, he said.

"This is slowing Russia's efforts to develop an alternative to Starlink — they need to launch a large number of satellites to do that. Their launch vehicles are expendable. They do not have a comparable reusable rocket and if their production capacity is reduced, they cannot put as many satellites into orbit, meaning the development of their own domestic equivalent of Starlink will be delayed," Suur said.

"This also hampers long-range strikes, as well as the use of smaller drones on the front line that require an internet connection or systems that need one for geolocation," he added.

Russian airstrikes have also caused extensive destruction, particularly in Kyiv. On August 20, Russian forces carried out one of their largest air attacks on Kyiv to date, killing at least 16 people.

"They used a highly coordinated combination of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles and drones, primarily to penetrate Ukrainian air defenses. There were various targets. Ukraine, of course, does not disclose everything that was hit or what it believes was being targeted, but various industrial facilities and warehouses were struck, as were some medical facilities and civilian infrastructure, including residential buildings," Suur said.

Fighting remains fiercest in Donetsk Oblast, while Russian forces have also begun putting pressure on Kharkiv from the north.

"The overall number of attacks is increasing, as are the numbers of indirect-fire attacks and drone strikes and some gains have been made here and there. In the direction of Kostiantynivka, the Russians are advancing slowly but steadily," Suur said.

Marten Suur and Reimo Sildvee. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

World.title: Photos: Roadworks uncover cobblestone road on Tallinn's Kreutzwaldi tänav
World.content:
Cobblestones uncovered during roadworks at a central Tallinn street cannot receive heritage status because it lies outside the Old Town.

The road and utility works began on Monday on Kreutzwaldi tänav, including milling, which involves removing the top surface of the road.

It was this process which uncovered the cobblestones — not an unusual occurrence in and around central Tallinn. However, such discoveries cannot be subject to heritage protection if they lie outside the Old Town (Vanalinn), which Kreutzwaldi does by more than a kilometer.

Triin Tõrs-Ojari, head of the advisory service at the City of Tallinn's heritage conservation department, noted cobblestone roads are one of the features of the historic Old Town and, as such, are protected only in that district. Outside the Old Town, cobblestones are usually concealed below more recent asphalt and other surfacing and are not restored, she added.

Where possible, the older roadways remain preserved beneath the newer asphalt. They may sometimes be reused elsewhere as an element of public-space design, Tõrs-Ojari said.

World.title: Oil shale producers warn EU plan would make oil production unprofitable in five years
World.content:
The heads of Estonia's two major oil shale companies told Prime Minister Kristen Michal that without a European Commission exemption, oil shale production would stop being economically viable within five years. Yet on Thursday, a new oil plant will be formally opened in Auvere.

The European Commission released proposals a month ago on how to change the greenhouse gas emissions trading system. Among other things, the commission suggested reducing free carbon quotas intended for industry.

Eesti Energia chief executive Andrus Durejko and Viru Keemia Grupp (VKG) chief executive Ahti Asmann sent a letter to the prime minister a few days ago, noting that if the quota system were truly redesigned as the commission proposes, all oil shale production would become uncompetitive as early as 2031–2033.

Reducing emissions extremely difficult

Free quotas for the oil shale industry would not directly disappear, but companies would be required to invest in reducing emissions in oil production. Eesti Energia said the catch is that decarbonizing or greening oil production is extremely difficult.

"Free quotas do not actually disappear, but they must be invested in the same facility as a mandatory requirement, which makes it unreasonable in terms of production cost. [...] Oil inevitably contains carbon. It cannot be eliminated; it is a fossil fuel. We cannot make this technology better," Durejko said.

Oil shale industry representatives want an exemption for Estonia that would remain in place as long as the European Union imports liquid fuels. This means free quotas should remain at the same level next decade as they are now, the producers wrote.

VKG chief executive Ahti Asmann said that if Estonia does not receive an exemption from the European Commission's plan, the company's tax burden would multiply at the beginning of the next decade.

"It is clear that if we currently pay €50 million in taxes annually and our tax burden doubles or triples, then very few companies can operate efficiently in such an environment," Asmann said.

Andrus Durejko Autor/allikas: Priit Mürk/ERR

Against this backdrop, Eesti Energia plans to officially open its newest oil plant in Auvere on Thursday. According to Durejko, the plant is now operating at its nominal capacity.

"This five-and-a-half-year construction saga has come to an end. Now the goal is to produce oil at the lowest possible cost and to market it and promote Estonia's exports," Durejko said.

If the laws remain as they are now, Eesti Energia has calculated that the new oil plant opening Thursday will be economically viable for 14 years.

Heat production in Iru may also become unreasonable

Under the European Commission's proposal, the emissions trading system would also extend to waste incineration.

In a letter to the Climate Ministry, Eesti Energia's head of government and partner relations Triin Reisner noted that taxing waste burned at the Iru power plant with carbon quotas risks making landfill disposal cheaper than exporting waste.

Iru plant near Tallinn. Source: Siim Lõvi /ERR

Eesti Energia's analysis showed that if the carbon quota price rises above €105 per metric ton, Iru would lose its competitive advantage in waste incineration compared to biomass, meaning wood chips.

Right now, the carbon quota price is about €80 per metric ton. The European Commission itself expects, according to Eesti Energia, that by 2030 the price will rise to €110 per metric ton.

If Iru is pushed out of Tallinn's heat market, Eesti Energia said landfill disposal of waste would increase and the city would have to burn significantly more wood for heating.

World.title: Tallinn mulls taking education ministry to court over new obligations
World.content:
Tallinn Deputy Mayor Andrei Kante said the burden of individually assisting young people who fail to meet compulsory education requirements could prompt the city to take legal action against the Ministry of Education.

As of Monday, there were 761 young people in Tallinn who had graduated from basic school but whose plans for continuing their education were not yet known.

Speaking on ETV's morning program "Terevisioon," where he gave an overview of the situation and criticized the ministry, Tallinn Deputy Mayor Andrei Kante (Center Party) said Tallinn and other local governments need more places in preparatory education to address the situation.

"The state needs to acknowledge this and begin negotiations with local governments now. Ministry officials have approached the Tallinn Applied College, but these cannot really be called serious negotiations because the school operator does not appear to be aware of what the state intends to do," Kante said.

Starting September 1, all local governments will automatically begin working with young people who do not have a school place. Kante said this requires an individual approach, with each family contacted and a counseling process initiated. Officials responsible at the Tallinn Education Department will make initial contact and if they are unable to help place the child in a school, child protection specialists will also be brought in.

"The administrative burden on Tallinn is enormous," Kante said, recalling that when the reform was being planned, the Ministry of Education said it would not increase the administrative burden on local governments.

Kante said the city could consider making a claim against the ministry as current estimates indicate that nearly 600 students will require this kind of individualized approach and one official will certainly not be enough. "We are talking about at least four or five new officials who will be handling these cases," the deputy mayor said.

Kante did not specify what such a claim might entail, but said taking the matter to court could not be ruled out.

The Tallinn deputy mayor believes the compulsory education reform needs to be reconsidered and redesigned. "In my view, no student should be able to graduate from basic school with inadequate knowledge, so the preparatory education function should remain with the student's home basic school, so that the connection between the school and the student is not broken and we do not have to track down these students one by one," Kante explained.

Kante said responsibility for implementing the reform should be shared with vocational schools, which could take responsibility for career counseling.

The deputy mayor said Tallinn is prepared to open new places in preparatory education and not only at Tallinn Applied College as other educational institutions have also expressed an interest in doing so.

"But we need certainty that the state will actually commission additional places. The law does not even provide for any other option because if young people qualify for preparatory education, they must be given those places," Kante said.

A shortage of teachers is also limiting the creation of new places. If additional places are to be created, recruitment of those teachers would need to begin now, but Kante said the ministry has yet to give the necessary signal.

Tallinn has typically had around 500 basic school graduates each year who have not continued their education.

Kante considers the compulsory education reform necessary in itself because only now has attention begun to be paid to young people who drop out of the education system after basic school. However, for the reform to provide young people with meaningful help, he said the role of basic schools should be strengthened and intervention mechanisms developed so that early identification is effective at the basic school level.

"Then we would not have to talk about young people dropping out after basic school. As it stands, however, the compulsory education reform is largely cosmetic," the Tallinn deputy mayor said.

World.title: Budget 2027: Reform wants to reduce deficit, Eesti 200 to support economy
World.content:
Negotiations for next year's budget started on Tuesday, and the coalition parties Reform and Eesti 200 want to prioritise cutting the deficit and supporting the economy.

Members of the coalition started budget discussions at Stenbock House on Tuesday for 2027 and the budget strategy for the next four years. The government will also shape Estonia's positions on the European Union's new budget period for 2028–2034.

Prime Minister Kristen Michal (Reform) plans to present the state budget to the Riigikogu in the last week of September.

Reform wants to cut the deficit by at least half a percentage point of GDP.

"At most, next year's budget deficit could be 4 percent. What makes achieving this goal easier is that our economy is growing – not vigorously, but still – people are working and taxes are coming in," Annely Akkermann (Reform), chair of the Riigikogu Finance Committee, told Monday's "Aktuaalne kaamera" evening news show.

Another favorable factor is the easing of inflation.

Annely Akkermann. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

"Indexed expenditures, pension expenditures – those indices will be relatively small next year. If pensions are indexed to inflation and wage growth, then that index will be smaller next year. There also should not be very great pressure from wage costs, because the purchasing power of wages has been maintained," she said.

Coalition partner Eesti 200 wants to support the economy and people.

"We have earmarked 5 percent for defense spending well in advance, and we should increase the rest of the state budget so that we can maintain economic growth and improve competitiveness. We should not reverse investments; investments make up a large part of the budget. Estonia is a major investor, but I think we should continue with that," said Education Minister and Eesti 200 chair Kristina Kallas.

Kallas wants to see a pay rise for teachers, additional funding for vocational education and digital development.

Kristina Kallas. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

"Reducing the budget deficit means the need to make cuts, and to cut education, healthcare and the social sector. At the moment, I do not see where those cuts should come from. We have slowed expenditure growth there quite significantly – by hundreds of millions. I do not see that we have any room to hold back there," she told "Aktuaalne kaamera."

As the coalition does not have enough votes to pass the budget by itself, it will need support from other parties or non-aligned MPs in the Riigikogu to do so.

Center Party MP Andrei Korobeinik says his party will not support a budget that does not improve the state of public finances.

"The main problem is the very large budget deficit, and the coalition has not proposed a single solution for how we will reduce it in the medium term, and there is a serious risk that before the elections there will be a desire to hand out money everywhere," he said.

If the budget is not adopted, the state will continue operating next year proportionally on the basis of this year's budget.

This article was updated to add the gallery and additional information about the budget negotiation process.

World.title: Former prime minister Siim Kallas' state funeral takes place on Saturday
World.content:
The funeral of Siim Kallas, former prime minister of Estonia and a former European commissioner, is to take place this coming Saturday, the government has announced.

Kallas passed away at the weekend at the age of 77. His death was announced by his daughter, Kaja Kallas, now the European Union's High Representative for Foreign Affairs and Security Policy.

The ceremony will be held with full state honors, at the Estonia Concert Hall in central Tallinn.

Flags on official buildings will be flown at half‑mast on Saturday, and the Government Office has declared Saturday, August 29 a day of official mourning. A moment of silence will be held at the start of the cabinet meeting on Tuesday morning.

State funerals are accorded to heads and former heads of Estonia's constitutional institutions, including the Riigikogu, the government, the Bank of Estonia, the Supreme Court, the Chancellor of Justice and the Auditor General. For former prime ministers, the ceremony is organized by the Government Office, with a funeral committee headed by the State Secretary and including a family representative as well as representatives of various government agencies. Expenses are covered by the Government Office.

A book of condolences is open to the public at the Stenbock House during working hours until Friday.

Siim Kallas, born on October 2, 1948, served as prime minister in the early 2000s and as a European commissioner and vice‑president for 10 years, from 2004 to 2014. He also held several other senior ministerial positions.

World.title: A look back at Estonia's presidential elections | Episode 1: Lennart Meri, 1992
World.content:
Thirty-four years ago, Estonia's first presidential election since restoring independence pitted four candidates against one another in a popular vote before the final decision passed to the newly elected Riigikogu and Lennart Meri emerged as president.

Estonia will hold its eighth presidential election this fall. Over the course of a week, ERR is looking back at the country's seven previous presidential elections, publishing one story each day featuring key figures from those elections. Tiit Pruuli, who was a member of Lennart Meri's campaign team, and Rein Taagepera, who ran for president, recall some of the key details of the 1992 presidential election.

Estonia's first presidential election after the restoration of independence, held in 1992, differed from all subsequent elections because it included a popular vote.

On August 20, Lennart Meri, who collected 11,491 signatures of support; Arnold Rüütel, with 21,009; Lagle Parek, with 10,839; and Rein Taagepera, with 14,887, were registered as presidential candidates.

On September 16, the four candidates took part in Estonia's first televised presidential candidates' debate on ETV.

Lagle Parek, Arnold Rüütel, Lennart Meri and Rein Taagepera on the ETV program "Presidential Candidates' Debates" in September 1992. Source: ERR archive / Heidi Maasikmets

Four days later, on September 20, the popular vote was held. Arnold Rüütel received the most votes, with 41.8 percent. Lennart Meri received 29.5 percent, narrowly beating Rein Taagepera, who received 23.4 percent.

However, because none of the presidential candidates received more than half the votes cast, no one was elected. Under the presidential election law, the decision then passed to the Riigikogu, with the names of the two most popular candidates, Arnold Rüütel and Lennart Meri, placed on the ballot.

As Isamaa had come to power in the Riigikogu elections held in September 1992 and Meri had been Isamaa's presidential candidate, it was no surprise that Meri received more votes than Rüütel in parliament. Meri received 59 votes and Rüütel 31, while 11 ballots were invalid. On October 5, 1992, Meri was elected the first president of Estonia since the restoration of independence.

Tiit Pruuli, who was a member of Meri's campaign team at the time, recalled that Rüütel's lead was secured by his down-to-earth, easily relatable image and his status as a symbol of the restoration of independence. Meri, meanwhile, was characterized at the time by a certain arrogance and deep intellectualism, which alienated some voters. To get closer to the public, Meri embarked on an extensive campaign, traveling around Estonia.

"Lennart stepped out of the intellectual's slippers — for the first time, though he would do so repeatedly later — and ran a very thorough campaign across Estonia. He traveled hundreds of thousands of kilometers around Estonia in the campaign car and met with people. So it was a tremendous amount of work," Pruuli said.

"The main strategy of Meri's campaign team from the very beginning was that we understood it would be impossible to beat Arnold Rüütel in the first (popular vote — ed.) round. The main strategy was therefore to make sure that Rüütel did not manage to win an absolute majority in the first round and that the matter would go on [to the Riigikogu]," Pruuli said.

Looking back at the contest between Rüütel and Meri, Pruuli also said he did not recall Rüütel presenting his views quite so explicitly during the campaign.

"His trump cards were his high name recognition and silver curls, and those certainly worked to his advantage. He didn't have to focus as much on setting out his views," Pruuli said.

In that respect, Pruuli said Rein Taagepera's decision to enter the race was very important. One of Taagepera's motivations was to support Meri and, in doing so, "eat into" Rüütel's share of the popular vote. Pruuli said, however, that Meri's team had no agreement with Taagepera.

"Taagepera was still an independent and autonomous candidate, so there were no agreements. Objectively speaking, Taagepera's entry into the race helped bring that about and we took into account that this could be the case, but there were no agreements."

Taagepera: I didn't like the prospect of the former chairman of the Supreme Soviet Presidium becoming president of a newly free Estonia

Rein Taagepera himself recalled that both the Popular Front, whose representatives even met him at the airport when he arrived in Estonia, and Lennart Meri wanted him to run. Taagepera himself hoped that his candidacy would help Meri's bid. He recalled that he initially said no to the Popular Front, but then received a phone call from Meri, who was in Helsinki and asked him to run.

"Why would anyone want a rival candidate? Lennart said he had health problems and that if something happened to him, there would be someone else. I knew very well what his 'health problem' was. It was the accusations from Lippmaa and Rüütel's circle asking why Stalin hadn't deported and killed his family. Why had he survived?"

"So, on the one hand, the Popular Front wanted to field its own candidate, while on the other, Meri's circle wanted to make sure Rüütel's supporters did not think that if they forced Meri out of the race with a smear campaign, the path would be clear for them. I agreed because I had been asked by both sides and I myself didn't like the prospect of the former chairman of the Supreme Soviet Presidium becoming president of an Estonia that was regaining its freedom," Taagepera said.

Lennart Meri and Rein Taagepera's election posters from 1992. Source: Urmet Kook's private collection

According to Taagepera, the fact that Meri finished behind Rüütel in the popular vote was a consequence of Taagepera's candidacy.

"When Lennart called me, I told him that if I entered the race, I would be running to win and would try to beat you, too. And he acknowledged that," Taagepera said.

According to Taagepera, Meri's team's calculation was that Taagepera would take more votes from Meri than from Rüütel, but would also take enough from Rüütel to prevent him from reaching 50 percent in the first round.

"Because Lennart and I were on the same wavelength and were competing for the same electorate," Taagepera said.

According to Taagepera, he finished behind Meri because the public wanted the president to come from Estonia and to be someone who had played an important role in restoring the country's independence. Taagepera said, however, that some calculations showed his popularity was on an upward trajectory and that if the campaign had lasted another week, he would have overtaken Meri.

Meri was elected president by parliament on October 5, receiving 59 votes to Rüütel's 31, with 11 invalid ballots. He was 63 when he became president.

Just one month later, in November 1992, Emor surveyed the public on how well Lennart Meri was performing his duties as president. Only 32 percent of respondents said Meri was doing a good job as president. Virtually the same proportion, 31 percent, thought he was doing a poor job. The remaining third had no opinion.

Such low support at the beginning of his presidency was understandable and could largely be explained by the fact that Rüütel had been the most popular candidate in the preceding popular vote. Meri's support, of course, did not remain that low. A year later, in December 1993, 58 percent already rated Meri's performance as president positively. The share with a negative view had remained essentially unchanged, at 34 percent.

The upward trend continued, and by March 1995, when Riigikogu elections were also held, 72 percent rated Meri's performance as president positively. Perhaps more importantly, the share of respondents who rated his performance negatively had fallen by half, to 18 percent.

World.title: Iraqi security recovers rare antiquities
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Iraqi National Security Service (INSS) arrested an antiquities trafficking network, recovering hundreds of unique artifacts from six different provinces.

The intelligence-guided operations, approved by the local judiciary, targeted black-market dealers and smugglers in Baghdad, Kirkuk, Nineveh, Anbar, Babil, and Wasit.

The INSS said in a statement that the recovered artifacts include five rare ancient statues seized in Baghdad, five historic pottery pieces, an ancient cylinder seal, hundreds of ancient metal and rare gold coins, and numerous ancient manuscripts.

The coordinated operations resulted in the arrest of several alleged antiquities smugglers, according to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA).

The suspects have been transferred to judicial bodies to face criminal charges under Iraq’s antiquities protection laws.

The items seized are being legally processed before being handed over to the National Museum of Iraq for preservation.

This campaign is part of Baghdad’s battle to reclaim its cultural identity.

Iraq’s rich legacy has suffered significant losses, beginning with the looting of approximately 15,000 items from the country’s national museum during the 2003 battle and continuing with widespread illegal excavations and black-market sales carried out by ISIS terrorists after 2014.

Over the previous few years, the government has recovered over 40,000 artifacts from global and domestic criminal markets following internal security operations and international initiatives.

World.title: German GDP growth revised upwards, defying Iran war turmoil
World.content:
Frankfurt – German growth rose faster than previously estimated in the second quarter thanks to strong exports, official data showed Tuesday, as Europe’s biggest economy defied the turmoil unleashed by the Iran war.

Gross domestic product grew 0.3 percent from April to June compared with the first three months of the year, according to revised data from the statistics office Destatis.

A first estimate in July had put growth at 0.2 percent.

“The German economy is maintaining the growth momentum seen at the start of the year”, said Destatis’s chief Ruth Brand, adding that “growth was primarily driven by the positive development of exports”.

The economy expanded 0.4 percent in the first quarter.

The revision to second-quarter growth is another sign that the eurozone’s manufacturing powerhouse may be weathering the energy shock unleashed by the United States and Israel’s war against Iran better than feared.

Factory output and exports have also been ticking up in recent months despite the fallout from the conflict.

The revised GDP data showed that exports rose two percent in the second quarter from the first, while imports were also up substantially.

Investment fell slightly, dragged down by a hefty fall in the field of machinery and equipment. Spending by both households and governments registered a small increase.

The German economy has stagnated for several years due to high energy costs, growing competition from China and US President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

Hopes had been high at the start of the year that it would stage a strong rebound thanks to Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s spending blitz on defence and infrastructure.

The outbreak of the Middle East war has dimmed those expectations after the hit to energy-intensive manufacturers, with the government now expecting growth of just 0.5 for 2026 as a whole.

World.title: Hyundai reaches tentative deal with workers after strike
World.content:
Seoul – South Korean automaker Hyundai Motor and the union representing its workers have reached a tentative deal on wages and bonuses, both sides said on Tuesday after a rare full-day strike.

Around 40,000 employees of a roughly 73,000-strong domestic workforce at the country’s largest carmaker walked off the job on Friday, according to union figures, in the first such action for a decade.

The union said on Monday that it had returned to talks with the company and had postponed shorter strikes planned for this week.

Hyundai said on Tuesday that the two sides had struck a “tentative agreement”, while the union indicated that the firm had agreed to partly meet its demands.

“We agreed to increase the basic monthly salary by 100,000 won ($72) and pay a bonus equivalent to four months’ salary,” the union told AFP in a statement.

The company would also meet another demand to raise the retirement age once the government passes legislation on a nationwide hike from 60 years to 65.

Hyundai will not apply the wage peak system, which gradually reduces the salaries of older workers in their final years, after the retirement age is extended, the union said.

Union members will vote on the proposals on August 31.

“We acknowledge the commitment of our employees and appreciate the efforts of our negotiating teams in reaching this tentative agreement,” a Hyundai spokesman told AFP.

He also said both parties recognised that advanced technologies such as “physical AI and robotics are essential part” of the future of mobility.

The company’s workers have staged a total of 60 hours of strikes this year, causing estimated losses of around $1.6 billion, according to calculations by local news agency Newsis.

Hyundai posted record second-quarter revenue of 49.2 trillion won, although operating profit fell 20.8 percent year-on-year amid weaker sales.

World.title: Six months into Iran war, Hormuz traffic way down, sailors stranded
World.content:
Paris – Six months since the start of the Middle East war, the strategic Strait of Hormuz remains largely paralysed, with thousands of sailors still stranded in the Gulf and commodity carrier traffic way below its normal level.

– Only a few transits per day –

Before Iran blocked the strait in response to joint US-Israeli strikes in February, around one fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas exports passed through the waterway.

Iran’s Guards have also warned of a “danger zone” covering 1,400 square kilometres where mines may be present.

After Iran closed the strait on March 1, commodity carrier traffic plummeted to an average of 10 transits per day, compared with a daily average of 95 in February, according to an AFP analysis of data from maritime tracker Kpler.

An agreement signed by the United States and Iran in June led to a temporary rebound to 36 transits per day, before they dropped back to an average of 15 between the resumption of hostilities on July 8 and August 22.

– New routes, ‘dark’ transits –

Before the war, vessels crossed the strait freely via a route through the centre of the waterway adopted by the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

There are now two distinct routes: one to the north, near the Iranian coast — the only one approved by Tehran — and another to the south, between the Omani coast and potentially mined areas.

During the relatively calm period between June 17 and July 7, an average of nine ships per day used the Iranian route and eight the Omani one. The rest transited via unidentified routes or the traditional IMO corridor.

Ever since the ceasefire collapsed on July 8, two-thirds of transits have become “dark”, or unknown, compared with less than one percent before the war, according to Kpler.

These transits involve vessels whose exact route cannot be confirmed due to insufficient data stemming from disabled transponders, jammed signals or missing satellite imagery.

– Thousands of sailors stranded –

Some 6,000 sailors and 500 ships have remained stuck in the Gulf since the beginning of the conflict, the IMO told AFP.

The organisation said there were “ongoing discussions” to ensure a secure maritime route, adding that their outcome “depends on de-escalation in the region”.

The IMO had begun an initiative in June to evacuate more than 11,000 seafarers stuck in the Gulf, but the effort was soon suspended following an attack on a vessel.

Over the past six months, at least 20 sailors and dockworkers have been killed in incidents or attacks in the region, according to the IMO.

World.title: Stocks stagger and oil rises as traders eye Iran threat, Nvidia results
World.content:
Hong Kong – Asian stocks fluctuated Tuesday while oil edged up as investors assess a US plan for the “economic asphyxiation” of Iran, while tech firms struggled following another down day on Wall Street and ahead of earnings from chip titan Nvidia.

With the war against Tehran now in its sixth month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the White House was declaring an “economic D-Day” on the Islamic republic and threatened to hit countries that trade with it.

The threat comes with talks to reopen the Strait of Hormuz stalled and neither side showing any sign of backing down — pushing oil prices up for most of August, which has in turn fanned long-term inflation fears and put pressure on bond markets.

“Around the globe, our objective is to sever every economic lifeline that sustains this tyrannical regime until Tehran stands alone,” Bessent told journalists Monday.

“We are going to hold everyone accountable, and this is economic asphyxiation of this regime,” he said, adding that countries not joining US sanctions would “share” in Iran’s isolation.

President Donald Trump was making phone calls to world leaders with requests to stop interactions with Tehran, Bessent said.

The Treasury Department said Iran’s digital assets, technology, gold, aviation and shipping sectors would be targeted for sanctions.

Both main contracts fell more than two percent Monday as Bessent’s comments appeared to suggest the US will hold off military action, but they ticked higher in early Asian trade.

His “increasingly aggressive economic campaign against Iran is designed to squeeze Tehran’s access to the global financial system while keeping the pressure economic rather than allowing the market to immediately price another military escalation”, wrote Stephen Innes, global strategist at Quintex Intel.

“For now, oil appears to have heard the message that way, which is doing Washington the considerable favour of taking some inflation pressure out of the system.”

Still, equities struggled as tech firms once again bore the brunt of selling, tracking a retreat in their counterparts on Wall Street.

Tech-rich Seoul sank more than two percent at one point as chipmakers SK hynix and Samsung retreated, while Hong Kong, Shanghai, Taipei and Manila were also off.

There were gains in Tokyo, Sydney, Singapore and Wellington.

The tepid performance comes ahead of much-anticipated earnings from Nvidia, which has become something of a bellwether for the AI boom.

With vast sums lavished on artificial intelligence investment over the past two years, markets are growing increasingly nervous about whether firms can deliver results to match.

And analysts have warned that even forecast-beating figures can sometimes not be enough.

Charu Chanana at Saxo Markets said: “Investors are not simply asking whether Nvidia can deliver another strong quarter. They are asking whether it can deliver enough upside to justify already-high expectations, especially with bond yields elevated.”

Eyes will also be on other tech names’ releases, including Salesforce and Marvell.

Also in focus is this week’s annual gathering of central bankers, economists and finance chiefs in Jackson Hole, Wyoming, where the Federal Reserve’s boss Kevin Warsh is due to speak.

His comments will be parsed for clues about monetary policy with inflation still stubbornly high and after Bessent said the Treasury would buy back more of its own bonds to push down borrowing costs after the 30-year yield surged to a 19-year high.

The Canadian dollar edged slightly higher after retreating against the US dollar Monday as Trump vowed to double tariffs on vehicles from its neighbour, fanning a trade war.

The US president’s threat comes after the two failed Friday to reach a deal to avert new 50-percent US tariffs on select Canadian goods. The duties took effect Saturday, and Ottawa laid out plans for retaliation.
