World.title: Fizz takes three in Mumbai rout
World.content:
Pace sensation Mustafizur Rahman recorded his best bowling figures of the Indian Premier League today when he finished with 3 for 16 in Sunrisers Hyderabad’s 85-run victory over Mumbai Indians at Vishakhapatnam.

The three-wicket haul took the left-armer to joint-second in the wicket-takers’ list with a total tally of 13 scalps from nine matches. He is one short of Mitchell McClenaghan, who has taken 14 wickets in 10 matches.

The 20-year-old currently has the best bowling average, 15.61, and best economy rate, 6.15, amongs bowlers who have played at least eight matches in the tournament.

The Sunrisers Hyderabad might have depended on Mustafizur a number of times in the ongoing Indian Premier League, but today was a collective effort. Ashish Nehra, Bhuvaneshwar Kumar and Barinder Sran had reduced the Mumbai Indians to 49 for 6 in nine overs before Mustafizur was given the ball.

The wily left-armer sent back Hardik Pandya with his first ball with a cutter which Pandya failed to adjust himself against. Pandya attempted a slice through point, but the ball curled away to the hands of the keeper, with the umpire judging that out even though the television replays were inconclusive.

Then in the very first ball of his second over again, Fizz bowled yet another slower delivery which moved away from the batsman, getting the edge of Tim Southee on the way to the keeper.

The man from Satkhira returned got the scalp of McClenaghan in the final delivery of his third over, getting the batsman to offer a loopy catch to midwicket.

Mustafizur did not get to bowl a fourth over as David Warner gave the other bowlers their chance to mop up the tail. And they did efficiently, bundling out the hosts for just 92 runs in 16.3 overs.

Earlier, brilliant performances from Hyderabad openers, Warner and Shikhar Dhawan helped the team post 177. Dhawan scored 82 off 57 while Warner smacked 48 off 33. Yuvraj Singh also had a good time with the bat, scoring 39 off 23.

World.title: Two die as scrub typhus spreads in Salyan
World.content:
Two die as scrub typhus spreads in Salyan

Four to five people are testing positive daily in Darma, fuelling fears of a wider outbreak as shortages of testing kits force patients to seek care elsewhere.

Locals take part in a scrub typhus testing camp in Darma. Post photo

World.title: 24 years after leaving Nepal, he came home blind and broken
World.content:
24 years after leaving Nepal, he came home blind and broken

Hom Bahadur Gharti went to Malaysia in search of work in 2002. He lost contact with his family, lived illegally for decades and returned this year after being found in a desperate condition.

World.title: NADA Auto Show 2026 opens in Kathmandu
World.content:
NADA Auto Show 2026 opens in Kathmandu

The six-day event brings together more than 150 brands and over 200 stalls, showcasing new vehicles, auto components and financial services while highlighting the industry’s role in creating jobs.

World.title: Lawmakers demand action over rape and killing of three-year-old in Bara
World.content:
Lawmakers demand action over rape and killing of three-year-old in Bara

National Assembly members criticise the government over rising insecurity, violence against girls and alleged pressure on the victim’s family during video filming.

World.title: Prime Minister Balendra Shah gets a medical pass for dark shades as Parliament bans them
World.content:
Prime Minister Balendra Shah gets a medical pass for dark shades as Parliament bans them

Doctors have advised the prime minister to wear sunglasses to protect his eyes from bright light, while lawmakers have been told to keep dark glasses out of the House.

Prime Minister Balendra Shah attends a meeting of the House of Representatives sporting dark sunglasses in this undated photo. Shah has been medically advised by doctors at Birendra Military Hospital to wear protective shades due to light sensitivity, making his condition an official exception as Parliament enforces a general ban on sunglasses inside the chamber. Post file photo

World.title: Trump administration plans to revoke visas of foreigners seeking asylum
World.content:
Trump administration plans to revoke visas of foreigners seeking asylum

The move could affect up to 200,000 business and tourism visa holders who have applied for asylum, as the administration intensifies its broader crackdown on immigration.

A general view of a US State Department sign outside the US State Department building in Washington, D.C., US, July 11, 2025. Reuters

World.title: Nepal’s parliament debates capital punishment following rape and murder of a three-year-old
World.content:
Nepal’s parliament debates capital punishment following rape and murder of a three-year-old

As public outrage mounts over the Jeetpur-Simara case, law and home ministers outline legal reforms while clarifying why the death penalty remains out of reach.

A demonstrator in Pokhara wears a sign demanding the death penalty for rapists following the rape and murder of a three-year-old girl in Bara. Despite mounting public outrage and calls for capital punishment, the government clarified that Nepal's constitution and international treaties prohibit the death penalty, leaving life imprisonment until death as the legal maximum sentence. Nepal Photo Library

World.title: Court orders government to ensure dairy farmers are paid on time
World.content:
Court orders government to ensure dairy farmers are paid on time

Court says government must ensure farmers are paid on time and warns that agreements should not become a tool to silence those without access to authorities.

The Dairy Development Corporation currently collects between 95,000 and 100,000 litres of milk a day from farmers across the country. Post file photo

World.title: Over 41,000 in Japan sent to the hospital for heatstroke in July
World.content:
The Fire and Disaster Management Agency said Tuesday that 41,174 people were sent to the hospital by ambulance for heatstroke nationwide in July, as many locations recorded temperatures of 35 degrees Celsius or higher.

The figure was the third highest for July since 2008, when the statistics were first compiled, following the 54,220 people logged in 2018 and 43,195 in 2024.

Among those taken to the hospital, 24,769 were age 65 or older, accounting for more than 60% of the total. Seventy-nine people were confirmed dead.

The agency calls on the public to stay hydrated and use air conditioners when necessary. It also encourages people to use designated cooling shelters equipped with air conditioning systems set up by municipalities.

World.title: Japan continues work to end drunken driving 20 years after tragedy
World.content:
Fukuoka Prefecture hosted a conference aimed at eliminating drunken driving in the nation on Tuesday, marking 20 years since a drunken driver rear-ended a car, which then fell off a bridge, killing three small children in 2006.

The incident became one of the turning points for the prefecture and the central government to impose stricter regulations on drunken driving.

“Us adults are the ones who can drive. It is the mission of the adults who create the base for a better society,” said Kaori Onuma, 49, the mother of the three children who died in 2006, on Monday ahead of the anniversary, adding that life should not be cut short because of drunken driving.

World.title: Firms in Japan seek new hedges, bracing for long era of yen weakness
World.content:
Taku Ueno buys beef from America, olive oil from Spain and tomatoes from Italy to stock his supermarkets south of Tokyo, imports that have more recently become costlier almost by the day as the yen falls relentlessly.

The yen has weakened despite currency intervention in 2022, 2024 and 2026, and the exchange rate is still under pressure, even after rare joint U.S.-Japan buying in August and July.

Ueno, chief executive of Takara MC, which operates 43 supermarkets, and his counterparts across Japan are losing patience, and looking for ways to insure against further weakness.

World.title: Six months on, grief still raw for Iran school parents
World.content:
For months, Masoumeh Zakeri has endlessly replayed the last night she spent with her 9-year-old daughter before she was killed in a strike on her school during the opening hours of the U.S.-Israel war with Iran.

Motahreh excitedly talked about upcoming holidays, planned weddings and the clothes she wanted to buy. She had a Ramadan pre-fast meal shortly before dawn and then Zakeri tucked her into bed.

“I never saw her again. (That was) the last time,” the 44-year-old mother said.

World.title: Hundreds of flights canceled as typhoon bears down on Okinawa
World.content:
An approaching typhoon has forced the cancellation of hundreds of flights in and out of Okinawa Prefecture, as Japan’s holiday period draws to a close.

ANA Holdings and Japan Airlines canceled a total of 279 flights affecting 41,688 people due to storm Saudel, which is expected to bring strong winds and high seas to the area from Tuesday night to Wednesday morning.

Okinawa, which hosts several U.S. military bases alongside its popular beach resorts, attracts more than 10 million visitors a year.

ANA said all of its flights to and from the airport in Naha will be canceled on Wednesday. Some ferry services are also canceled.

The Japan Meteorological Agency said winds may reach speeds of up to 40 meters per second. After crossing Okinawa Prefecture, the storm is expected to move westwards, hitting the coast of China later in the week.

Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi urged the public to pay close attention to weather forecasts and evacuation information. “If you sense the slightest danger, don’t hesitate to take action to protect your lives,” she said in a post on X.

World.title: Shortage of engineers creates opportunities to advance in Ukrainian defense tech
World.content:
The speed of innovation on the Ukrainian battlefield means frontline troops may need a new drone design within weeks — but the country’s defense industry faces a critical labor shortage that threatens to derail that pace.

Tens of billions of dollars in investments and wartime demand have fueled the creation of thousands of defense companies in Ukraine, but the supply of workers has failed to keep up. Yurii Faraponov, chief operating officer of BlueBird Tech, said his company can’t respond to some frontline requests because he doesn’t have enough engineers.

Another company recently poached a production manager by offering him three times his previous salary, along with paid housing, said Sergii Vysotskyi, vice president of the National Association of Ukrainian Defense Industries. Some companies are tracking down retired specialists and begging them to return to work.

World.title: Japan’s only high-speed trader Dharmacapital moves to Singapore citing tax rates
World.content:
Japan’s high-frequency trader Dharmacapital moved all its staff to Singapore earlier this month, according to people familiar with the matter, effectively leaving Tokyo with no such firms operating out of the city.

The country’s high tax rate compared to other Asian financial hubs, such as Singapore and Hong Kong, was partly behind the decision to relocate, according to one of the people, who asked not to be identified discussing private information.

“The major reason of relocation is to get better access to global markets,” Akiyoshi Shiotani, CEO at Dharmacapital, wrote in an email. “Japan remains our most important market and we’ll continue to provide liquidity and contribute to efficient trading.”

Among 53 high-frequency trading units involved in Japanese markets, Dharmacapital was the only firm located in Tokyo as of July according to a registered list maintained by the Financial Services Agency (FSA). Most peers, including Citadel Securities, Virtu Financial and Jane Street, trade from Singapore or Hong Kong.

Tokyo has struggled to cement its status as a major international financial hub. Comparatively high income tax rates and language barriers are among the factors cited by some finance professionals for choosing other cities over the Japanese capital.

Singapore this month unveiled a proposal for tax exemptions for fund managers, as rival Hong Kong sees a resurgence in its fortunes and an influx of returning talent.

Market-making firms accounted for more than 30% of trading value in the Tokyo Stock Exchange since at least 2024, according to a survey by the FSA.

World.title: Laundry businesses in quake-hit Kumamoto wash evacuees’ clothes for free
World.content:
Local dry cleaning and laundry businesses in Kumamoto Prefecture are washing clothes without charge for disaster evacuees following last month’s magnitude 7.1 earthquake.

A laundry facility affiliated with the White Express dry cleaning and laundry chain in the Miyahara district of the town of Hikawa has sent a vehicle every morning on business days since Aug. 7 — 10 days after the July 28 quake — to collect bags of clothing from evacuation centers. It washes and dries more than 1,000 items, including towels and underwear, each day and returns them to evacuees.

“We owe our business to the local residents,” said Hiroaki Sekihara, the 36-year-old head of the facility. “We want to give back to the community even a little bit, especially at a time like this.”

Kiyomi Matsumura, a 53-year-old employee, visited an evacuation center to return washed clothes and was greeted by a staff member there. “Someone once thanked me for all that I do, which made me feel glad that I was doing this,” Matsumura said.

Folding freshly dried T-shirts and trousers, 64-year-old employee Mihoko Tsukamoto said, “We want to help disaster-affected people whose homes have been destroyed and who cannot even take a warm bath.”

Amid consecutive days of scorching heat, many locals wash their clothes by hand at evacuation centers or return to their damaged homes to do laundry.

“I want to help the disaster victims live more comfortably,” Sekihara said.

Behind the initiative is the Disaster Sentaku Assistance Team (DSAT), a volunteer network of professional cleaners launched after a powerful quake in the Noto Peninsula in Ishikawa Prefecture, in January 2024. Sentaku means washing in Japanese.

In collaboration with a laundry and dry cleaning industry association in Kumamoto, the team called on local businesses in the cities of Yatsushiro and Uki to join the initiative. Laundry costs under the initiative are covered by support funds given to the DSAT and other sources.

“It’s important to maintain a hygienic environment for people in evacuation centers in extreme heat,” said Yuichi Nakamura, the 42-year-old head of the DSAT.

Expecting a potential increase in demand for laundry services for clothes retrieved from collapsed houses, Nakamura said, “We want to keep supporting people as long as there are requests.”

World.title: Hong Kong’s Chinese Medicine Hospital to start 24-hour inpatient services in December
World.content:
The Chinese Medicine Hospital of Hong Kong will launch 24-hour inpatient services in December, the first of its kind in the city, and charge patients HK$980 (US$125) per day for subsidised care, more than three times the fee at public hospitals.

The city’s first dedicated traditional Chinese medicine hospital will also launch 10 additional special disease programmes within this year to help treat conditions such as eczema and Parkinson’s disease.

The hospital, which was opened last December in Tseung Kwan O, aims to provide services for more complex cases under a model that features Chinese medicine as the primary approach, integrated with Western medicine.

The expansion of services, announced on Tuesday, includes the provision of 24-hour inpatient services from December 11.

The hospital will provide 93 inpatient beds – consisting of 60 government-subsidised and 33 non-subsidised ones – as well as 20 beds under its clinical trial and research centre and two high-dependency beds.

The subsidised inpatient option will cost HK$980 a day – a fixed, overall package price that covers all treatment-related services, such as room fee, visits by registered practitioners, Chinese medicine interventions, tests and medication.

World.title: Hong Kong jewellery shop slapped with 30-day tour group ban over coerced sales
World.content:
Hong Kong’s tourism watchdog has suspended a jewellery shop from receiving tour groups for 30 days after finding it failed to stop a guide from coercing mainland Chinese visitors into making purchases.

The Travel Industry Authority (TIA) said on Tuesday that Kaiser Jewellery International would be barred from receiving any inbound tour group visitors from Wednesday until September 24.

“The authority adopts a zero-tolerance approach towards coerced shopping and any conduct that damages the reputation of Hong Kong’s tourism industry,” it said in a statement.

A check by the South China Morning Post found two locations operated by the company under the TIA’s list of registered shops, including one on the first floor of Hankow Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui trading as “KJI Super Mall”, and another location at Harbourside HQ in Kowloon Bay.

The Kowloon Bay branch has been marked as “registration suspended”, though the company has filed an appeal for review and a hearing has been scheduled, according to the authority.

One of Kaiser Jewellery’s shops is located at Hankow Centre in Tsim Sha Tsui. Photo: Handout

The disciplinary action stemmed from a case involving a tour group from the mainland in February.

World.title: Hong Kong power firms to raise fuel charges from September amid geopolitical tensions
World.content:
Hong Kong’s two electricity suppliers will raise fuel-related charges from next month, citing geopolitical tensions and volatility in international energy markets.

As electricity costs rise, CLP Power and HK Electric have introduced rebate and relief schemes as grass-roots households face higher air-conditioning expenses after a summer with an unusually large number of very hot days.

HK Electric, which supplies electricity mainly to Hong Kong Island and Lamma Island, said on Tuesday that its fuel clause charge would rise to 60.7 Hong Kong cents (7.74 US cents) per kilowatt-hour (kWh) in September.

The charge will increase by 3.4 cents, or 5.9 per cent, from August, marking the fourth consecutive monthly increase since May.

Together with the basic tariff, the average net tariff will rise to 188.6 cents per unit in September, an increase of 1.8 per cent from August.

“International energy prices remain volatile, with spot prices for liquefied natural gas having more than doubled compared with levels before the geopolitical developments earlier this year and still rising,” HK Electric said in a statement.

World.title: Hong Kong exports jump 50.7% in July, driven by growth in AI-related electronics
World.content:
Hong Kong exports surged by 50.7 per cent year on year in July, driven by “impressive growth” in artificial intelligence-related electronic products, with the government expecting the robust demand to continue supporting trade development despite geopolitical risks.

Provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Tuesday showed that the value of exports jumped to HK$672.5 billion (US$86.2 billion) last month after a 53.4 per cent rise in June.

A government spokesman attributed July’s strong performance to growth in AI-related electronics and a visible increase in exports to most major markets.

“The value of merchandise exports grew by 50.7% over a year earlier, with exports of AI-related electronic products again registering particularly impressive growth,” he said.

The spokesman said global demand for AI-related electronic products was expected to continue to bolster the city’s exports, but warned of geopolitical risks in the Middle East and rising trade protectionism in some advanced economies.

Imports rose by 41 per cent year on year to HK$677.4 billion last month. The city still recorded a trade deficit of HK$4.9 billion, equivalent to 0.7 per cent of import value.

World.title: Hong Kong government statistician cleared of loitering charge near girls’ school
World.content:
A Hong Kong court has acquitted a government statistician accused of loitering near a girls’ school and outside a classroom to photograph a pupil, ruling that his conduct did not pose an actual threat despite leaving the girl feeling unsafe.

Eastern Court Magistrate Kestrel Lam Tsz-hong on Tuesday found 59-year-old Patrick Lam Win-hon not guilty of one count of loitering causing concern, despite acknowledging that the defendant had loitered at one of Causeway Bay’s leading girls’ schools on July 5 last year.

The court heard that the statistician entered the school on its open day and spent 14 minutes on the fourth floor, where the classroom of the pupil he allegedly targeted was located.

Other students alerted teachers to the defendant’s suspicious behaviour, including his taking photographs through the classroom window.

The court heard that the target was a 16-year-old girl, who said the defendant had followed her during her daily commute to school for two to three years.

The girl said she first noticed the defendant showing interest in her by smiling and nodding at her on the MTR in late 2022. She said she later spotted the same man in the same carriage while travelling from Olympic to Hong Kong station on her daily commute.

World.title: 3 helpers sacked, issued warnings over use of employer data to secure loans
World.content:
Three domestic helpers in Hong Kong have been sacked and issued warning letters after providing their employers’ personal data without consent to secure loans, resulting in the households being harassed by debt collectors.

Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data Ada Chung Lai-ling said on Tuesday that, in each of the three cases, the names, phone numbers and addresses of employers were originally obtained solely for work purposes.

“However, the domestic helpers in question subsequently provided the employers’ personal data to financial institutions for applying for loans,” she said. “And I would say that this went beyond the original purpose for which the data was collected.”

In one of the cases, which happened in 2025, the helper provided her employers’ phone number and address to a moneylender in the Philippines as proof of work, but later defaulted on payments due to the high interest rate.

The moneylender then texted the employer, requesting that the helper be reminded to make the payments, and threatened to send debt collectors to the address if the transaction was not completed by a deadline.

The other two cases took place in January and May this year and involved the helpers disclosing their employers’ personal information to several financial institutions without consent to apply for loans, resulting in their employers being harassed.

World.title: 58 evacuated, woman taken to hospital after fire at Hong Kong flat
World.content:
About 60 people were evacuated and a 98-year-old woman was taken to hospital after a fire broke out in a flat in Hong Kong on Tuesday.

Police said they received multiple reports of the blaze at 488 Hennessy Road in Causeway Bay at 10.59am.

The 58 people evacuated comprised 25 women and 17 men from the building, plus another 11 men and five women from a bank on the ground floor.

The elderly woman reported feeling unwell and was taken to Ruttonjee Hospital in Wan Chai, police said.

At 11.39am, the Transport Department said all lanes on the section of Percival Street between Hennessy Road and Russell Street remained closed due to the incident, adding that traffic in the area was heavy.

Tram services on the Happy Valley loop were suspended, bus routes 108 and 117 were diverted, and motorists were advised to use alternative routes.

World.title: Construction safety design needed to reduce fatal accidents in Hong Kong: experts
World.content:
Hong Kong should make safety design a part of all building development plans and address the culture of rushing work at construction sites, industry leaders have said after the city recorded 15 fatal industrial accidents earlier this year.

Their calls followed the warning by Construction Industry Council chairman Thomas Ho On-sing on Monday that the number of such accidents was on the rise despite stiffer penalties, reflecting that a safety culture had failed to take root.

Ho pointed out that up to 70 to 80 per cent of accidents at worksites were caused by bad habits and poor mindsets, while all 15 fatal accidents were triggered by the pressure to finish projects quickly, which he described as among the deadliest factors on construction sites.

Chau Sze-kit, chairman of the Hong Kong Construction Industry Employees General Union, said on Tuesday that safety awareness had improved but had yet to become second nature in a sector where “rushing culture” was still prevalent.

“For instance, the media recently exposed workers on exterior scaffolding without wearing safety belts or hooking on to independent lifeline ropes. This is a clear case of safety measures not being properly implemented. Ultimately, we need to embed a safety-first culture,” he said.

Chau said the issue stemmed from both worker habits and a lack of management supervision, while the provision of safety tools and improved design at the outset of construction would also minimise risks.

World.title: Education, health fees among key concerns
World.content:
China to legislate on preschool education

China will push for legislation on preschool education to provide a legal guarantee for the operation and management of such institutions, Vice-minister of Education Tian Xuejun said on Nov 30.

Tian made the remarks at a news conference organized by the State Council Information Office regarding a child abuse case at RYB Education New World Kindergarten in Beijing that received widespread attention in November. He said the Ministry of Education was already doing research on the legislation.

"The ministry will also complete the requirements on qualifications of teachers engaged in preschool education and is considering formulating a code of ethics for them," Tian said.

He also said a plan is on the way to step up supervision of kindergartens and solve the problem of insufficient resources for preschool education. Tian said the case exposed the conflict between public demand for preschool enrollment and insufficient development of preschool education.

"It also showed that some local authorities and kindergartens still have problems of unsound management and failure to implement or fully implement regulations," he said.

Rural health fee increase explained in detail

The National Health and Family Planning Commission recently responded to public concern of newly increased fees for a new rural cooperative medical system.

Fees charged in the new rural cooperative medical system have recently been raised from 30 yuan ($5.5) to 180 yuan.

The NHFPC explained that while fees for individuals have been raised, government financial subsidies to individuals have also been raised accordingly in recent years from the previous 20 yuan per person to 450 per person. At the same time, the government has a comprehensive medical assistance system for those unable to afford such fees. Also, the reimbursement proportion for hospitalization costs for those in the new rural cooperative medical system has also been raised from 35 percent to 75 percent.

Anti-espionage law will help national security

The State Council issued a circular on China's anti-espionage law on Wednesday with detailed rules for implementing the law.

The circular explains several terms in the law, including overseas institutions and organizations, individuals, spy organizations, spy organization agents and hostile organizations. It was made clear that national security departments under the State Council will identify unacceptable behavior.

According to the circular, providing funds, venues and materials to spy organizations and individuals will be identified as helping them.

Conducting espionage activities in the territory, accepting overseas funds to endanger national security or connect them for spying activities will also be deemed as collusion.

Staff members at national safety departments are authorized to arrest and hunt criminal suspects, and their anti-espionage activities will not be interrupted by any other illegal actions.

It said that Chinese people and organizations retain the right and privilege to secure national safety, and their contributions such as providing clues about spying activities, collaborating with national security departments and fighting espionage activities will also be rewarded.

World.title: International group praises green revival
World.content:
High-level advisory panel pitches 15-year pollution fight, but holds China up as model

A high-level international advisory body applauded China's efforts to improve the environment and suggested a 15-year strategy against pollution in a draft recommendation report on Monday.

China has made building an ecological civilization an important goal and has taken comprehensive measures to improve the environment. This has resulted in positive results, including improved air quality, Vice-Premier Zhang Gaoli said when chairing the annual meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body.

Like Zhang, Erik Solheim, executive director of the United Nations Environment Programme, said he was impressed by China's tremendous achievements regarding its environment in recent years, in particular curbing much of the smog problem.

"China is capable of solving the environment problems themselves," said Solheim, the council's vice-chairman, adding the best practices taken by China could provide guidance to other areas facing similar issues.

His praise of China's approaches to move toward being an ecological civilization won wide support from other members of the environmental council, which includes senior officials and experts from home and abroad.

The council's draft recommendation presents highlights of the war against pollution in air, water and soil, and suggests the creation of a 15-year strategy that will be "focused on cost-effectiveness, synergies and ways to build public confidence about eventual results".

Ideally, the integrated rollout should be ready before 2020, to be in line with the 2035 pivot point, when China expects to be a "basic modern country", the draft said.

Solheim said he is confident that China can reach the 2035 goal to build a "beautiful China", considering the determined and effective efforts adopted in recent years.

Along with the longer-term strategy to curb pollution, council members suggested creating conditions for fair competition and incentives for green industries.

Based on the input from Monday's meeting, the advisers and their support teams will modify their proposal and provide a final version to the State Council through the Ministry of Environmental Protection.

zhengjinran@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Beijing, Moscow drill for potential missile warfare
World.content:
China and Russia kicked off their second joint computer-assisted anti-missile drill on Monday, a move experts said could deter potential missile threats amid rising tensions on the Korean Peninsula.

The drill began on Monday in Beijing and is expected to conclude on Saturday, China's Defense Ministry said on its website on Monday. "This is a practical measure in fulfilling the important consensus reached by both countries' leaders on deepening Sino-Russian antimissile cooperation," it said.

"It will strengthen Sino-Russian mutual strategic trust, improve anti-missile cooperation between the two militaries and has great significance in jointly dealing with regional ballistic and cruise missile threats," the ministry said.

The exercise does not target any third party, it said. "China and Russia oppose the development of global anti-missile systems. The two militaries will increase practical cooperation in anti-missile defense, and jointly safeguard Chinese and Russian security interests and regional strategic balance."

The goal of the exercise is to "jointly train for anti-missile combat planning and preparation, launch command and firing coordination," Senior Colonel Wu Qian, the Defense Ministry spokesman, said in a news briefing in November.

Tension on the Korean Peninsula has been mounting since the Democratic People's Republic of Korea launched its Hwasong-15 intercontinental ballistic missile in November. DPRK media reported the missile could carry nuclear warheads and reach the continental United States.

Su Hao, a professor at the China Foreign Affairs Academy, said that it is crucial for China and Russia to bolster strategic trust and cooperate in anti-missile defense to protect their nations from potential threats.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Memorial Day a time to 'remember', 'inspire'
World.content:
A memorial service to mark the 80th anniversary of the Nanjing Massacre committed during the War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression (1931-45) brought together hundreds of activists and members of the Chinese and other Asian communities on Sunday in San Francisco.

The memorial, organized by the Rape of Nanking Redress Coalition, the Committee to Promote Reunification of China, the Alliance for Preserving the Truth of Sino-Japanese War and Comfort Women Justice Coalition, has been held annually for the past 20 years with the aim of exposing the Japanese Imperial Army's war crimes and encouraging people to understand and never forget the dark chapter of history.

"The Japanese army blatantly violated international conventions and committed the extremely cruel atrocity in Nanjing, where 300,000 Chinese were murdered and one-third of the buildings were destroyed," Zha Liyou, acting Chinese consul general in San Francisco, said at the service.

Japanese troops captured Nanjing, which was China's capital at the time, on Dec 13, 1937. It then began a slaughter that lasted more than 40 days. Tens of thousands of women were raped.

"Our stories are linked. The fate of over 400,000 women sexually enslaved by the Japanese Imperial Army during World War II is part and parcel of what happened during the Nanjing Massacre," said Judith Mirkinson, president of the Comfort Women Justice Coalition.

She said the 20th century has been called the most violent century in the history of the world, and that one way to ensure peace in the 21st century is through truth and reconciliation.

"Reconciliation does not come without truth. So the Japanese government must acknowledge their crimes," she said.

"They must give justice to those few people who still survive from the Nanjing Massacre and to the memory of what happened there," she said.

From the time that Japan invaded Northeast China in September 1931, followed by a full-scale invasion that started on July 7, 1937, around 35 million Chinese soldiers and civilians were killed or injured during the occupation, which continued until 1945.

To honor the victims and the survivors and to pursue justice and an enduring peace, the Chinese community worldwide joined hands this year to commemorate this historic event, which was designated by the Chinese government as National Memorial Day for Nanjing Massacre Victims.

"To remember the atrocities committed by the Japanese army during World War II does not mean to pass on the enmity but rather to remind people not to forget the history and inspire them to love peace," said Zha Liyou.

In 2015, the Nanjing Massacre was entered onto the UNESCO Memory of the World Register, a compendium aimed at preserving documented heritage of universal value.

liazhu@chinadailyusa.com

World.title: More military technologies targeted for civilian sector to boost economy
World.content:
Greater integration will spur innovation and cultivate new engines of growth

China will strengthen innovation by developing high-tech industries with military technologies to boost military-civil integration, a move that aims to cultivate new growth drivers and boost the economy, said a recent State Council guideline.

This was one of the seven key tasks set by the guideline on deepening the military-civil integration in the defense technology industry, which was released by the State Council, China's Cabinet, on Monday last week.

The guideline targets sharing technological innovation bases and facilities between military and civilian sectors while more efforts will be made to apply military technologies to non-military areas.

The military integration will also focus on key areas such as space, cyberspace and maritime sciences, while private capital is encouraged to enter military industries, the document said.

The guideline was the latest move by the central government to promote the military-civil integration to widen military contract orders to civilian sectors and apply high-end military technologies for civilian purposes as part of the supply-side structural reform.

In June, the General Office of the State Council released a guideline on civil aviation development to open airspace less than 3,000 meters in altitude and other industries such as cybersecurity and satellite navigation.

Shi Haiming, an associate professor at the National University of Defense Technology, said the guideline brings benefits for both private and military enterprises while pre-entry approvals will be changed into post-entry reviews to streamline administration, except those linking strategic weapons.

Meanwhile, Shi said the guideline lowers the access threshold for enterprises to enter the field of weaponry equipment and will make the process more transparent.

The document also will further reduce institutional costs for private enterprise by building better platforms to promote military-civil integration, he said.

In fact, many developed economies are highly reliant on military-civil integration.

For example, the United States' airplane maker Boeing sells China civil aviation aircraft worth billions of dollars each year and is known for its high-end military aircraft. Many Japanese multinational companies such as Toshiba and Mitsubishi have a department to take military orders.

The integration is a worldwide trend to fully improve the national defense capability, said Jiang Luming, a professor at the National Defense University of the People's Liberation Army.

In countries such as the US, the United Kingdom and Germany, less than 15 percent of military technologies are solely for military purposes and more than 80 percent are used for civilian purposes, Jiang said.

Jiang said in October last year that China has about 290,000 national defense intellectual property rights not being used due to the previously separated military and civil industries.

For example, breakthrough technologies such as engines and aluminum alloy materials can help ease production overcapacity and transform China's economy, he said. These new technologies can essentially boost economic growth and national defense, Jiang said.

The military industry has the priority to apply cutting-edge technologies and also make breakthrough innovations, Lu Guangshan, chairman of the Avionics System Co under the Aviation Industry Corporation of China, was quoted by Shanghai Securities News as saying.

"For example, virtual reality headsets were first used in helmets for fighter jets and my company has developed six civilian industries such as virtual reality, drones, robotics and smart wearing," Lu said.

Military companies are encouraged to work with local governments to promote their advantageous expertise and develop a large number of new high-tech industries, Long Hongshan, chief engineer at the State Administration of Science, Technology and Industry for National Defense, told a news conference last week.

These new industries will play a vital role in promoting local economic growth and creating new employment opportunities, Long said.

Currently, 30 percent of products made by China's military companies are for military purposes and the other 70 percent for civilian purposes, he said.

In the future, high-tech industries will cover half of the military-related economy, Long added.

World.title: Dangerous stunts get thumbs-down from video platforms
World.content:
Multiple social media and video streaming platforms will limit who can view videos that depict dangerous stunts - and may even prohibit such material - in an effort to discourage imitators.

In November, daredevil stunt climber Wu Yongning fell to his death while scaling a skyscraper in Changsha, Hunan province. Wu, 26, had more than 1.3 million followers on social media who regularly devoured his breathtaking videos and photos. He climbed with no protective gear.

Last month, Wu's account on Sina Weibo stopped updating, leading followers to worry about his well-being.

On Friday, Wu's girlfriend confirmed on social media that the "rooftop daredevil" had fallen and died.

"Today is Dec 8. It makes me think of Nov 8, the day that you left us, left this world," she wrote.

Wu's family also confirmed his death to Jiefang Daily, a newspaper in Shanghai.

Meipai, Kuaishou, Xiaohuoshan and other video platforms on which Wu posted content, expressed their condolences, according to ThePaper.cn. Platform representatives told the news outlet that China currently has no law regulating extreme stunt videos, but each platform will update its content policy to discourage imitators.

Kuaishou said Wu's account had been restricted - meaning that only the uploader can see it - in September because of its depictions of dangerous acts.

Xiaohuoshan said it will ban video livestreams of dangerous stunts because live interactions between the performer and the audience could be a distraction and lead to catastrophic results.

The platform also said it will respect the desires of Wu's family in dealing with the videos.

All of Wu's stunt videos on the three platforms had been restricted or taken down as of Monday. A cellphone video of Wu performing his last stunt and falling to his death on Nov 8, has also been taken down.

Wu was part of an informal community of young thrill-seekers around the world who engage in "roof-topping" - climbing to the top or to high ledges of buildings, often without a permit or protective gear, to take stomach-churning pictures and videos. The activity is generally illegal.

In January, an 18-year-old identified as Alexander Sh, fell to his death from Europe's second-tallest building - the 350-meter OKO Tower in Moscow. He was trying to take a selfie when he slipped and fell, Russian media reported.

zhangzhihao@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Taiwan's New Party vows to help improve relations
World.content:
Delegation to Beijing reaffirms support for one-China, rejection of agitators

Top political adviser Yu Zhengsheng met with a Taiwan delegation representing the island's New Party in Beijing on Monday to discuss the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations and how to achieve the "great rejuvenation" of the Chinese nation.

Yu praised the New Party's unbroken stance upholding the 1992 Consensus, which embodies the one-China principle, since the party's establishment, as well as its peaceful approach to relations.

The 19th National Congress of the Communist Party of China, which was held in October, further clarified the guidelines and policies addressing Taiwan, Yu said.

In his opening address to delegates during the congress, Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Central Committee of the CPC, called the one-China principle the political foundation of cross-Straits relations, and said that attempts to move toward "Taiwan independence" in any form will be defeated.

Taiwan will share development opportunities on the Chinese mainland, and its residents will enjoy the same treatment as mainland people as they pursue studies, start businesses, seek jobs or come to live on the mainland, Xi said in the address.

Yok Mu-ming, chairman of the New Party and head of the Taiwan delegation, said the party has firmly upheld the one-China principle and promoted peace.

The delegation also met on Monday with Zhang Zhijun, head of the State Council's Taiwan Affairs Office.

Zhang and Yok agreed that the one-China principle must be upheld going forward, expressed firm opposition to separatist activities and vowed to make efforts toward peaceful relations.

Both sides agreed to establish and improve mechanisms of communication, share opinions on major issues in the relationship and promote exchanges and communication in all fields - especially between youth. They further agreed to create a constructive and convenient environment for the development of Taiwan youth on the mainland.

Zhang said cross-Straits relations have faced challenges because the island's Democratic Progressive Party has refused to clearly express support for the one-China principle, which led to the mainland suspending official communications with the island.

He said that a "Taiwan independence" force had recently stirred up the island, proposing the removal of Chinese mainland elements in a variety of fields.

"Its aim is to cut the historical ties between Taiwan and the mainland, reduce public awareness that Taiwan people are part of the Chinese nation and limit many cultural influences on the island," he said.

Some people advocating "Taiwan independence" have pushed for amending the law, and have proposed changing the island's constitution. "This shows that separatist activities and the group supporting 'independence' pose the most serious threat to the peaceful development of cross-Straits relations," Zhang said.

He warned that people from both sides should be vigilant and firmly oppose such activities.

luowangshu@chinadaily.com.cn

World.title: Former Chongqing political official facing corruption investigation
World.content:
Sun Zhengcai, the former secretary of Chongqing Municipal Committee of the Communist Party of China, has been placed under investigation on suspicion of accepting bribes, according to the Supreme People's Procuratorate on Monday.

According to the procuratorate, Sun has been placed under "coercive measures", which may include summons by force, bail, residential surveillance, detention and arrest.

The investigation is underway, the procuratorate said in a statement released on Monday.

In July, the CPC Central Commission for Discipline Inspection launched an investigation into Sun for "serious violations of Party discipline".

The CCDI said in a news release that Sun betrayed Party principles and ignored the Party code of conduct and rules.

He was found to have seriously violated the CPC's eight-point code on frugality and maintaining close ties with the masses, seeking pomp, ostentation and privileges, according to the CCDI.

The CCDI said he was guilty of nepotism and seeking benefits in selection of officials. He was found by the CCDI to have leaked confidential Party information and seriously breached Party rules on integrity.

Moreover, he abused power and used his job to gain benefits for others, then accepted their huge bribes in return, either paid in cash or properties, the CCDI said. He was found to seek substantial benefits for his relatives' businesses and accepted valuable gifts, the CCDI said.

The anti-graft inspectors also accused Sun of bureaucracy and sloth in work and degradation and power-for-sex trades, according to the CCDI.

Sun totally deviated from the Party spirit and political requirements of senior officials, the CCDI said in the statement, adding that his misconduct betrayed the trust of the CPC Central Committee and the public, inflicting huge harm to the Party and the country with "extremely bad" social influences.

The CCDI transferred the criminal evidence involving his case to judicial authorities for further investigation.

In September, the Political Bureau of the CPC Central Committee expelled Sun from the Party and dismissed him from public office.

China Daily - Xinhua

World.title: Tracing the Route of ‘Cathay’
World.content:
Eighty years ago, Roy Farrell and Sydney de Kantzow — two ex-air force pilots who had supported China’s War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression during World War II — purchased a Douglas DC-3 twin-engine propeller airplane. After establishing an import-export company in Shanghai, they soon relocated to Hong Kong and officially registered their new venture: Cathay Pacific Airways.

Today, Cathay Pacific is ranked as a 5-star airline and flies to 60 countries worldwide. Less recognized is the origin of “Cathay” as a common term. Chosen by the founders as a nod to their China connection alongside “Pacific” to capture their ambition for their enterprise to one day cross the world’s largest ocean, the word itself tells a story of communication and misunderstanding between ancient China and the West.

Indeed, for centuries, the name “Cathay” haunted the European imagination. It conjured visions of a distant, mythical realm of silk and spices beyond China — even as European merchants and missionaries quietly traded with the immense state. The great irony is that for nearly 300 years, Europe operated under the profound delusion that these two magnificent empires were separate neighbors, and perhaps even rivals.

This mismatch in geographical understanding can be traced back to a difference in terminology, itself a byproduct of accounts from travelers who visited different parts of the region amid shifting names for the north and south. According to the Oxford English Dictionary (OED), “Cathay” can be traced back to “Khitan,” the name of the nomadic people who established the Liao dynasty in the north from the 10th to the early 12th century. The Khitan name was then absorbed by the powerful Kara-Khanid Khanate to the west along the Silk Road, which subtly altered its pronunciation. As the word flowed westward into Persian (as Katā), then post-classical Latin (Cataia or Cathaia), and in Marco Polo’s accounts as Catai, “Cathay” came into being.

And yet, a linguistic rift began to appear as Europeans who landed on China’s southern coast found themselves dealing with a country named “China,” an older word derived from Sanskrit. On 16th-century maps, “China” was thus often depicted as a mere coastal strip known to Portuguese sailors, while “Cathay” loomed as a vast, mysterious inland empire to the north.

This was no mere academic error; it had monumental, real-world consequences. In fact, this geographical schism served as the very engine of the Age of Discovery. When Christopher Columbus and John Cabot set sail for the New World — with a heavily annotated copy of Marco Polo’s book of travels — they were convinced they were heading toward Cathay. Driven by the desperate hope of finding this elusive northern empire, Humphrey Gilbert penned his 1576 treatise, “A Discourse of a Discoverie for a New Passage to Cataia.”

Yet, the human drive to uncover the truth is a powerful instinct. The reconciliation of “Cathay” and “China” belongs not to kings or cartographers, but to the walkers — specifically, the missionaries who refused to accept that the map was complete. When Matteo Ricci arrived in China in the late 16th century, he noticed that the “Cathay” described by Polo perfectly matched the empire of the Ming dynasty (1368–1644). To settle any lingering doubts, the Portuguese Jesuit missionary Bento de Góis then embarked on a grueling overland expedition from India. Crossing the unforgiving Pamir Mountains and the Gobi Desert, he searched for the legendary kingdom of Cathay. Though he died waiting for permission to enter Beijing, his ultimate sacrifice proved that the Silk Road led directly to the seat of the Ming’s rule, not the separate land of “Cathay.”

By the early 17th century, Western travelers like Ricci, de Góis, and Martín de Rada had conclusively established that the China reached by sea could be accessed by following Marco Polo’s land route across Central Asia. When their letters finally reached Europe, the phantom of “Cathay” vanished from the maps, leaving behind only the tangible reality of China.

One might expect the word “Cathay” to have perished alongside that geographical revelation. Instead, it transformed. As the OED notes, from the beginning of the 17th century, “Cathay” was gradually superseded by “China,” and by the century’s end, the process was complete. Stripped of its geographical necessity, the word was reborn as an archaic, highly connotative strand of poetic use. In the early 18th century, poet James Thomson wrote of caravans bending “to the golden coast of rich Cathay/With news of human-kind.” By 1823, Lord Byron was similarly invoking “far Cathay” alongside Ceylon and Inde in “Don Juan.” In 1859, Harper’s Magazine placed Cathay alongside Atlantis and El Dorado as a land now “peopled with beings of flesh and blood.” By 1871, Joaquin Miller mused, “Where the winds come in from the far Cathay/With odor of spices and balm and bay.” Through these verses, the word had become a timeless vessel for exotic mystery and richness.

Perhaps most fascinating is the OED’s entry for the phrase “cycle of Cathay,” defined as “a period of time which is long-lasting but during which little changes.” Popularized by Lord Tennyson’s poem “Locksley Hall” (“Better fifty years of Europe than a cycle of Cathay”), the phrase reflects a complex, heavily Eurocentric Western gaze assuming cultural superiority. This cultural bias was further cemented in an 1886 issue of the North American Review, which claimed that “the world has made more progress in that time [...] than in many cycles of Cathay.”

The name then found a romantic revival in the bustling commercial heart of the East. In the cosmopolitan Shanghai of the 1930s, “Cathay” was embraced as a symbol of ultimate luxury and modernity. The legendary Cathay Theatre and the grand Cathay Hotel (now the Fairmont Peace Hotel) adopted the ancient name to evoke timeless elegance and prestige. When the theater’s name was localized into the Chinese characters pronounced Guotai, evoking an auspicious idiom meaning “peace and prosperity,” it marked a brilliant fusion of Western phonetics and Eastern cultural values. Here, Cathay was no longer just a distant Western fantasy, but a glamorous reality woven into the very fabric of the city’s urban memory.

Decades later, this evocative name took flight, finding its most enduring manifestation in the clouds. By reusing the beloved “Guotai” moniker, Cathay Pacific’s founders seamlessly carried that century-old promise of peace and prosperity into the jet age.

The story of Cathay teaches us that names are far more than mere labels; they are the enduring vessels of our shared history. The long journey from “Cathay” to “China” charted a passage from fragmentation to wholeness, from distant myth to tangible reality. It serves as a poignant reminder that while maps and misunderstandings may carve the world into “us” and “them,” the human spirit — propelled by the footsteps of explorers and the verses of poets — can’t help but try to blur such divides. In the end, we are all, in some way, still searching for Cathay, hoping to discover that behind the ancient myth lies a shared humanity.

(Header image: Visuals from VCG, reedited by Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018933/China’s Beloved Beef Noodles Are Getting a Rebrand
World.title: China’s Beloved Beef Noodles Are Getting a Rebrand
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018933/China’s Beloved Beef Noodles Are Getting a Rebrand
World.content:
China’s signature local specialty Lanzhou lamian, or Lanzhou pulled noodles — named after the capital city of the northwestern Gansu province — are undergoing a rebranding. At many noodle shops across the country, the dish will now be known as “Qinghai lamian,” as the northwestern Qinghai province strives to build its own regional brand.

More than 1,000 noodle shops nationwide have made the shift, state broadcaster CCTV reported on Saturday. In June, 72 noodle shops in the northern port city of Tianjin first changed their names to bear the words “Qinghai lamian,” followed by hundreds of shops in several other provinces in the months since.

Composed of hand-pulled noodles in a clear broth, sliced beef and radish, and chili oil, the dish traces its history back to the turn of the 19th century in the central Henan province. After being brought west, they took on the name of Gansu’s capital, a stop on the old Silk Road — where the halal noodles first became a hit in part owing to its significant Muslim Hui population. They were further popularized as a local specialty by Hui noodle maker Ma Baozi in the 1910s.

Later, as China opened up in the 1980s, entrepreneurs from poverty-stricken counties in Qinghai, such as Hualong, began capitalizing on the noodles’ popularity, opening small, mom-and-pop restaurants across the country.

“There was little brand awareness back then, and hardly anyone had heard of Hualong, Qinghai. However, Lanzhou is close by, so (noodle shop owners) thought they’d just call them ‘Lanzhou noodles,’ because everyone knows Lanzhou,” Ma Liping, president of the Qinghai Noodles Industry Association, told local media.

The shops have become a familiar sight nationwide. As of the end of February 2026, there were 31,000 noodle restaurants operated by owners from Qinghai in more than 330 cities across China, generating more than 24 billion yuan ($3.5 billion) in annual revenue, according to data from the Qinghai Noodle Industry Association.

But tensions over the use of the dish’s name have grown among Lanzhou and Qinghai residents, as people from Lanzhou call it “Lanzhou niurou mian” — Lanzhou beef noodles — while people from Qinghai call it “Lanzhou lamian,” or “Lanzhou pulled noodles.”

The dish has also evolved two differing preparation methods among Gansu and Qinghai restaurant owners, fueling debate. Lanzhou noodle makers have made efforts to preserve its traditional flavors, while Qinghai shop owners have adapted to local tastes — for instance by using less oil and salt in Guangdong, or adding more pepper in the southwestern Sichuan province.

To distinguish their wares from the noodles sold by people from Qinghai, local authorities in Lanzhou registered a trademark featuring a bull’s head for “Lanzhou Beef Noodles” in 2007, marking the city’s first step toward building a formal regional brand.

The recent rebrandings are part of Qinghai’s broader effort to build a provincial brand. About one-fifth of the rebranded shops have adopted a “three-in-one” model, adding in-restaurant sales of local specialties such as yak jerky and highland barley products, as well as tourism promotion, as new revenue streams.

Online, users voiced their support for the change. “After all, the two noodle dishes differ significantly in taste and texture, so distinguishing them clearly will help consumers make informed choices,” one user wrote on microblogging platform Weibo.

In a commentary, state-backed Haibao news wrote that “the rebranding reflects the growing push to standardize China’s grassroots food industry.”

The push is evidenced by multiple regions recently moving to standardize the production of local dishes. Gansu began regulating Lanzhou lamian in 2023, while a vocational college in the southern Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region launched a course dedicated to standardizing and promoting its river snail rice noodles in 2020. In July, the catering industry association of the eastern Zhejiang province also introduced a standard for preparing duck heads, a Quzhou city specialty.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A Lanzhou lamian shop in Yichang, Hubei province, Aug. 11, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018935/Inside the Chinese AI Studio Shrinking Short-Drama Crews to One
World.title: Inside the Chinese AI Studio Shrinking Short-Drama Crews to One
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018935/Inside the Chinese AI Studio Shrinking Short-Drama Crews to One
World.content:
Editor’s note: This is the second of a two-part series on how AI is reshaping China’s ultrashort-drama industry. Read part 1.

JIANGSU, East China — Chen Hao’s old desktop still has more than 10 versions of Nuke, a standard editing tool in the visual-effects industry. Over nearly a decade, he learned each new release, picked up 3D animation software Autodesk Maya and the 3D graphics game engine Unreal Engine, and taught himself enough English to use them.

Today, as a technical director at Qidian Interactive, a new AI-video studio in Wuxi, eastern China, Chen is helping build a platform that can compress much of that accumulated expertise into a few prompts.

By last year, he said, AI video had improved enough to rival work that took him days. Then ByteDance’s text-to-video model Seedance 2.0 arrived, making it much easier to generate studio-grade footage, prompting his company to move more aggressively into AI, and put Chen on a project to create their own model.

“I don’t like AI, but I was forced to use it,” Chen tells Sixth Tone. “When I realized one click could sometimes produce something better than two or three days of work, I had to use it.”

The company calls the system Yudian. Chen began building it in April, drawing on programming skills he had taught himself years earlier to automate repetitive VFX work. He produced the first version in about a month.

It can suggest a premise based on trending topics from social media, draft dialogue, create storyboards, arrange characters and objects in three-dimensional space, and assess whether an ending has a strong enough cliffhanger to keep viewers watching.

The goal, one Qidian executive says, is for every employee to be able to make a drama independently.

Auto play

But first, lighting artists, animators, and cinematographers are needed to translate their craft into instructions for the Yudian machine.

Inside Qidian’s production hub, rows of employees sit at brand-new computers behind glass walls, some working across multiple monitors. Team leaders sit alongside their members, while directors occupy small rooms at the far end.

On one screen, a production prompt reads:

“45-60 seconds. Setting: watch repair shop. Barton lunges for the pocket watch as Eliza twists her wrist and shatters its central gear. The action should be extremely fast and explosive, giving the audience no time to breathe.”

It specifies an Arri Alexa 65 IMAX camera, Panavision Primo V/C/T lenses, cinematic lighting and camera movement, no music or subtitles, practical light sources, and smooth continuity.

“Shot 1, 45-48 seconds. Medium shot. 35mm lens. Length: 3 seconds. Barton roars “like a crazed beast,” lunges forward, and reaches for the watch.”

Another screen displays a digital prop room of sorts: characters, locations, objects, and lighting setups that can be reused across future scenes and productions.

Nearby, artists are testing several costumes for the female lead of a romance drama aimed at overseas audiences. They refine her through prompts such as “simulate natural daylight,” “increase skin texture,” and “preserve natural imperfections” to make her look less artificial.

Over the past year, similar AI production studios have proliferated across China, while established film and television companies have opened AI divisions or shifted existing teams into AI production. In some cities, local governments are accelerating the shift with computing-power subsidies and other support.

On the day Sixth Tone visited Qidian, Chen Hao had just updated a plug-in for the new AI platform that lets users position characters and objects in three-dimensional space, giving the model a clearer map of where each belongs within a shot.

Typing a single word — “script” — into the system produces an outline within seconds, generated from recent viral online trends and popular dramas. A team leader checks the output before the system moves on to dialogue and storyboards.

One chat box is used to develop a character. In another, a shot is divided second by second, its prompt altered until the movement or composition works. On more demanding projects, teams may spend hours or days refining what the model produced almost instantly.

A separate model assesses the project across more than 10 criteria: Was the cliffhanger strong enough? Did the emotions build at the right pace? Were scenes being used efficiently? Could any of it run into content-review problems?

“The goal is to shorten the learning curve,” says Chen Jie, a project director at Qidian, not related to Chen Hao. “We are trying to make production faster internally so we can stay profitable even as prices keep falling.”

Like Chen Hao, much of the team behind Yudian came from traditional visual production: lighting artists, animators, key-frame artists, and cinematographers whose craft now lives partly in the platform’s prompts, workflows, and presets.

One of those veterans is Ma Shuan, a lighting artist who spent nearly two decades in film production and worked on visual effects for movies including the science-fiction blockbuster “The Wandering Earth.”

At Qidian, Ma now uses AI partly to repair live-action footage. In one scene set on an ancient battlefield, modern concrete structures had slipped into the background. In another, crew members’ hands holding arrows needed to disappear, leaving the arrows suspended beside an actor’s face before they shot forward.

Some of the cleanup Ma once did frame by frame can now be finished in about half a day instead of two or three, he says. Other jobs, including some background fixes, are still faster with conventional tools.

“To me, AI is only an assistant,” Ma says. “Traditional production is controllable. If I want to change something, I can. With AI, every generated result is a gamble.”

Take two

Across the industry, that gamble is known as “drawing cards.” Some studios even employ dedicated “card operators” whose job is to generate shot after shot until one works.

Huang, 26, who works at a Shanghai production company, spends much of her day generating the same shot three to five times before getting a usable result.

Each attempt may take only a few minutes, but during the afternoon rush, when demand on the system peaks, the wait can stretch to 10 or 20 minutes. Then Huang checks the result and decides whether to generate it again.

“For instance, a sofa that appears as a single-seater in one shot may return as a two-seater in the next,” says Huang, who asked to be identified only by her surname for privacy reasons. “Or leather upholstery may suddenly become fabric.”

For shots that need greater consistency, Huang and her colleagues give the model reference images, then generate again.

“You never know what you’ll get, so it becomes a little addictive,” says Huang. “I think the fun is never knowing when the AI will suddenly cooperate and give you a whole take that works. You just keep repeating the process.”

Until recently, both Huang and the company worked mainly in live action. Founded in 2014, the studio produced web series and films before it began experimenting with AI short dramas late last year.

Huang now works entirely on AI dramas for overseas audiences, moving between story planning, directing, generation, and editing.

On live-action sets, Huang says, actors bring their own understanding of a scene, while cinematographers might improvise a camera movement. “It was still a collective creative process.”

“But with AI, the density of decisions becomes much higher. Almost every creative decision is made by just one or two people. Even the actors’ performances are completely under your control, so those pleasant surprises almost disappear.”

Back at Qidian, dramas still need a team, too.

A typical production moves through three small groups. One builds characters and settings, another generates the footage, and a third edits it together, with one or two people at each stage. A team leader — usually someone with more experience in film, animation, or advertising — reviews the work throughout and decides what needs another pass.

The company’s Wuxi production base opened only in April. Within a month, it had recruited more than 50 employees, nearly half of them recent graduates. By June, the studio was producing four or five short dramas a day, each comprising 30 to 44 episodes.

For Qidian founder Wang Ting, one shelved project became an early test of what AI could make possible.

Drawing on Wuxi’s traditional Huishan clay figurines, the project follows two characters, A Xi and A Fu, through a fantasy adventure set among local landmarks. It had already cleared China’s broadcasting regulator, but the original plan called for three years of work and a budget of 8 million to 10 million yuan ($1.19 million to $1.49 million). Qidian shelved it.

Using AI, Wang says, Qidian eventually finished the project in two months for around 1 million yuan.

“This shows how traditional filmmaking — from shooting and editing to visual effects production — can now be replaced,” she says.

Qidian now uses the same workflow for work far beyond short dramas. During Sixth Tone’s visit, one team was making a Dragon Boat Festival promotional video for a local government, generating scenes of racers paddling across the water. Other teams handle corporate s or use AI to repair and supplement live-action footage.

For one electric-vehicle campaign, the car itself never had to enter the studio. “We simply tell the AI what kind of vehicle we want and what actions it should perform,” says Chen Jie. “And a promotional video can be generated almost instantly.”

The next generation

The faster Qidian generates footage, the more Chen Jie has to review. In the past, he might review 20 shots in a week. Now he goes through dozens — sometimes hundreds — every day.

“It’s exhausting because the videos are generated so quickly,” he says. “I’m almost numb to it now.”

AI-generated characters can still look “oily,” he adds, while fine details often fall apart when he freezes a single frame. “The quality isn’t terrible, but it still hasn’t reached the standard of traditional filmmaking.”

Yet what all that speed ultimately buys is less clear.

On one earlier job, Chen Jie spent weeks perfecting the opening few dozen seconds of a promotional video for a major game company. When he later checked it, the video had received 48,000 likes.

“It was promoted by a big company, and it still only got this much attention. What’s the point?” He pauses, then answers himself: “None.”

“I still have things I want to pursue,” he says. “But my pursuit now is simply to deliver what the client is paying for. That’s all.”

When he started using AI, Chen says, everything he created looked terrible. “Later I realized we have to adapt to it. You can’t fight against the model,” he says. “You have to work within its strengths, compromise with its limitations, and gradually learn how to control it.”

Younger workers have often adapted more quickly. Wang Zheng, who graduated this year in advertising and art design, already leads a small team working on AI-generated videos, character assets, and scene design.

A teacher encouraged him to enter the AI industry, while most students who graduated before him went into traditional advertising. “The training I received still helps,” Wang says. “It taught me visual logic and developed my sense of aesthetics.”

AI, he adds, has given him more freedom to pursue ideas that would once have been difficult to realize. While waiting for the model to finish generating footage, he experiments with projects of his own.

“My dream is to become an AI film director,” says Wang. “I want to create a complete feature film entirely from my own ideas using AI.”

Qidian is already planning an AI feature film of its own, hoping to build a reputation beyond commissioned work.

Feature films, however, are also where Chen Hao still sees limits to replacement. He has friends working on complex visual effects for major productions, where demanding standards for quality and stability still make much of the work difficult to hand over to AI.

Some of Chen’s peers have no intention of following him into AI, even if those technical barriers fall. “One of my friends told me that if visual effects disappear in the future, he’d rather become a livestream dancer than work in AI,” Chen says with a laugh.

He understands the resistance, but believes that if a single sentence can eventually generate 10 — or even 90 minutes — of finished video, many of the jobs that now make up a production may simply no longer be needed.

Through the studio’s glass walls, Chen watches young employees working on Yudian — the AI platform he helped build — some typing prompts, others retouching AI-generated faces in Photoshop.

Qidian now plans to license Yudian to other studios.

“One day it might replace me as well,” Chen says.

He pauses.

“But you still can’t afford not to do it.”

Additional reporting: Lü Xiao; editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Yudian, a system built by Chen Hao, generates story ideas, dialogue and storyboards, and simulates multi-camera setups in 3D space in Wuxi, Jiangsu province, June 2026. Reedited by Ding Yining; photo by Lü Xiao/Sixth Tone)

World.content:
China’s ultrashort-drama boom built a sprawling live-action industry of actors, directors, crews, and filming bases. Now, as AI drives down production costs, shoots are disappearing and companies are cutting staff. In Zhengzhou, filmmakers reckon with the slowdown; in Wuxi, former film and animation workers are building AI production systems that can turn scripts into finished videos with only a handful of people. Sixth Tone follows both sides of the shift to see how AI is changing not just how short dramas are made, but what filmmaking work itself is becoming.

Additional reporting: He Qitong; story editors: Apurva and Qi Ya; video editor: Lü Xiao

World.title: Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1018928/Chinese Mother Buys Daughters Extra Train Seat, Sparking Debate
World.content:
“We bought three tickets,” a teenager says to a woman asking to use the empty seat beside her — occupied by snacks — her sister sitting on the other side.

“We’re all in the same carriage,” the standing woman says. “Shouldn’t we help each other out?” She calls a train attendant for help.

“Places 5, 6, and 7 — those seats are theirs,” the attendant says after checking the teens’ tickets. “You need to talk to them about it. Telling me won’t help.”

This scene, which took place Aug. 18 on a slow train traveling from Shanghai to the southwestern city of Chengdu — a 27-hour journey — was captured in a video that went viral in China this past week.

Online, people heatedly discussed whether the girls should have shared the seat or whether they were entitled to keep it for themselves. The topic rose to the second-highest place on Chinese microblogging platform Weibo’s trending list, receiving over 37 million views and 12,000 discussions as of Monday.

Many were in support of the girls’ decision, arguing that giving up their seats would be a favor, not an obligation, as the teens themselves had paid for the three tickets. Others said that they were “wasting public resources.”

Still others contended that the train attendants should have been more proactive, pointing to railway ticketing rules that say customers can only buy one ticket for themselves per train and that if the ticket holder does not board, their seat should be reassigned by train attendants.

Despite these stipulations, passengers can buy tickets for others using their identification information on train ticket purchasing platforms.

The girls’ mother did just that, buying their tickets as well as entering her own information for the third seat, according to a now-deleted post she made on Aug. 20 on Douyin, the Chinese version of TikTok.

“My original intention was to keep them from taking up other people’s space because they had too much luggage, so I bought an extra ticket,” she wrote. “Since they’re both girls and didn’t want to sit with others, I bought three tickets together.”

In response to the issue, 12306 — China’s official train ticketing and service platform — told Shanghai-based media outlet The Paper that in the event that a passenger does not board the train, their ticket remains classified as “sold” in the train’s online system. In addition, if a ticket is purchased for a passenger but they do not board, the person whose ID was used to buy the ticket retains the right to decide how the seat is used.

On Aug. 21, the Chengdu Bureau of China’s National Railway responded to the controversy, seemingly contradicting 12306: “If a passenger fails to board after purchasing a ticket due to personal reasons, the passenger is considered to have forfeited their right to use the seat … according to the rules, the seat cannot be occupied by a third party.” The bureau noted that such instances should be reported to the train staff.

But a day later, the case shifted from a dispute over passengers’ rights and entitlements to discussions on the lack of support for children traveling alone, as well as the difficulties faced by migrant families. The girls’ mother, speaking to domestic media on Aug. 22, explained that she works in Shanghai and was sending her two daughters back to their hometown. She added that she did not have enough time to escort them and wanted them to “develop their independence.” The extra seat, she said, could also serve as a place to lie down for the two, as she worried about male strangers sleeping beside them in sleeper cars.

She also noted that, under ticketing rules, minors cannot buy tickets themselves and their tickets must instead be purchased alongside an adult ticket.

In a commentary, The Paper wrote that “behind the purchase of the three tickets lies a harsh reality faced by millions of working families, leaving migrant families with no alternative.” It recommended that the railway system follow airlines — which allow parents to apply for service for unaccompanied minors in advance — as an example.

Editor: Marianne Gunnarsson.

(Header image: A video screenshot shows the empty seat that gave rise to a national debate. From Weibo)
